en: *Baifa lun xianyou chao*, Scroll One, End: "Seeing, etc.

Second, regarding the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): both afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) each possess a view of a self; therefore, this [view] does not function in this stage (*bhūmi*).

For this reason, it is said that in the fourth stage one abandons one delusion: first, the delusion of craving for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), which is precisely the craving for concentration (*dhyāna*) within this context.

"Accompanied by" means that one simultaneously gives rise to craving and attachment toward meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); thus, it obstructs the four stages. Attachment to meditative concentration is a fetter for a bodhisattva.
Regarding "delusion regarding craving for dharmas": this refers to the attachment to the reality of the body accompanied by craving for dharmas within this context;
this is called craving for dharmas. It is an obstruction to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). These delusions regarding the path of cultivation are all... [as previously stated].

Regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is clarified that these are not afflictions (*kleśa*). "Attachment" refers to craving (*rāga*). By severing these two types of delusion, one enters the fourth stage (*bhūmi*).

From here below, the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), involves the severance of the obstacles to the *parinirvāṇa* of the two vehicles; this refers to those [obstacles] within the cognitive obstructions that are concomitant with...

To give rise to even a single portion [of such a mind] that causes one to weary of birth and death and aspire to enter nirvana is identical to the followers of the Two Vehicles who loathe suffering and rejoice in quiescence;
this constitutes an obstruction to the distinct path of non-attachment on the fifth stage, for the means of realization and the object realized are called "undifferentiated."
Regarding the distinction of names: the wisdom that realizes *tathatā* (suchness) is called the "path of non-distinction.
This is because one perceives that there is no further distinction between *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*; how, then, could there be joy or aversion? One sees that the existence of *saṃsāra* is illusory;

now that one knows *saṃsāra* is fundamentally non-existent, it is itself *nirvāṇa*. It is like seeing that the snake [one perceived] is actually nothing but hemp. This should be contemplated. Entering...
At the time of the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), this obstacle of the self (*ātma-āvaraṇa*) can be permanently severed.
In this fifth stage, one contemplates that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are entirely equal, with no further distinction between them.

This is because, whereas in the fourth stage one’s wisdom is similar to that of the śrāvakas—practicing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) and likewise feeling weary of saṃsāra while hastening toward nirvāṇa—one is able to permanently sever [this attachment] upon entering the fifth stage. For this reason...
The fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*) is said to eliminate two delusions (*moha*) along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*).

First is the delusion of exclusively attending to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), which is precisely the aversion to the suffering of *saṃsāra*. Second is the delusion of exclusively attending to *nirvāṇa*, which is the longing for *nirvāṇa*.
These two delusions consist of aversion to suffering and longing for quiescence; upon entering the fifth stage, one is able to sever them forever.
Next, the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), eliminates the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics.

This refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). As for this "innate portion," it pertains specifically to the level of the cognitive obscuration; therefore, it must be severed.

This is because in the preceding four stages, one clings to the realized principles within the Four Noble Truths as being characterized by defilement and purity. Since suffering and its origin are the causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), [one must abandon such clinging].

The fruit is called "defiled" (saṃkliṣṭa). Cessation and the Path are the causes and fruits of returning to cessation; they are called "pure" (śuddha). Because one perceives these causes and fruits of defilement and purity, it is termed the "coarse characteristic" (audārikalakṣaṇa).

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She lun) states: "It is also called the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics," which is the same as [the definition in] the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Because this is taught with reference to the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), it is called "coarse characteristics. The seventh stage is called "subtle.

Upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to permanently sever [these characteristics]. That is to say, within the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths regarding cause and effect, there are two aspects of defilement and two aspects of purity.

The *tathatā* (suchness) realized in this sixth stage is called the "stainless and non-pure *tathatā*. The realization itself is also called "stainless and non-pure wisdom" (*jñāna*), because it is not—

Because of its establishment, these six stages are said to abandon two types of ignorance along with their coarse residues (*dausthulya*). First is the ignorance regarding the observation of the actual process of saṃsāra;
this is precisely the grasping at the existence of defilement and purification within this context, as it is comprised by the defiled portion of the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Grasping at the existence of defilement constitutes an obstacle to observing suffering and its origin as the cause and effect of this defiled flow; because it obstructs the sixth stage, it is abandoned there. Second is the [ignorance regarding] characteristics...
The delusion of frequent manifestation is the contemplation of the path of cessation and return, because it is characterized by purity;

yet, because one perceives many coarse appearances therein, it directly obstructs the wisdom of the non-defiled and non-pure *tathatā* of the sixth stage. This is also called the "wisdom of non-defilement and non-purity.
On this stage, one no longer contemplates the Four Noble Truths as being either defiled or pure; they are fundamentally pure and ultimately unobtainable.

From here below, within the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), one abandons the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle signs. This refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because one clings to the existence of arising and ceasing, that which manifests as subtle signs is precisely "having signs" (*animitta-saṃjñin*).

Since signs are diminished in the sixth stage, that obstacle obstructs the sublime contemplation of signlessness (*animittadhyāna*) in the seventh stage. At the time of the eighth and seventh stages, one is then able to abandon it forever.

Because the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—observing the process of evolution and involution—is performed during the first six stages, and because there is still the subtle characteristic of arising and ceasing regarding that which is grasped, it is called an "obstruction.
Since the seventh stage consists of purely signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), it obstructs this signlessness;

thus, the *tathatā* realized therein is called the "undifferentiated *tathatā* of diverse phenomena," and the wisdom that realizes it is called "sublime signless wisdom" (*animitta-jñāna*). Upon entering [this stage]...

At this stage, the obstacles consisting of subtle signs are permanently severed. For this reason, it is said that on the seventh stage, two types of ignorance along with their coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) are abandoned:
first, the ignorance of the active manifestation of subtle signs, which is the grasping at birth within the obstacles;

this is because one still perceives the subtle signs of birth within the process of saṃsāra, namely the truths of suffering and its origin. Second, the ignorance of exclusively applying mental attention to seek the signless; this is the obstacle [within the obstacles]...
Those who cling to cessation still grasp at the subtle marks of returning to cessation and extinction;

thus, while they diligently seek through the mental application of signlessness (*animitta-manasikāra*), they are unable to give rise to superior practices within the gateway of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*).

Now, in this stage, having removed this obstacle, one no longer seeks with exclusive diligence in the gateway of signlessness, but rather gives rise to superior practices within emptiness. That which is called "emptiness" is...

Regarding the principle of signless emptiness: because one simultaneously gives rise to practice within both the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, one is able to give rise to the conventional contemplation within the ultimate contemplation, and give rise to the ultimate contemplation within the conventional contemplation; that is, within the contemplation of signless emptiness.
Thus, one initiates superior practice. Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Within the seventh stage, by means of the wisdom of skillful means regarding emptiness, one initiates superior practice within existence. In this stage, these two delusions are abandoned."
From here on, within the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacle consisting of the application of effort toward the signless (*animitta*).

This refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents the contemplation of the signless from becoming spontaneous, because it involves the wisdom of applied effort (*prāyogika-jñāna*).
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "To apply effort toward the signless (*animitta*) is synonymous with [the stage of] Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is because in the first five stages, there is much contemplation of signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) and little contemplation of the signless, due to the inferiority of the contemplative mind.

In the sixth stage, there is little contemplation of signs and much contemplation of the signless, because one dwells frequently in the signless by means of contemplating the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the equality of defilement and purity. In the seventh stage...

In the middle [stage], because the characteristics of subtle arising and ceasing are severed and the continuity of the signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is maintained, this is precisely the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*).
It differs from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) because, due to the presence of application within the signless, one has not yet attained spontaneity;
thus, one lacks mastery in entering the signless contemplation and has not yet been able to manifest the body and the land. Such obstacles of application are absent in the effortless eighth stage.
Because of this, if one enters the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to sever [these afflictions] forever; thus, one attains the two masteries (*vaśitā*).

Prior to the eighth stage, when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it is triggered by the mental intention (*āśaya*) immediately preceding the concentration. Furthermore, although the manifest land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*) appears, it is not yet termed "mastery."

Because one cannot act spontaneously—since at the time of entering the eighth stage, there is no intentional effort required to initiate application—one immediately manifests infinite transformation bodies.
Therefore, the manifestations of the eighth stage consist of the spontaneous appearance of gold, silver, jewels, and so forth.
The manifested lands may be large or small, both being attained; because both the signs and the lands are sovereign, it is called [the Stage of Sovereignty].

One attains two types of mastery. For this reason, it is said that in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons two delusions (*moha*) along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless (*animitta*); second, the delusion of lacking mastery over signs (*nimitta*).

Because of this, one cannot attain mastery over signs; thus, one also lacks mastery over the Buddha-lands (*kṣetra*). This is due to the obstruction of these delusions. From the eighth stage upward, [the practice] is purely...

Because the untainted path arises spontaneously and the afflictions of the three realms never again manifest, the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness may still arise;
this is because the fruit of the wisdom of self-emptiness does not contradict them.
Having severed these two delusions, one attains the stage of the path of no-more-training (*anāgamya-mārga*), wherein the characteristics, functions, and lands are all brought under mastery.
From here on, in the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacle of non-zeal regarding the door of benefiting others.

This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes one not to desire to apply oneself diligently to activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and instead takes pleasure in cultivating one's own self-interest.
That obstacle pertains to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "One is unable to skillfully benefit [others]."

This is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Vasubandhu states: "Because one is unable to practice for the benefit of sentient beings. The general meaning is the same.

This is because, within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one attains signless conduct (*animitta-caryā*) and becomes attached to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Unwilling to advance in cultivation, one becomes intoxicated by the wine of quiescent extinction;
thus, one does not perceive the mark of a sentient being in relation to living beings, and consequently does not deliver sentient beings. Furthermore, one does not perceive...
The characteristic of the Buddha’s bodhi is that one does not seek bodhi; therefore, it is only through the exhortation of the Buddhas that one is able to advance in practice. The Buddha said:
"Good son, since your cultivation of the Path has reached the end of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and you are on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, why do you remain attached to the signless?
Your original vow from the past was to deliver boundless sentient beings and to seek bodhi through your solemn resolve. You should..."
When one is no longer obstructed by the signless, one is then able to proceed with the quest as encouraged by the Buddha.

Within the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacle to altruism consisting of the lack of desire to act for the benefit of others, which hinders the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). These four analytical knowledges are: first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*);

second, that of expression (*nirukti*); third, that of meaning (*artha*); and fourth, that of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). This should be understood. Upon entering the ninth stage, one is then able to abandon this [obstacle] within the context of benefiting others.

This refers to the obstacle to the desire to teach. Consequently, at the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*), it is said that two types of ignorance (*moha*) along with their corresponding latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) are abandoned.
First, there is the ignorance regarding the mastery of *dhāraṇīs* and wisdom concerning the infinite teachings, the infinite names, phrases, and syllables, and their successive [elaborations].

Second, there is the ignorance regarding mastery of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). These two ignorances constitute the obstacles to the factors associated with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Thus, these two ignorances are the actual hindrances.

The first ignorance among the former [three] obstructs the first three analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The second ignorance, that of lack of mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna*), obstructs the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
Now, regarding how the first ignorance obstructs the first three analytical knowledges:

it obstructs the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) with respect to mastery over the dhāraṇīs of the immeasurable teachings that have been spoken, specifically within the meanings that are expressed.
First is mastery over dhāraṇī, which manifests all meanings within a single meaning. Second is mastery over dhāraṇīs of immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables;

this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), for by means of mastery over the dhāraṇī of the expressive [words], one manifests all names, phrases, and syllables within a single name, phrase, and syllable. Third is mastery over progressively superior wisdom...
Furthermore, the "mastery of dhāraṇīs" refers to the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

This is the mastery of retention (*dhāraṇī*) in the successive interpretation and explanation of words and sounds; within a single sound, one manifests all sounds, namely, all regional dialects and languages.

It is from which the vocal sounds of all sentient beings emerge. When this ignorance is completely severed, one immediately gives rise to the three types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Second, regarding the ignorance that obstructs the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): it is the ignorance concerning the mastery of the two forms of eloquence.
This ignorance acts as an obstruction to this analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); therefore, it is called the delusion regarding mastery of eloquence.
Because it renders this eloquence non-mastery, yet because one possesses the analytical knowledge of eloquence, one is able to skillfully penetrate the appropriate capacities [of sentient beings].
This refers to skillfully expounding the profound Dharma to others; that is, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the seven analytical knowledges.

Regarding the "four and seven analytical knowledges," these are the wisdoms of the four unhindered understandings (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*); here they are called the "four unhindered wisdoms. The underlying principle is the same:

the four unhindered wisdoms take the untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their essence. Among them, the unhindered understanding regarding meanings (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) partially encompasses the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Therefore, among the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the first is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*). This is because "phenomena" refers to the teaching, which is the means of expression;

that is, names, phrases, and phonemes. One is unimpeded regarding these, and thus understands all names, phrases, and phonemes. Second is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
This means that because one understands all principles that are expressed, there is no obstruction whatsoever. Within that which is expressed, there is ultimate truth;

because this is what fundamental wisdom expresses, it is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). Third is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), which is the understanding of various dialects and the sounds of the six realms of existence and four modes of birth, all of which are without obstruction.
"Language" (*nirukti*) refers to sound itself. Question: What is the difference between this and the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?

Answer: They are also distinct. The former dharmas are provisional designations consisting of names, phrases, and syllables; the latter, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), is sound itself, which is substantial.
Therefore, there is a distinction between them. Regarding the fourth, the analytical knowledge of eloquence: it consists in preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Question:

How does this preaching of the Dharma differ from the aforementioned analytical knowledge of dharmas? Answer: It is also distinct. The former concerns the conceptual understanding of dharmas, whereas [the latter]... [does not].
This refers to verbal expression. Here, the focus is on the capacity to speak, rather than the content of what is spoken;

thus, within the context of unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*), seven types of eloquence are further distinguished. As for these seven: first is *mukha-pratibhāna* (eloquence of the mouth). This means that when speaking, words flow without obstruction.
"Obstruction" (*sai*) refers to stammering, and "stuttering" (*ke*) refers to redundancy. Because this Bodhisattva’s preaching is neither stammered nor redundant, it is called *mukha-pratibhāna*.

Second is "swift eloquence" (*pratibhāna*): because one expounds the treatises like a cascading river without delay or stammering, it signifies that the Bodhisattva’s flow of preaching is rapid. Third is "appropriate eloquence": because it accords with the time and the capacity [of the listener] without adding or subtracting. "Accordance with the time" means the moment when the faculties of the assembly have matured. "Accordance with the faculties" refers to the distinctions among the three types of faculties; in all cases, one preaches in accordance with those faculties. Regarding the phrase "without adding": [The text continues: ...it is not excessive. "Without subtracting" means it is not deficient. It is neither too much nor too little; it is precisely what is required. This is called appropriate eloquence. Furthermore, regarding "swift eloquence," there are two aspects: first, swift eloquence in the sense of non-retrogression, meaning that once one has attained eloquence, one never regresses from it; second, swift eloquence in the sense of non-interruption, meaning that the flow of eloquence is continuous and uninterrupted. Regarding "appropriate eloquence," there are also two aspects: first, appropriateness in terms of the dharma, meaning that the dharma taught is profound and subtle, and the words used are skillful and expedient; second, appropriateness in terms of the person, meaning that the teaching is delivered according to the specific capacities of the listeners. Because these four types of eloquence are present, they are collectively termed "unimpeded eloquence. Furthermore, regarding "swift eloquence," there are two further aspects: first, swift eloquence in terms of the object, meaning that one can explain all dharmas without obstruction; second, swift eloquence in terms of the mode of expression, meaning that one can manifest various sounds and voices to teach and transform sentient beings. Regarding "appropriate eloquence," there are also two further aspects: first, appropriateness in terms of the dharma, meaning that one can preach the Dharma without error or confusion; second, appropriateness in terms of the person, meaning that one can preach the Dharma by discerning the differences between superior and inferior faculties. If sentient beings are fit to hear a small amount of the Dharma, he speaks little; if they are fit to hear the Hīnayāna, he teaches the Hīnayāna.
Regarding "not diminishing": if sentient beings delight in much, he speaks much; if they delight in the Mahāyāna, he teaches the Mahāyāna Dharma. Fifth, "discernment free from negligence and error":
that which is spoken accords with principle, hence it is called "free from negligence"; because it is neither deviant nor mistaken, it is called "free from error. Fifth.

6. Uninterrupted and inexhaustible eloquence: Because it continues in succession and returns [to the source], it is called "uninterrupted"; because it never reaches exhaustion, it is called "inexhaustible. 7. Abundant flavor and meaning in all that is proclaimed:
Because every single phrase and word contains many principles and facts—meaning that while the words are few, the principles are many—this is the eloquence of a Bodhisattva.
When ordinary people preach the Dharma, their words are many but their principles are few; therefore, this is distinct from them. 8. All that pertains to the world...
He is fully endowed with the most supreme and wondrous eloquence. It is as profound as thunder, clear and penetrating, heard from afar.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of vocal sounds that issue from the Buddha’s mouth. The first is "profound as thunder":

just as when a clap of thunder resounds, all the hundred grasses sprout buds and hibernating insects open their burrows, so too does the Buddha’s voice cause the noble paths of the Three Vehicles to arise and all sentient beings [to awaken].
It opens the door between birth and death. First, it is pure and clear, heard afar. Second, it is delightful; as the Sūtra says, "it gladdens the hearts of all.
Third, it enters the mind with reverence and love. Fourth, it is understood with clarity and ease. "Clarity" (di) means reality (truth).
"Thoroughly understanding" (*liao*) means to penetrate and realize; it is the skillful exposition of all phenomena. Fifth, the listener never tires;
the characteristics of this practice are as can be known. Because this ignorance obstructs the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), it is subsumed under the ninth obstruction.
This ignorance is precisely what prevents the attainment of the four and seven types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
From here on, in the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacles regarding the lack of mastery over all phenomena.
This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents one from attaining mastery over all phenomena; it is precisely this clinging to [subject-object] duality.
To grasp at all phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); this constitutes a lack of mastery over the Great Dharma.
It obstructs the tenth stage, which is the Cloud of the Great Dharma Wisdom (*mahā-dharma-jñāna-megha*), as well as the activities arising from what it contains and preserves.

"Great Dharma Wisdom" refers to the wisdom that takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object; because it is like a great cloud, it is called the "Cloud of Great Dharma Wisdom. Furthermore, it includes that which is contained and preserved therein.
This refers to the hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates, the hundreds of thousands of *samādhi* gates, and all dharmas of merit.
It is the great cloud of Dharma-wisdom that contains the waters of manifold virtues and fills the body. It is the activity arising from the various dharmas of merit it contains and preserves;
it is the various great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These dharmas of merit of the ten stages have not yet [manifested] of their own accord.
All that exists [as obstacles] arises from this very hindrance. Upon entering the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to sever it forever.

For this reason, the tenth stage is said to eliminate two types of delusion (*moha*) along with their corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*): first, the delusion regarding supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which refers to the activities arising within this hindrance;
second, the delusion regarding the subtle penetration into secrets, which refers to the great cloud of Dharma-knowledge within this hindrance.
And it refers to the dharmas contained therein. It should be understood as being analogous to the obstructions.

"Subtle and secret" refers to the wisdom, qualities, and merits of the subtle and wondrous objects that are obstructed. Regarding the obstruction within the mind emerging from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*):

although one has attained mastery over the dharmas in this tenth stage, there remain further obstructions that have not yet been called ultimate; that is to say, there is the innate (*sahaja*) [obstruction].

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the seeds of spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) are all severed instantaneously, and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata.
Although one has attained mastery over the ten dharmas, one is still not yet called a Buddha.
These extremely subtle two obstructions must reach the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) before they can be completely severed; this occurs precisely at the tenth [stage].

It emerges from within the mind, thereby opening this obstruction. Since the treatise does not provide a separate name for the eleventh obstruction, it simply refers to the two types of ignorance found in the *Buddhabhūmi*.
The treatise states: "By virtue of this, the *Buddhabhūmi* is said to sever two ignorances and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*).
First, there is the ignorance of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge; this is precisely the 'subtle' [obstruction] within this category."
It is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Second is the subtle obscuration of delusion regarding the extremely minute;
this refers to all the seeds of spontaneous afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within this [cognitive obscuration]. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"When a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment, they simultaneously sever the afflictions and the cognitive obscurations, becoming a Great Arhat and a Tathāgata, and realizing Great Nirvāṇa and Great Enlightenment."
Thus it is. The ten stages (*bhūmi*) mentioned above involve the severing of eleven layers of obstructions and the remedying of twenty-two types of delusion;

this, in its entirety, constitutes the clearing away of the dark alleys [of ignorance]. This refers to the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*para-sambhogakāya*), which clears away the dark alleys of others. Question:

Since these are all Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who personally give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and personally sever their own afflictions, how can it be said that the Buddha is able to clear away the dark alleys?

[Question: Is it so? [Answer: In truth, it is indeed self-severance; however, by taking the Buddha’s teaching of the untainted (*anāsrava*) doctrine as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), one causes that [obscuration] to be severed.
For this reason, it is also called "opening the dark path for others. [Question: By what wisdom is it opened? [Answer: It pertains to all four types of severance (*prahāṇa*).
If we rely on the ultimate meaning, only the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) opens it. [Question: Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*)...

Question: Do both paths arise when severing hindrances? Answer: Both paths do arise. The path of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the seeds and the manifest [hindrances], while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) severs the heavy habitual tendencies (*dausthulya-vāsanā*).

Question: Since it is stated that hindrances are severed upon entering the mind of each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), could there not be afflictive hindrances during the periods of abiding in and emerging from those minds?
Answer: According to the *Abhidharma-samaya-pradīpikā* and other treatises, there are indeed hindrances during the periods of abiding and emerging; that is to say, at every...

Each of the three stages (*bhūmi*) possesses three minds, and each involves the severance of obstructions; thus, there are thirty layers of obstructions in total. For each mind, the severance of delusions gives rise to two paths:
namely, thirty paths of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) and thirty paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

When it is said that "obstructions are severed," this refers exclusively to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). As for the afflictive obstructions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), these are suppressed regarding their active manifestation throughout the ten stages. Regarding the afflictions:

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are severed by the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in each stage (*bhūmi*). Question: Over what duration of time are the thirty layers of obstructions completely severed? Answer:
Jianfu says that for each stage there are three moments of mind, each requiring one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; thus, across the ten stages, it takes thirty *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to sever them all.
Question: One *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is spent before the stages; from the first stage to the seventh stage, it is the second...
[The first] asaṃkhyeya [kalpa], from the eighth bhūmi to the tenth bhūmi; the third asaṃkhyeya [kalpa], when causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.
How can it be said that there are thirty asaṃkhyeyas? The answer is: the Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* translates here as "countless time.
When it is said that one attains Buddhahood after three countless kalpas, this refers to the "great" countless time. This statement of "thirty asaṃkhyeyas" refers to the "small" [countless time].

This concludes the preceding section, which has consistently distinguished and elucidated the meaning of the "dark path. This marks the completion of the second two lines, which extol the *saṃbhogakāya*.
From here below, the third section consists of two lines extolling the *nirmāṇakāya*, which is divided into two parts; the first line concerns its manifestation in the world.

The second phrase distinguishes the preaching that accords with the capacities of sentient beings, such as the dispersal of the Dharma-rain. The preceding phrase [refers to] the great trichiliocosm, which refers only to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The second phrase [refers to] the ten billion [worlds], which refers only to sentient beings. The former phrase describes the manifestation within the great trichiliocosm;

the second phrase describes the moistening and nourishing of the sentient beings of the ten billion worlds. Were it not so, there would be no distinction between them. The Commentary states: "The compassionate clouds gather... up to "the hundred [billion]."
"Yi" (億) means "numerous. "Ai" (靉) describes the appearance of clouds gathering; it describes the appearance of clouds arising. "Ci" (慈) refers to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
this is the transformation of the mental action (*manas-karman*). The term "clouds" is a metaphor; it is a metaphor for the transformation of the Tathāgata’s bodily action (*kāya-karman*).
The particle "ér" (而) is an auxiliary word used to connect clauses. "Yòu" (誘) means to lead; it also means to guide or to bring forth. "Xiù" (秀) means to emerge.

That is, to draw forth sentient beings and cause them to leave the ocean of suffering. Because the Tathāgata possesses definitive compassion, the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) flows forth from the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Since great compassion exists within this subsequently attained wisdom, he manifests transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, he transforms those three...
Those who ride upon the five natures are the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, all of whom can be transformed; this great trichiliocosm is the realm of those to be transformed.
As for the "lofty clouds of compassion," it is like the Nanda Dragon King, who, wishing to send down sweet rain, first spreads clouds of compassion.
For seven days, he causes sentient beings to know that his intention is fixed and that he does not harm things, so as to nourish the hundred grasses;
only then does he send down rain. This dragon is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s own body; the clouds are a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
The rain contained within the clouds and poured forth nourishes all sentient beings; this is the *nirmāṇakāya* preaching the Dharma, nourishing those of the three vehicles.
This is a person. "Clouds follow the dragon; rain follows the clouds. Here, the cloud is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), which arises from a mind of compassion;

thus it is called the "Cloud of Compassion" (*cimegha*). That is to say, based on the mind there is the body, and based on the body there is the speech. Based on the compassionate mind, the *nirmāṇakāya* arises; and based on the *nirmāṇakāya*, one then preaches the Dharma.

This is like how, based on the dragon there are clouds, and based on the clouds there is rain. This refers to the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, which are like the dragon giving rise [to the clouds].

Because it is a transformation-body of compassion (*karuṇā*). Furthermore, "compassion" refers to the transformation of mental action (*manas-karman*); "clouds" refer to the transformation of bodily action (*kāya-karman*);

and "drizzling the rain of Dharma" refers to the transformation of verbal action (*vāk-karman*). Moreover, "the gathering clouds of compassion" carries the same meaning as the scripture’s description of them "gathering and spreading downward.
As for "clouds," they possess seven virtues: first, the virtue of containing rain; second, the virtue of radiance; third... [and so forth].
The virtue of awakening; the virtue of delighting the fourfold assembly; the virtue of eclipsing the sun; the virtue of coolness; and the virtue of universality.

Thus, a sutra says, "The cloud of wisdom gathers in the intercalary month. It is like the Dragon King of Compassion who raises clouds containing rain, but does not let it fall for seven days, waiting until the farmers have finished their work before finally releasing the rain. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s cloud of compassion, which internally contains all myriad [virtues].
Virtue: When the capacities of sentient beings have matured, one proclaims the teaching in accordance with their faculties; this refers to the twenty-first day. Second, the flashing of lightning:
this is a metaphor for the brilliance of the Buddha’s transformative path. Third, the distant thundering of a voice: this awakens all living beings. For those who oppose it, it engenders terror;
this is a metaphor for the fear that arises among various demons when the Buddha appears in the world.

Fourth, "causing the assembly to rejoice" refers to the joy of the multitude; "clouds arising to provide shade" is a metaphor for sentient beings seeing the Buddha and giving rise to a heart of admiration and longing.
Fifth, "the sunlight being eclipsed" is a metaphor for the sun that removes afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the eclipsing of the sun of false views. Sixth is "the earth being cool above ground.

This is a metaphor for sentient beings within the scorching pool of birth and death attaining the coolness of nirvāṇa. Originally, the sun shines upon the earth; its heat scorches and afflicts sentient beings.
Now, by eclipsing the sun of false views, they immediately attain coolness within birth and death. Thus, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the earth.
"Seventh, [the clouds] hang down in dense masses as if they could be grasped. 'Ai' (靉) means dark; 'dai' (靆) means black. This describes the appearance of clouds rising in profusion.
'As if they could be grasped' is a metaphor for the Buddha’s descent of his spiritual power to establish great models and norms.

Through the resonance of his compassion, he causes beings to give rise to joy, so that they shall attain Buddhahood. 'Chenglan' (承攬) is the sense of being able to obtain. 'Fei' (霏)..."* *(Note: The provided text fragment ends with "霏者" [as for "fei"], suggesting the source was cut off. The translation reflects the available portion.)*
This is the appearance of fine rain. As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The arising of the transformations of the three karmas and so forth" refers to the essence of the Dharma;

"rain" is a metaphor. That is to say, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha preaches the Three Vehicles, the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so on—whether it be the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates or the methods of skillful means—which, like fine rain, nourishes and causes [sentient beings] to grow.
The sprouts of the path for all sentient beings grow, just as a fine rain moistens and nourishes the hundred grasses and other plants;
"moistening" means to nourish. "Ten billion" refers to the sentient beings to be transformed. "A great trichiliocosm" refers to the container world (*bhājana-loka*).

Some say that "a great thousand" and "ten billion" are correlative terms and have no further meaning; however, this remains unclear. This refers to the transformation of the great trichiliocosm by the *nirmāṇakāya*.
For all sentient beings, it is called the "drizzling rain of Dharma" that nourishes ten billion worlds. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"That rain falls equally and simultaneously upon the four quarters," which is a metaphor for the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).

"Flowing in streams through immeasurable lands, filling and saturating them" refers to the teachings issued by the Tathāgata, which universally benefit ten billion sentient beings. From the five continents, he preaches the Four Noble Truths.
He then spoke gradually, up until the six *pāramitās*, which are the "fine rain" (*fei*). Question: Of which Buddha’s transformed realm do these ten billion [worlds] constitute the domain?
Answer: They are the realm transformed by the Great Transformation Body (*mahā-nirmāṇakāya*). A Small Transformation Body transforms only a single four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*).
A single four-continent world is precisely one country. Question: How is this known? Answer: The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says:
I, now Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal; Upon the thousand petals surrounding me, there appear again a thousand Śākyamunis.
On each petal are ten billion lands, and in each land is one Śākyamuni; Each sits beneath a Bodhi tree, simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood.
Regarding the statement that "upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central lotus], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis," this refers to the Great Nirmāṇakāya (Great Transformation Body).
Regarding the statement that "on each petal are ten billion lands, and in each land is one Śākyamuni," this refers to the Small Nirmāṇakāya (Small Transformation Body).

Furthermore, the "great trichiliocosm" refers to ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, and so forth; thus, one should know that this refers to the small transformation body.
It transforms only a single set of four continents. This thousand-petaled lotus seat is the first tier; it is the lotus seat produced by the *parabhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others).
Furthermore, regarding the term "ten billion" (*koṭi*), there are four categories in total. First, one hundred million is a "billion," and there are ten billion of these;
this refers to the great transformed realm. Thus far, the explanation has been based on the literal text. Above, there were two [sections]. The first...

The profound analysis of the three bodies (trikāya) and the second section, which assigns them according to the text, together constitute the analysis of the second [part]: the object of refuge and veneration.

Thus far there have been two sections: first, the analysis of the ritual of the one who takes refuge; second, the analysis of the object of refuge. This constitutes the entirety of the first [major section], which is the general praise of the three bodies, exhorting the practice of taking refuge and paying homage.
From this point downward is the second section, concerning those sentient beings who, having failed to respond, all returned to the cool state [of extinction]. This is divided into three parts:
First, the two characters "Thus" (然) and "Therefore" (以) serve to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one. Second, the phrase "Sentient beings harbored no response;

they destroyed my Dharma-hero" identifies the causes and conditions for the exhaustion of the responsive manifestation. Third, the phrase "Thereupon, the teaching ceased at the Golden River and the light was withdrawn beneath the Crane Tree" identifies...
This is the time and place of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. It consists of three distinct sections. First, regarding the section that concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent:
"Now" (ran) serves to conclude what precedes. One might ask: "In what way does 'now' conclude the preceding and introduce the subsequent? The answer is as follows:
This means that the previous praise of the three bodies as all being eternally abiding is something I now also grant; thus it is so. "Thus" (*ran*) is a term of permission.
The previous statement that the three bodies are eternally abiding is logically correct. Question: How is it that we do not see the Buddha-body? Answer:
[The following] is the text concerning those born after [the Buddha's passing]. "Because sentient beings harbor [delusions] and fail to evoke [his response]" refers to what was stated previously.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Although the three bodies are eternally abiding," it means that because sentient beings lack the conditions for resonance, the Buddha does not appear;

this refers to the text following the account of the Buddha’s birth. Since the Buddha-body is in reality eternally abiding, the Buddha himself stated, "My body is precisely the eternal body, the Dharma-body.
It is merely that the Tathāgata employs skillful means to manifest extinction. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "He is truly present..."

Regarding the term "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*): because sentient beings constantly perceive a self, they give rise to a mind of arrogance and indulgence; it is solely because sentient beings lack the capacity for spiritual resonance that the Tathāgata enters extinction.
This refers to the period after birth. Regarding the term "conceiving life" (*saṃjīva*): "conceiving" (*huái*) carries the sense of "containing.

It means to be born while containing emotional consciousness; therefore, it is called "conceiving life. Furthermore, it is so named because one contains the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus, it is called "conceiving life."

Furthermore, within the eighth self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of sentient beings, because they harbor afflictions and karma, these two obstacles—afflictions and karma—trigger the arising of karma and provide the moisture for rebirth;
therefore, they are called "those who harbor birth" (*saṃjīva*). Moreover, "harbor" (*saṃ*) is a synonym for "ordinary beings," "sentient beings," and "living beings.
Because they are born while harboring afflictions, they are called "those who harbor birth. This has ten names; the first is called "the class of beings" (*nikāyasabhāga*).

The second is named "those born from a storehouse" (zàngshēng); the third, "those born in groups" (qúnshēng); the fourth, "those who harbor life" (huáishēng); the fifth, "the azure masses" (cāngshēng); the sixth, "sentient beings" (zhòngshēng);

the seventh, "beings containing [life]" (hánshēng); the eighth, "distinct beings" (yìshēng); the ninth, "dependently arisen beings" (yuánshēng); and the tenth, "sentient beings" (yǒuqíng). Thus, there are ten such names.
"Mo" means "non-existent. "Gan" means "response. Thus, "mo-gan" refers to the absence of a stimulus for sentient beings;

because sentient beings do not stimulate the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, it is called "no stimulus. Furthermore, "gan" is like the harmony and abundance found in a household, which is termed "stimulus-response.
Here, "gan" refers to the maturation of the roots of goodness in sentient beings, which then stimulates the Buddha’s appearance in the world; this is termed "stimulus-response."
Since the roots of goodness in sentient beings have not yet matured, they do not elicit the appearance of a Buddha in the world; therefore, it is said that there is no elicitation. Question:

Although there is no elicitation from sentient beings, what is the purpose of knowing that a Buddha appears in the world? Answer: There are two meanings. First, the Buddha fundamentally appears in the world [for his own sake].

This is for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings whose faculties have matured. However, since the faculties of the multitude of beings have not yet matured, if a Buddha were to appear in the world, those beings would not resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
Since it would be impossible to transform such sentient beings and there would thus be no benefit, what advantage would there be in appearing in the world?

Therefore, when sentient beings lack the capacity for response, a Buddha does not appear in the world. Second, if sentient beings lacked the capacity for response and a Buddha were nevertheless to appear in the world, then [the beings]...

Because one might develop weariness toward the Buddha and thus fall back into the state of ordinary beings, the Sūtra says that they are unable to conceive the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter.
Out of the Buddha’s compassion, fearing that they might fall back into the state of ordinary beings, he manifests the appearance of entering *parinirvāṇa*. Question:
When is it said that a Buddha appears in the world? Is it when the roots of goodness have matured? Answer: It is simply said that [he appears] in accordance with the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

The roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and the untainted roots of goodness (*anāsrava-kuśalamūla*) are accomplished.

Since these are not merely the accomplishment of the roots of goodness for humans and devas—which is mundane—they are called "conducive" (*anuloma*) because they do not merely produce rebirth as a sentient being. Question:

The roots of goodness conducive to liberation and the roots of goodness conducive to penetration of the three vehicles, as well as the roots of goodness of humans and devas, are all of one kind in being tainted (*sāsrava*). How is it that only [the former] are termed "conducive"?

Regarding the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and those conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*): when these roots of goodness have matured, one transcends the world. The answer is:
the roots of goodness of humans and devas merely seek the worldly, out-flowing fruits (*sāsrava-phala*) of humans and devas; thus, they accord with birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

However, because the roots of goodness conducive to liberation and penetration of the three vehicles can seek the supramundane, outflow-free fruits (*anāsrava-phala*) of benefit and liberation, they accord with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world for those whose untainted roots of goodness have reached maturity.
Since there are currently none whose roots of goodness for liberation have matured, the Buddha does not appear in the world; thus it is said that sentient beings fail to evoke his response. Question:
Upagupta converted immeasurable people, all of whom attained the fruits of sainthood. How can you say that the Buddha does not appear in the world? Answer:
This refers to a class of sentient beings who make a vow, aspiring to attain the fruits of sainthood within the Buddha’s True Dharma.

Consequently, after his parinirvāṇa, immeasurable sentient beings will attain the fruits of sainthood within that True Dharma. Because these beings lack the karmic affinity for the Buddha, the Buddha does not appear in the world for their sake;
thus it is said that "sentient beings do not evoke [his response]. The term "jīan" (殲) means "exhaustion" or "termination"; that is to say—
He manifests the same appearance as those of the two vehicles and enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, wherein neither body nor cognition remains; therefore, it is called "exhaustion.
As for "I," this refers to the Master Ci'en’s own self-designation. As for "Dharma Hero" (*dharmavīra*), this refers to the Buddha.

Because he is uniquely honored throughout the three realms and his wisdom is fierce and majestic, he is named the Dharma Hero. Thus, a sutra says: "The Great Hero, the Fierce World-Honored One. Above.
This is the reason why [the Buddha] must necessarily pass away.
Thirdly, from here on, we shall correctly examine the time and place of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. Question: At what time and in what place did he enter parinirvāṇa? Answer:
There are two ways of correctly examining the time and place. One says it was the *renshen* day during the reign of King Mu of Zhou.
Regarding the year: one source states it was the fifty-second year of King Mu, the year of *Guiyou* (癸酉), on the fifteenth day of the second month.
This corresponds precisely to the second interpretation. The preceding *Renshen* (壬申) year was the first year of his teaching, and the *Guiyou* year was the second;
thus, he entered *nirvāṇa* at midnight during the *zi* hour on the fifteenth day of the second month. As for the location: it was Kuśinagara in Central India.
To the west of the city, more than five li away, there is the Golden Sand River (*Suvarṇavālukā-nadī*). This river flows from south to north.

On the western bank of the river is a *śāla* grove, which is the place where [the Buddha] entered *parinirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is called the "place of entry into extinction. Thus, the commentary states:

"He ceased his teaching at the Golden River and withdrew his radiance beneath the Crane Trees. Regarding the phrase "ceased his teaching" (*xi-chàng*): "ceased" (*xi*) means to stop, to end, or to rest; "teaching" (*chàng*) refers to the turning and proclaiming [of the Dharma].

This is because sentient beings lacked the conditions for resonance; thus, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa and ceased his preaching of the Dharma. Therefore, it is said that he "stilled his proclamation.

According to the account in the *Chavibhāga* (Section on Cremation), at the middle watch of the night, the Tathāgata was tranquil and without sound; hence, it is said that he "stilled his proclamation."
Regarding the term "Golden River" (Jinhe), it is so named because there is much gold sand within its waters.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that he entered nirvāṇa on the banks of the River Araluvati; this is the Sanskrit name for the River Araluvati.
This is called the River of Gold Sand. A question was asked: "What is the underlying significance of the Tathāgata entering nirvāṇa by the side of this river?
The answer was: "Because it serves as a symbolic representation. For within this river there is gold, yet the water of the river flows and changes from moment to moment."

Because there is no gold sand therein that does not flow. As for the water flowing from moment to moment, it is a metaphor for sentient beings who, possessing afflictions, drift through birth and death like water that never stays still.
The pure Buddha-nature within their bodies is precisely a metaphor for the gold sand in the river.

Because there is fundamentally no coming or going. That gold is produced in the Li-shui River is what is transmitted in Eastern customs; that the *Tīrthika* River contains gold is what all in the Western lands know.
This means that birth and death are like a river that never ceases, while *nirvāṇa* is like gold because it is worthy of being treasured and honored.
Thus, it signifies that *nirvāṇa* exists within birth and death. It is like sand, which does not flow; therefore, there is something signified. The Buddha, regarding the river...

He entered parinirvāṇa at the edge [of the world]. Thus it is said that he ceased his teaching at the Golden River (*Suvarṇanadī*). Regarding the phrase "concealing his radiance" (*tāoguāng*): "concealing" (*tāo*) means to store away or to hide.
"Radiance" (*guāng*) refers to the Tathāgata’s constant light of one *vyāma*, which is the golden light; it also includes the halo (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) and so forth.
Furthermore, whenever the Buddha preached the Dharma, he invariably emitted light. Moreover, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that from his mouth (*mukhadvāra*), he emitted various kinds of...

As for "retracting the light" (*tāoguāng*): after entering *parinirvāṇa*, he no longer emitted light; hence it is said that he "retracted the light. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "retracting the light":
at the time of his *parinirvāṇa*, when he was about to undergo cremation, there was an arhat named Kāśyapa who came from the mountains.
He went to the family of the disciples and requested one thousand pieces of white cotton cloth to wrap the Tathāgata’s golden-hued body. With the golden-hued body [placed] therein...
Because he was concealed within those white cotton cloths, it is called "Concealing the Light" (*tāoguāng*). As for the term "crane-tree" (*héshù*), this refers to the twin *śāla* trees.
When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, they turned white, resembling crane-trees. To the west of the Kinnara River, there were four pairs of these trees;
in this grove, with his head to the north and facing west, the Buddha entered nirvana. At the time of his passing...

These four trees then made a dry sound and turned white. Yet the four original trees remained green and did not change. The one named "Self" (*ātman*) is a tree that turns white; the one named "Non-self" (*anātman*) is a tree that does not turn white. On the northern side there are two trees:
the green one is named "Purity" (*śubha*), and the one that turns white is named "Impurity" (*aśubha*). Question: Why is it that among these eight trees, four turn white while four do not? Answer:
These white colors represent the Tathāgata’s [teaching on] impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), non-self (*anātman*), and impurity (*aśubha*).

This demonstrates the manifestation of entering parinirvāṇa. As for the "four blue [trees]," they represent the unchanging nature of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, signifying that the Tathāgata abides eternally;

thus it is said: "This body of mine is itself the eternal body, the Dharma-body. Regarding the term "Kūṭāgāraśālavana" (the Śāla Grove), it is named after the fact that the trees turn white at the time of transformation.
This concludes the second section, which correctly establishes the time and place of the Tathāgata’s entry into parinirvāṇa.

From here below is the third section, which distinguishes how the Dharma has been transmitted through the succession of the holy teachings as being of a single flavor. This is divided into four parts: first, distinguishing the chronological periods;
second, distinguishing the persons who transmitted the teachings; third, distinguishing the teachings that were transmitted; and fourth, answering external objections.
First, regarding the determination of the dates: the commentary states, "prior to one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

As for the term "Buddha," it is called *buddha* in the Western [language], which is the Sanskrit term. In the language of Tang, it is translated as "Awakening" (*jue*), which is a shortened form that omits the syllable *ta*.
Thus, "Awakening" refers to the Buddha. Furthermore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha do so by uttering the word "Buddha" in order to generate wholesome roots.
If one were to address him as "The Awakened One" (*Buddha*), it would not give rise to wholesome [reverence].
If we follow the Sanskrit manuscripts of various sūtras, they all refer to our Original Teacher by the name *Bhagavān*. Because this single word contains all virtues, it encompasses the six meanings.
Since it possesses the six qualities such as sovereignty (*vaśitā*) and so forth, the master translators intended to employ abbreviation; thus, following the preceding...

Because he gives rise to goodness, he is called a Buddha (*buddha*). If explained according to its meaning, it is the sense of "awakening" (*bodhi*). Since this sense of awakening possesses three meanings, he is named *Buddha*.
If even one of these meanings were lacking, the definition of *Buddha* would not be established. Question:

Regarding the meaning of "awakening," is the name "Awakened One" applied only to the Buddha, or is the meaning of awakening also applied during the causal stage? Answer: The meaning of awakening also exists during the causal stage.

Because they lack [these qualities], they are not called Buddhas. Only a Buddha possesses the three types of awakening; namely: first, self-awakening (*svabodha*); second, awakening others (*parabodha*);

and third, the perfection of the practice of awakening (*bodhicaryā-paripūri*). Only by possessing these three meanings of awakening is one named a Buddha. Regarding the first, self-awakening: this distinguishes [the Buddha] from all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
From beginningless time until now, ordinary beings have constantly dwelt in the long night of birth and death, shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*).

They are shrouded and do not realize it for themselves; furthermore, they are blinded by birth and death, which obstructs their eye of wisdom so that they do not see the Noble Path and do not realize it for themselves.
Therefore, the Buddha is called "Self-Awakened" (*svayaṃbuddha*) to distinguish him from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Second, he is called "Awakening Others" (*parabodhaka*) to distinguish him from those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), who awaken themselves alone but do not awaken others, as they seek only their own benefit. Question: Ordinary worldlings do not awaken for themselves.
Ordinary beings are not called Buddhas. As for those of the Two Vehicles, since they have already awakened for themselves, they may be granted the name of Buddha. Answer:

Although those of the Two Vehicles awaken for themselves and also awaken others, they are permitted to be called Buddhas. However, because the Two Vehicles consist solely of practices for self-benefit and cannot awaken others, they are not included within the category of [true] Buddhas;
this is because the conduct of the Two Vehicles involves revulsion toward suffering and a longing for quiescence, and thus lacks the practice of benefiting others.
Question: If one is designated a Buddha based on both self-awakening and awakening others, then the practitioners of the Two Vehicles—who achieve only self-benefit—cannot be called Buddhas.
However, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages possess both benefits and possess both self-awakening and awakening others; they should therefore be called Buddhas. Answer:

While it is true that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages possess the two types of awakening—benefiting themselves and benefiting others—and that in principle they are Buddhas, their awakening and practice are not yet perfected at the Ten Stages. Therefore, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages are not called Buddhas.

Because even a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva) still possesses subtle, innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that have not been completely severed, they are not yet fully perfected;
they are merely those of the Path of Liberation. Only the Tathāgata of Sublime Enlightenment, who possesses the threefold meaning of "enlightenment," is truly called a Buddha.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), like awakening from sleep, like a lotus flower [opening]."
"Opening" refers to the wisdom of the fundamental nature (*mūla-jñāna*), which is able to awaken itself, just as one awakens from sleep or a dream.

"The wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākāra-jñāna*) is that which is able to awaken all sentient beings, like the blooming of a lotus flower; this is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The "knower of all" (*sarvajña*) is the wisdom that contemplates emptiness; it is solely principle and solely truth, for it is free from conceptual discrimination.

The "knower of all aspects" (*sarvākārajña*) is the wisdom that contemplates existence; this is conventional wisdom regarding phenomena. "Like awakening from a dream": "like" (*yathā*) means "resembling."
This is like awakening from a dream. For example, when a person dreams, they perceive various objects and grasp them as real things, unaware that it is a dream.
Once they have awakened from the dream, they realize that all dream-objects are empty. Now, fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is likewise.

Previously, before the arising of awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*), while within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*), one grasped at all worldly objects as real. Now, one attains the realization of the outflow-free fundamental wisdom.
Because this is the truth, one knows that delusive objects are entirely empty. Thus, birth and death are now understood as a dream.

"Like a lotus blooming" refers to the subsequently attained *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), which resembles the blooming of a lotus. When the lotus blooms, its fragrance spreads afar; when *sarvajñatā* arises, [its radiance likewise extends].

It rescues sentient beings and brings them to liberation, resembling the flourishing of a lotus. Alternatively, it is said that "like a lotus blooming" means that by the blooming of the flower, the flower is revealed;
the "flower" here refers to the seed. When the wisdom of the seed (bīja-jñāna) arises, it transforms sentient beings because they have already attained the fruit.
It is like seeing the pedestal when a flower blooms. Question: Why is it called "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*)? Answer: "Aspect" (*ākāra*) means category;
that is, the various types of the faculties and natures of all sentient beings. Because this wisdom can know the distinctions among all these categories, it receives this name.
Furthermore, "awakening" (*jue*) is precisely the Chinese term for it. Now, [this teaching] gives rise to goodness according to the local conditions.
