Thus, each of the Four Kings took one portion for worship. This explains the second Teacher’s period of transformative activity; his transformative activity was now complete.
Next, to identify the third Teacher: he is Maudgalyāyana (Madiande). "Madiande" is an archaic translation; "Madiandikā" is the correct form.
This refers to Maitreya (Madiande), which translates as "Golden Ground. [He was so named] because Ānanda transformed water [into gold for him].

When he was the Elder Kāñcanamuni, he was called "Golden Ground" (Kāñcana-bhūmi) because he had attained the fruit [of Arhatship]. Second, he is called Madhyāntika, which means "Golden Head" (Kāñcana-śiras);
he is named "Golden Head" because his hair resembles the color of gold. As Ānanda said: "The World-Honored One entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa;
he entrusted the Dharma to me; I have now entrusted it to you, Madhyāntika. Thus, he entrusted it to both individuals simultaneously.
He also asked: "These two individuals were contemporaries; how is it that Madhyāntika was already the third patriarch?
He replied: "This is according to their sequential rank. That is, Śāṇakavāsin should be considered the third patriarch.
This is because Śāṇakavāsin had a karmic affinity with Upagupta and took him as his disciple; thus, with Upagupta being the fifth [patriarch], [Śāṇakavāsin] is reckoned as the third."
Because he was a Teacher of the Doctrine, there is no error in designating Śāṇakavāsin as the fourth Teacher. Question:

Where did Madhyāntika go to convert beings? Answer: While the Tathāgata was still in the world, he led a group of bhikṣus, flying through the air on a journey until they reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You should know..."
"Fifty years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a great arhat named Madhyāntika who will convert this land and establish five hundred monasteries;

this person was prophesied by the Buddha in advance. Upon hearing the Buddha’s profound prediction, Madhyāntika thought, "I have now attained the Way and brought it to completion," and his heart was filled with joy. He then went to that place where the great nāga...
He went into the pond; it was Maudgalyāyana. He had previously made a request from another dragon king, who became greatly enraged.
This Venerable One, realizing his supernatural power, was a great Arhat who manifested eighteen transformations as a great divine feat.
Because the dragon king possessed the power of karma, he immediately fell under [the Venerable’s] influence. Thus, the dragon appeared three times.
The Venerable One’s majestic power was so fierce that the great earth trembled. The Dragon King asked the Venerable One, "If you request the entire great lake, it cannot be granted;
however, if you request but a small portion, I shall grant it. The Venerable One replied, "I wish to build a vihāra here to propagate the treasury of the Dharma.
As the Tathāgata prophesied in secret, I am to rule as a king over this land; therefore, I shall establish it."
He did not ask for much; he simply required the space of one *āsandī* (seating mat) or one knee’s breadth, though it was not fixed.

Upon hearing this, the Naga King immediately granted his permission. As the Venerable One thus spread out his seating mat, the water gradually receded while the mat gradually expanded, until five hundred monasteries (*vihāra*) had been constructed. The pond remained only on the west side.
At the southern corner, a small portion of water was left remaining; it is fifteen *li* in circumference. The Dragon King dwells here at the southwest corner.

After this pond, five hundred monasteries were constructed. When one thousand years had passed, as there were already vihāras, the community of monks required attendants (*karmadāna*) for their service.
Consequently, they engaged in trade with various countries; these very attendants have since passed a great deal of time.
The number of monks gradually diminished, while the number of *karmadāna* (lay attendants) increased. Consequently, these *karmadāna* supported one another and established themselves as kings.
Neighboring countries all referred to them as "the country of slaves" (*kīla*, which here means "purchased"). All nations held them in contempt and would not engage in mutual intercourse with them.
Later, at that time, an Arhat in this very country manifested fire to cremate his own body and entered Parinirvāṇa;
this is precisely the kingdom of Rājagṛha, or as it is called Kaśmīra. This explains the third Teacher.
The fourth section from here below distinguishes Śāṇakavāsa, also known as *Tāyi* (a term from the old translations).
According to the new translations, his name in Sanskrit is Śāṇakavāsa, which means "Grass-Robed.
Long ago in the distant past, this Venerable One was once a traveling guest who entered the sea to seek pearls. There he encountered an Upādhyāya who was a Pratyekabuddha, whose body was clad in...
The one clad in grass garments was none other than this merchant leader. Having offered his robes to this Buddha and made offerings to him, he then made a vow, saying:
"May I, in a future life, resemble this preceptor by likewise wearing grass garments;
and may the preceptor whom I serve be ten thousand times superior to this present preceptor. This was Ānanda. Having made this vow, when the time came for his final birth, he entered the womb.

This robe was born together with [the Buddha] and grows along with his body. At the time of his renunciation, it transformed into a garment of grass; thus, it is called the "womb-robe" (*garbha-vastra*).
Later, at the time of his *nirvāṇa*, he left this robe behind to symbolize the Dharma. As the tradition says: "If this robe is damaged, the Dharma will also gradually perish.
Indeed, when the Tripitaka Master from the Western Regions arrived, he saw that this robe had already been damaged. He took...
Knowing that the Buddha was gradually approaching his parinirvāṇa, it is said that the robe has something symbolic.

Thus, Śāṇakavāsin received the entrustment from Ānanda, whereupon he propagated the Dharma-treasury and extensively delivered those with whom he had a karmic connection. This accords with the Buddha’s profound prediction:
"In the kingdom of Magadha there shall be an elder named Kautika. Kautika shall have three sons; the youngest son shall, under my True Dharma..."
“Dharma, you shall attain the fruit of sainthood. The Venerable Śāṇakavāsin immediately recalled the Buddha’s profound prediction.
Later, he went with a thousand disciples to that householder’s home and became a preceptor to the householder Kautika.
After some time, he departed again, and his disciples gradually diminished in number. Following a further period of time, the Venerable one went alone to Kautika.
The householder of the Ti family asked, "Previously you had many disciples; why have you come alone this time?
The Venerable One replied, "My disciples have abandoned me and departed. He then asked the householder, "Would you be willing to become my disciple?
His intention was not to take the householder himself as a disciple, but rather his third son. This...
The householder Kukkuta had no son. The householder said, "I cannot become a disciple of the Venerable One;
it is because I have not yet renounced wealth and sensual pleasures. If, at a later time, I have a son, I shall then become a disciple of the Venerable One.
Having received this promise regarding the son, the Venerable One departed. Later, the householder fathered a son named Ānanda-Kukkuṭa. The Venerable One...
He then begged the householder for [the son]. The householder was unwilling, saying, "My household estate is vast; I must trade this son away.
If there were a second son, I would certainly give him to you, Venerable Sir. When the Venerable Sir gave his consent, he departed.
Later, a second son was born, named Aṣṭabhujiṣya. The Venerable Sir again begged for him, but the householder was once more unwilling.
"My second son knows external affairs; my first son knows internal affairs. If there is a third son, you may take him as you please.
The Venerable One then departed. Later, the elder had a third son named Upagupta.
When the Venerable One requested him from the elder, the latter was unwilling to give him up. The Venerable One then proceeded to instruct and convert this third son, saying: "You..."
The Sūtra states that for Kṛtaka, white thoughts were more numerous than black thoughts. He asked, "What constitutes a white thought and what a black thought?
The Venerable One replied, "A thought that benefits others is a white thought; a thought that does not benefit others is a black thought.
Kṛtaka replied, "I have only black thoughts. The Venerable One said, "You should [use] two stones, one black and one white."
"Son, for every act that benefits others, place a white pebble; for every act that harms others, place a black pebble.
Later on, when there were only pure white pebbles remaining, the Venerable One then preached the Dharma. This Kukkuta [monastery] became known as "Skilled in Speech."
He attained the first fruit of the path. Regarding the "black mind," it refers to greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth; the "white mind" refers to the eleven dharmas beginning with faith.
Thus, through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure of four motions), the Venerable One attained the fourth fruit.
Having converted disciples, he himself did not enter *nirvāṇa*, but remained in a certain mountain range leading his disciples, practicing there within that mountain.
He proceeded.

This is the fifth patriarch from below, namely Upagupta. Having received the entrustment, he widely proclaimed the treasury of the Dharma, delivering those with whom he had a karmic affinity and benefiting all sentient beings.
If there were a husband and wife who loved one another, he was able to transform them.
Those who attained the fruits of sainthood used split blades of fine grass as counting sticks (*śalākā*). Each stick was four inches long. They were kept in a stone chamber;
its width was sixteen feet, though some say it was thirty feet—the latter being uncertain. When the chamber became full of these counting sticks, he later entered *nirvāṇa*.
He took enough [sticks] to cremate his body. Every time he preached the Dharma, there were those who attained sainthood. Later, when he preached the Dharma...
Many among those seated below had not yet realized the fruits of the Path. Mahākātyāyana thought to himself, "When I preach the Dharma, there is no one who does not attain the fruit of sainthood.
Those in this assembly today who lack the karmic affinity with me must be those whom my teacher alone can transform.
At that moment, Śāṇakavāsin, while in the mountains, perceived Mahākātyāyana’s thoughts from afar and immediately exercised his supernatural powers, arriving [at the assembly].
Kumuda was away; Kumuda was not present. Once he had arrived, he sat upon the rope-couch.
Kumuda’s disciples, seeing that his hair and nails were long and sharp, did not realize he was a great Arhat. They immediately began to revile him, saying, "Old monk from what region are you?
Why are you sitting on my preceptor's rope-couch? They then pushed and pulled him, yet he remained as immovable as Mount Sumeru. He would not budge.
Nengdong then reported this to Jueduo. Jueduo said, "It must have been my Great Master who arrived there. Indeed, it was as he had said.
Nengdong immediately prostrated himself with his head at [the master's] feet and inquired after his well-being. However, the various disciples did not cease their arrogance.
"Although he prostrated before my teacher, it does not necessarily mean that his virtue and wisdom surpass my teacher’s. Thus, one knows that the disciples' arrogance had not yet been eliminated.

While sitting at ease, [the Buddha] emitted five hundred rays of divine light from the tips of his fingers—some say five hundred streams of fragrant milk, though this is not certain. Śāṇakavāsin then said to Kuṭadanta: "You..."

Kukta wondered from which meditative concentration this auspicious sign had arisen. Having seen it, he immediately entered into samādhi and exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he was utterly unable to know its source.
He then addressed the Upādhyāya, saying, "I have exhausted my supernatural powers, yet I cannot understand this miraculous transformation.
The Master said, "You should not expect to know it; even Mahākāśyapa could not understand the samādhi and supernormal powers of the World-Honored One."
"Ānanda cannot know the *śāla-vṛkṣa-samādhi*, nor can you know even my *abhijñā-samādhi*.
This is the *nāga-pracalita-samādhi*; I now entrust it to you, and you should receive this entrustment.
Thereupon, all pride was completely eliminated from the minds of the disciples, and they all realized the fruits of sainthood upon hearing these words. Śāṇakavāsin then, at that very place—
He entered into *nirvāṇa*. Jutuo (Kukta) then collected his relics and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
Later, when Jutuo preached the Dharma, there was no one among those in his assembly who did not attain the fruits of sainthood. He extensively transformed those with whom he had a karmic connection;
people of the time called him the "Buddha Without Physical Marks. On one occasion, during a discourse on the Dharma, the celestial Māra conceived this thought: "This is a Great Arhat..."
"Arhat, you are skilled at converting those with whom you have a karmic connection. My disciples all belong to others.

I shall employ supernatural powers—either transforming myself into a woman, or becoming one of your own kind, or raining down the seven treasures and such—to harass and disturb Kūṭadanta, so that he will not be able to know when it is time for me to preach the Dharma.
Later, at the place where the Dharma is being preached, there will not be a single person among the listeners who attains realization."
Regarding the "Noble Fruit" (āryaphala), Kuṭadanta said: "This must be a celestial Māra who is harassing my disciples.

He then entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to observe the matter and saw that a celestial Māra was indeed harassing his disciples, preventing them from realizing the fruit. Furthermore, the Māra took his crown and placed it upon Kuṭadanta’s head;
amidst the great assembly, he danced about, brandishing it. Since the celestial Māra acted in this manner, Kuṭadanta then took three...
The corpses—namely those of dogs, monkeys, and snakes—transformed into necklaces (*mālā*). They said to Pāpīyas:
"Since you, the celestial Māra, are thus, then that Kūṭadanta shall offer you his head-garland; we now give it to you, and we give you these necklaces.
Pāpīyas, taking this to be true, accepted them. Consequently, Kūṭadanta placed [the garland] upon his head, and he returned to his original state.

The stench of their forms was so foul as to be unbearable. Through his supernatural powers, Pāpīyān ascended to heaven and entered the earth, performing all manner of deeds, yet he could not eliminate it.
He then went up and informed the Brahmā King, saying: "This is a transformation produced by a disciple of the One of Ten Powers;
I am ultimately unable to remove it. You must return to the place of Kuśa, seek mercy, and repent. Only those who know these three corpses shall remain; all others shall not."
"It is possible. Pāpīyas returned to that place and offered an apology. Kuṭadanta granted his request and said to Pāpīyas:

"I have heard that you are skilled at manifesting the form and the marks of a Tathāgata. Since I have not seen the World-Honored One, you must manifest for me the form and marks of the World-Honored One;
his majestic demeanor must be exactly like his. Once I have gone away, [you may depart]. Pāpīyas replied, "I shall do so."
The Venerable One manifested his own body; the Venerable One was not permitted to prostrate.

Pāpīyān entered the forest and manifested the body of the Tathāgata, golden-hued like refined gold, sixteen feet tall, with Śakra leading before him and Brahmā following behind, surrounded by the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly.
Guṇabhadra, unaware, prostrated himself. He then said to Pāpīyān: "From this day forward, you shall be mine..."
He made two kinds of vows: "I shall cause no one who preaches the Dharma to be disturbed;
nor shall I allow anyone sitting in meditation or practicing the Way to have their body or mind distracted. Pāpīyān replied, "I can comply with and carry out these instructions.
From that time until now, all practitioners of the Way have not dared to be disturbed. Should they be disturbed, they immediately die twenty-three times over.
The fifth master has completed the transmission of the teachings. Altogether, these five masters spanned approximately one hundred years.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "Prior to the hundred-year mark, there were five masters; all were 'extraordinary persons' (i-jen). They were extraordinary because they differed from ordinary beings;

thus they are called 'extraordinary persons. They emerged preeminently among the multitude of sages. The preceding section constitutes the entirety of the second [section]: those capable of transmitting the teachings.
Furthermore, the third section from below, which distinguishes the teachings transmitted, states in the *Sūtra Commentary*: "The pure source still draws upon the true track, remaining identical.
The explanation says: this refers to the discernment of the Dharma; that is, the Tathāgata’s truly correct teaching, which is free from error or delusion. Because...
It is no different from when the Buddha was alive; therefore, it is called the "True Track" (zhēnguǐ) because it remains identical. Regarding the term "pure" (chún), there are two interpretations.
First, some say that "pure" signifies being unmixed, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which speaks of "pure, singular, and unmixed. Second, others say it does not signify being unmixed;
this is the sense of the character "pure" used in the commentary (*shù*), because the character for "to offer" (*xiǎng*) is composed of the "water" radical, and thus it does not mean "unmixed."

Regarding the meaning: this character "pure" (*jun*) signifies essence; it also signifies clarity, and is thus glossed as "clear. "Source" (*yuan*) means beginning. The initial emergence of water is called a source.
The intended meaning is that these five people transmitted the Dharma as a single flavor. Thus, the true and correct teaching is named the "Clear Source.
If there were any confusion or disorder, it would be termed "turbid. There is also an explanation for the term "source": [text continues].

There are two interpretations. First, it is said that "source" (*yuan*) refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*); that is, the original source, for all phenomena (*dharmas*) flow forth from within True Suchness.
Second, it is said that the twelvefold teachings spoken by the Buddha’s golden mouth are, from the very beginning, born from the Buddha’s mouth;
thus, the golden mouth is the original source. This is also like water emerging from its primary source. As for the word "yet" (*shang*):
"Yu (猶)" means "near. "Yi (挹)" means "to draw [water]. Furthermore, "yi" describes the manner of personally receiving [the teaching].
The intended meaning is that the Dharma taught by these five people is still profoundly tranquil; thus, "yi" implies it is not yet diminished.

The intended meaning is that for a hundred years prior, the five people transmitted the teachings no differently than when the Tathāgata was alive, personally beholding the very root of the Buddha’s True Dharma.
The source is similar; hence it is called "drawing from" (*yi*). "True" (*zhen*) means reality and correctness; that is, the true and correct Dharma, and thus it is named "true.
"Track" (*gui*) refers to a standard or model, a pattern for conduct. "By" (*you*) means cause or that which is followed.
The commentary states: These five masters transmitted the teachings in strict accordance with the principle of ultimate reality; they are no different from the teachings spoken by the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that their true tracks are identical. Thus concludes the third section above, which discriminates the teachings transmitted.
The fourth section below explains the objections raised by outsiders. The commentary states: "Although the various sages maintain [the Dharma] in harmony with the transformation of the Tathāgata.
An outsider objects: "If, during the Buddha’s lifetime, only the Buddha alone preached the teachings, one could say that the teaching was of a single flavor."
Now that there are five individuals transmitting the teachings, each is distinct; how then can it be said that the Dharma-teachings are of a single flavor?
Thus, the meaning of "the true track remains the same" is not established. Regarding the formal response below, the *Sūtra* (commentary) states:

"Although the various sages maintain [the teaching], their transformations are in harmony with those of the Tathāgata. The word "although" (*sui*) implies a dual sense of both gain and loss. The intended meaning is: although the five individuals are not the same...
Because the Dharma entrusted [to him] through his insight was entirely pure and correct, this is also a term of approval. "The assembly of sages" refers to the five individuals.
Some interpretations state that the "assembly of sages" refers to the group of five hundred arhats; however, for now, we take the names of these five as the "assembly of sages.
As for "upholding," it means to sustain and maintain the Buddha-Dharma; that is to say, it is the Correct [Dharma].

Regarding the person who maintains the Dharma: furthermore, "maintaining" means there is no violation or transgression; thus it is called "maintaining. As for the term "harmony" (*yè*), it means union or accord.
The meaning lies in the previous explanation: although the five people are distinct, their views and understandings are harmonious.
Alternatively, they are in accord with the Buddha’s teachings and the Dharma. Because they are of a single flavor without contradiction, it is called "harmony."
"Yi" (also) means "like" (*yǐrú*). That is to say, as the World-Honored One has taught, because there is nothing else different [from it], it is like the Dharma during that Buddha's lifetime;
therefore, it is called a transformation that exists "as if present. Thus, these various sages who sustain the Buddha-Dharma are all transformations manifested while the Buddha was present.
The above constitutes the fourth section, which explains and resolves external objections. The four preceding sections, though distinct, collectively [form the whole].
This concludes the third section on the single flavor of the Dharma transmitted through the succession of the noble teachings of the great texts.

Below this, the fourth section distinguishes how heterodox followers arise in competition and various views proliferate; it is divided into three parts: first, a general distinction of the differences in the teachings in a single sentence;
second, the presentation of analogies; and third, the formal exposition. Regarding "heterodox views," the Commentary states: "Heterodox followers cause confusion to the very core. Up to...

This is correct; the three sections are distinct. Furthermore, this commentary (*śāstra*) is divided into two parts. Regarding the section where "heretical followers arise in competition and divergent views proliferate," it is divided into two:
first, a general discussion of the differences in teaching through both doctrine and analogy; second, a specific exposition of their divergent attachments.

The commentary states that from the words "heretical followers" onwards constitutes the first part, the general discussion through doctrine and analogy, which is further divided into two: first, the doctrine; and subsequently...
As for the analogy: "Furthermore, as for the Dharma," it refers to the fact that after this point, the Dharma diverges from its single flavor (*ekarasa*).
Regarding the first point, which generally distinguishes the differences in the teachings: this refers to the divergence of the Dharma from its single flavor according to the *Siddhānta-śāstra*.

As for the term "after this" (*zihou*): "this" (*zi*) means "from" (*cong*), and "after" (*hou*) refers to the period after one hundred years; that is, starting from the completion of the first century.

"Later" refers to having divergent views and discordant realizations. For the five hundred years prior [to this], the teachings transmitted by the five masters were all of a single flavor without divergence.

"Divergence" (乖) means to turn one's back on; some say it means to dispute, but here we take it in the sense of turning away. That is, to turn one's back on my pure and correct Dharma, hence it is called "turning away.
To turn away is to be in discord. From the time of Upagupta onwards, after the first five hundred years, during the second five hundred years...
First, the various disciples diverged into conflicting views; they were no longer of one flavor in the Dharma as it was during the Buddha’s lifetime.
At the beginning of the second century, they immediately deviated from that single flavor. Question: During the Buddha’s lifetime, he preached both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings and others;

these were not uniform. How can you say the Dharma was of one flavor? Answer: It is true that the teachings were of many kinds, yet for the sake of the Buddha’s preaching, they constitute a single flavor.
At that time, it is fully endowed with its five virtues; therefore, it is called "one flavor" (*ekarasa*). First, the virtue of being able to transform those who are difficult to transform.

Second, the virtue of severing doubts and providing acceptance. Third, the virtue of being revered by humans and devas. Fourth, the virtue that the Dharma is not established in vain; once established, it necessarily brings benefit.
Fifth, it is able to subdue heterodox factions. Because it possesses these five meanings, it is called the "Dharma of One Flavor" (*ekarasa-dharma*).
At the beginning of the second century, because this Dharma of One Flavor was violated, a question was asked: "What was the transmission of the teaching that violated the Dharma of One Flavor?

The answer is: "It was Mahādeva’s recitation of verses; this was the very first violation of the Dharma of One Flavor. He then expressed his own sentiments, speaking whatever came to mind in verse form.
Therefore, it is said that this contradicts the sacred teachings. As the *Treatise on Tenets* (*Siddhānta-śāstra*) states:

"More than one hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Bhagavat, much time having passed since the Sage, he was like the sun long set. The *Commentary on the Treatise on Tenets* (*Siddhānta-śāstra-ṭīkā*) composed by Cien (Kuiji) says:
"Outside of one hundred years after the Tathāgata’s extinction, there was a king named Aśoka in the city of Suma in the kingdom of Magadha. No [further text provided].
Udayin was the prince Ajātaśatru. At that time, the Buddha’s Dharma was first divided by dispute. [The interlocutor] asks: "Who was Mahādeva? [The respondent] answers:
"In the west, there is the country of Mathurā; he was the son of a merchant leader (*śreṣṭhin*).
That merchant leader took a young wife, and later they bore a son of handsome and upright countenance, named Mahādeva. Later, the merchant leader, taking his..."
He possessed great wealth and traveled to various other regions for trade. There, he encountered a rebellion and was detained, unable to return for a long time.

Mahādeva grew up and eventually became sexually involved with his mother. Later, when his father returned, Mahādeva, fearing that the matter would be exposed, conspired with his mother and killed his father.
Fearing further discovery, he then took his mother and fled to a distant land.
In the city of Pāṭaliputra in the kingdom of Magadha, during the lifetime of his father, there was a disciple who was constantly supported by the household as an arhat.
Later, while traveling on pilgrimage, this arhat happened to arrive at the house of Mahādeva.
Upon seeing him, Mahādeva feared he would speak ill of others; thus, he used a stratagem to invite the arhat into his home and killed him. Having done so—
"This was an evil deed. Heaven did not protect him; later he became impoverished and worked as a hired laborer for others.
His mother had committed adultery with another man, and when Mahādeva learned of this, he killed her as well. Thus he committed the sins of the three karmas.
Because he had not severed his roots of goodness, he felt deep remorse and reflected: 'I have previously committed such transgressions; by what means can I extinguish them?'"

This is a transgression; this is an act of parricide. Yet, even such a person’s roots of goodness are not severed. He said to himself, "I have heard that śramaṇas possess a dharma for extinguishing sins.
He immediately went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery and inquired about the method for extinguishing sin.

Having reached the interior of the monastery gate, he encountered a bhikṣu walking in meditation (caṅkrama), who recited a single verse (gāthā): "If a person commits a grave offense, By practicing virtue, it may be extinguished."
He was able to illuminate the world, like the sun emerging from the clouds. Having heard this verse, he immediately went to where the bhikṣu was and said, "I desire to leave the household life.
If you are a noble one, please accept me as a disciple. The bhikṣu then examined his faculties and received him into the Way.

However, upon examining Mahādeva, he saw that he had committed three heinous crimes and was unwilling to ordain him. He went from room to room asking the noble ones, but they all likewise refused to grant him ordination. Finally—
There was an ordinary monk who, without inquiring into the circumstances, immediately granted him the tonsure. Mahādeva was by nature intelligent;

before long, he had memorized and upheld the Three Piṭakas of the holy teachings, mastering them all completely. His speech was clear and refined, and he was capable of guiding others through his teaching.
Later, the king repeatedly invited him into the palace to provide offerings and requested that he preach the Dharma, whereupon he served the kingdom.

The Master, it is said, had previously engaged in sexual relations with the Queen. Later, while at a monastery, he gave rise to improper thoughts and uttered a great falsehood, claiming, "I have attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Subsequently, in a dream, he discharged impurity that stained his robe and ordered his disciple to wash it.
The disciple said, "I have heard that for an Arhat, all outflows (āsravas) are exhausted; how is it that my Preceptor still has outflows?"
He discharged impurity. He immediately asked his teacher, "How can an Arhat still have such a thing?
Mahādeva falsely replied, "You should know that there are two kinds of outflows (*āsrava*). The first is the outflow of afflictions (*kleśāsrava*), which Arhats have forever eliminated.
The second is the outflow of impurity, which Arhats still possess; this refers to things such as excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva. Thus [said] I.
"Leakage [of semen]—this too is the work of Māra, the Heavenly Demon, who has disturbed me; it is only then that this impurity occurs. This is the first matter.
Furthermore, I shall grant successive predictions of enlightenment to my disciples: 'After you have attained the first fruit, the next shall attain the second fruit.'"
[The Buddha] even went so far as to bestow the sequential predictions for those who had attained the fourth fruit. The disciples were filled with doubt and asked their teacher:
"We have heard that one who has realized Arhatship knows all things by himself; yet we do not know anything at all now.
Mahādeva replied: "You do indeed know. There are two kinds of ignorance: first, defiled ignorance, which [Arhats]..."
It has already been severed. Second is non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). Because it exists, you possess this non-afflicted ignorance;
that is, attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Thus, its existence is not precluded. This is the second point. Furthermore, at a later time, the disciples asked:
"Master, you said that we have attained the fruit of Arhatship; therefore, we ought to be without doubt. Doubt gives rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). [Upon entering...]
Upon seeing [the truth], it was immediately eliminated. "How could I have harbored doubts regarding the Triple Gem and the Four Noble Truths? Mahādeva replied, "There are two kinds of doubt.
The first is doubt concerning principle (*tattva-saṃśaya*), which the Noble Ones have already severed. The second is doubt concerning phenomena (*vastu-saṃśaya*).
For instance, there is the case of an Arhat who doubted whether black and red salt were a type of insect; this was the third matter. Furthermore, at a later time, his disciple..."
He asked: "Various sūtras state that an arhat possesses the wisdom-eye and is able to personally realize and know his own liberation.
Why is it that he realizes this only through the entry into transformation, while others have no personal realization at all, such as: 'I am one beyond training'?"
"You have already been ordained; do you not know this at all? Mahādeva replied, "There are two kinds of Arhats.
The first are those of dull faculties, who do not know anything themselves and must be ordained by others. The second are those of sharp faculties, who know it for themselves.
Even among those of sharp faculties, there are still some who do not know, such as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who were foremost in wisdom."

Before the Buddha had granted him the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), he was entirely unaware of it; because he did not know when he would attain Buddhahood, it was only after the Buddha granted him the prediction that he finally understood.
This is the fourth matter. Furthermore, at a later time, Mahādeva reflected upon himself and thought of the many evil transgressions he had committed.
Overwhelmed by anxiety and dread, he cried out in a broken voice, "Alas! Alas! When his disciples heard this, they...
When morning arrived, he asked the Master, saying, "I heard the Great Master chanting 'Alas, alas! last night.

Since you are one who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and has completed what was to be done, for what reason did you chant 'Alas'? Mahādeva replied, "Why do you find this strange? This year I am old and decrepit;
though I have entered the Noble Path many times, I cannot attain it. Only by calling out aloud can I finally see before me. For my sake...
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he invoked the Noble Path; thus, failing to realize this, he cried out, "Alas, what suffering! This was the fifth matter.
It is recorded that there were these five kinds of false speech. Later, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, during the *poṣadha* ceremony of the assembly of monks...

Next, Mahādeva should reflect upon the precepts. Having completed this reflection on the precepts, he shall take the five preceding matters and compose them into a single verse, reciting it while seated among the assembly:
"The causes of leakage for those beyond training are the disturbances of Māra; ignorance and doubt are overcome by others."
The Noble Path does not manifest; it is invoked by means of sound. This is the Tathāgata’s truly pure teaching. If one refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (or *Śāstramūla*), a verse therein states:

"Those who are led by others, being ignorant and full of doubt, enter [the path] through the influence of another; because the cause of the Path arises from sound, this is called the True Buddha-teaching.
If the fourth line were reversed to say, "What you say is not the Buddha-teaching," the meaning would be the same as before. Having thus concluded this...

Verse: When the noble ones—those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who are learned, uphold the precepts, and cultivate pure meditative concentration—hear what he says, there is none who does not express shock and reproach:
"Alas, you foolish man! How could you speak such words? This has never been heard before within the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
They rebuke Mahādeva by reversing the fourth line [of his verse]: "Whose words are these? It is not the Buddha's teaching! Because of this, there subsequently arose...
The dispute arose and continued until dawn without ceasing; there was no peace for the community in the monastery, and all the monastics and laypeople were distressed by it.
After many days had passed and the quarreling still did not subside, the King learned of this and, having prepared his carriage, went to the monastery to settle the matter.

He immediately [inquired] who was right and who was wrong. Mahādeva said to the King: "In the Vinaya scriptures, it is taught that if it concerns the Dharma of Cessation (nirodha-satya), one should accept it."
Regarding the "majority decision": they proceeded by means of a majority vote. Within that assembly, those who were noble ones (*ārya*) were few, while the ordinary ones (*pṛthagjana*) were many.
The noble ones formed one faction, and the ordinary ones formed another. The King issued an order to distribute two kinds of voting sticks (*śalākā*), white and black;

whichever was more numerous would be deemed correct, while the fewer would be incorrect. Thereupon, those noble ones who took up the white sticks were few, while the ordinary monks who took up the black sticks were many.
There is a sacred teaching which says that it was because the Māra King came to cast black voting-slips that [the schism] became so prevalent.
Consequently, the two factions were divided into two schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Sthavira.

When King Aśoka heard that the Sthavira school was small and acting improperly, he became enraged. Upon hearing this, the noble ones departed from the kingdom, whereupon they constructed a leaky boat and...

In the Ganges River, they were about to be drowned and killed. When the Noble Ones realized this, those who had already attained the state of a Noble One lent their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to those who had not yet attained it.
Upon reaching the Ganges, they protected their teeth by holding them with their hands, supporting one another as they flew up into the air like a flight of geese and departed toward the northwest.
Sometimes they transformed themselves into pigeons, and sometimes into geese, heading toward the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
Aśoka saw this and realized with certainty that what the holy ones had said was not false.
He then dispatched a messenger to that country to invite the holy ones to return to his own kingdom. The holy ones all refused.

Consequently, the King went to that country himself and constructed five hundred monasteries, naming them the Pigeon Park Monastery (Kākaṇḍī-vihāra). Later, while traveling, Mahādeva encountered a physiognomist who said of him: "This man..."
"Seven days from now, I shall die. Having heard this, Mahādeva immediately informed his disciples: "In seven days, I shall enter parinirvāṇa...
until at a later time I am cremated with the excrement of white dogs. This was the first division into two schools.
It arose from this. In Sanskrit it is called Mahāsāṃghika; here it is translated as "Great Assembly. In Sanskrit it is called Sthavira; here it is translated as "Elders.
These refer to the five propositions of Mahādeva, which were the cause for the division of the schools. Thus, there are the two aforementioned divisions: the Mahāsāṃghika and the Sthavira.
According to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it says: "The Mahāsāṃghika school distinguishes and explains existence."
Seven; the Mahīśāsaka has eleven. These are called the twenty schools. The eighteen together with the two original ones all emerged from the Mahāyāna.
There is neither right nor wrong; I have spoken this as a prophecy for the future. That is, seven schools branched out from within the Mahāsāṃghika.
The Sthavira school split into eleven sections. To briefly explain the verse: "The Mahāsāṃghika branch is said to have seven divisions" refers to the second line.
Regarding "Tāmraśāṭīya, eleven": this means that eleven sections were split off, making twenty schools in total.
As for "eighteen plus the two original," the Mahāsāṃghika split into seven and the Sthavira split into eleven. This is...
Eighteen [schools], together with the original two, constitute the twenty schools.

As for the statement that "all emerge from the Mahāyāna," this means there is no Hīnayāna that does not branch out from the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is the root, while the two vehicles are the branches.

Regarding the statement that "there is neither right nor wrong," it refers to the fact that each established doctrine is merely a self-clinging to one's own position, which ends in refutation. Therefore...
It is not that these names do not exist; for all twenty schools are the true words of the Buddha, it is also not that these names are incorrect.
When I spoke of my "prediction of the future," the Buddha said: "Within one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall remain of a single flavor, and no disputes shall yet arise.

Beyond those one hundred years, various schools will emerge in confusion. This is what is called the "prediction of the future. If one follows the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* (or *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*), the Mahāsāṃghika...
From within that school, eight branches were divided; together with the root school, there were nine. From the Sthavira school, ten branches were divided;
together with the root school, there were eleven. Previously, according to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, there were eight including the root school, which did not include the Prajñaptivāda school.
However, the Mahāsāṃghika school was generally vast while the Ārya schools were small; therefore, within two hundred years, there were frequent disputes. During this period:
Because their interpretations and views differed regarding the meaning [of the teachings], they subsequently divided into three schools. The first is the Ekavyāvahārika (One-Exposition) school;

since they maintain that both the mundane and the supramundane are all explained as being merely one conventional designation (*prajñapti*), it is called "One-Exposition. For example, when one calls out "fire," it does not burn the mouth and so forth.
The inclusion of other dharmas is termed "the non-attainment of functional efficacy. Second is the Lokottaravāda school.
The tenet of this school is that mundane dharmas arise from inversion, whereas the supramundane dharmas do not arise from inversion;
since both the essence of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) truly exist and can be relied upon, it is called the "Supramundane" school. Third is the Kukkutika school.
This refers to an ancient seer who, driven by lust, fathered offspring upon that mother hen; because they were transmitted through this lineage, they were called the Kukkutika (Chicken-clan).

This school propagated only the Abhidharma and did not propagate the Sūtras and Vinaya, as the Sūtras and Vinaya are considered worldly, expedient teachings. They were ordained monks who lectured on the Sūtras.
They will inevitably give rise to arrogance; because arrogance arises, they shall not attain liberation. Only the Abhidharma is the correct principle.
Later, when two hundred years were nearly full, another school branched out, named the Bahulika (The Many-Hearing School).

These masters extensively studied the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka and profoundly realized the Buddha’s words; they were named the Bahulika after their practice of extensive learning. Not long thereafter, yet another [school] emerged...

It split into one school called the Prajñaptivāda. When two hundred years had passed, there was a renunciant heretic who abandoned his original false teachings and took refuge in the Buddha’s true Dharma;

he was also named Mahādeva. He resided within the Mahāsāṃghika school, and because he re-examined the previous doctrines regarding the five points of Mahādeva—determining what was acceptable and what was not—a dispute arose, leading to a division into three schools, the first of which was the Caitika school.
This refers to the caitya where Mahādeva resided; "caitya" here is translated as "spiritual temple," meaning a shrine where the holy spirit is enshrined.
Thus, it was named after the mountain. Second is the West Mountain Dwelling School (Aparaśaila), and third is the North Mountain Dwelling School (Uttaraśaila).
Since these two schools were not in harmony with this Mahādeva, they consequently resided in the northwest of the mountain. They were named after their locations. In this manner, they were divided.
This constitutes eight schools; including the original [Sarvāstivāda], there are nine. From the beginning of the third century, the Sthavira school remained in harmonious unity.
During the preceding two centuries, this school had no disputes whatsoever. At the beginning of the third century, Kātyāyanīputra entered the order within the Sthavira school;
he first propagated the Abhidharma of the Sthaviras and later propagated the Sūtras and Vinaya. Having thus diverged...
Regarding the fundamental tenets, a dispute subsequently arose, leading to the emergence of the Sarvāstivāda school.

This school maintains that although there is a distinction between the ultimate and the conventional regarding conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, all are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because the three time periods and so forth are substantially existent.
Subsequently, from within the Sarvāstivāda, another school branched off named the Vātsīputrīya; it was so named because its founder was the son of the ancient seer Vātsī. Next, within...
From within the Vātsīputrīya school, four sub-sects branched out. The first is the Dharmottarīya. "Dharmottara" is the title of the master of the Vinaya;

it means that there is a Dharma which can be exalted, or that there may be a Dharma that stands above the multitude, or that he was exceptionally skilled at preaching the Dharma and was thus named Dharmottara, or it is simply the name of the leader of the sect.
The second is the Bhadrayānīya. "Bhadra" refers to the name of the leader of the sect, while "yāni" (or "yāna") refers to lineage or descendants.
The *Arthasiddhāntika* school is the sprout of the Arhat lineage. Third, as for the *Saṃmitīya* school: they establish the definitive meaning;

because their measures and cognitions are without error or delusion, they are termed "correct" (*saṃmita*). All the profound doctrines established by this school are definitively settled and free from error;
therefore, it is called the *Saṃmitīya*. Fourth, as for the *Gokulika* (or *Tāmraśāṭīya*) school: this school is near mountain forests, and because those forests are lush and dense, [it is so named].
This is its name. Next, from within the Sarvāstivāda school, another sub-sect was further divided out, named the Mahīśāsaka.

The founder of this school was originally a sovereign who transformed and governed the land; later, he left the household life to study the Way and returned to his own country to govern through the transformation of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is called Mahīśāsaka (Transforming the Land). Furthermore, from within the Mahīśāsaka school, another sub-sect was divided out, named the Dharmaguptaka, also known as...
The Dharmaguptaka school. This master received and preserved the True Dharma, much like the Sarvāstivādins; thus, it is named after its founder.
Subsequently, from the end of the third century, another school branched out from within the Sarvāstivāda, named Kāśyapīya.

Kāśyapa is a Brahmin clan name. In ancient times there was a rishi whose body was golden-hued; because his radiance eclipsed that of the sun (Kāśyapa), he was named Kāśyapa. He is the founder of this school.
These are their descendants; they are named according to their origin. Next, from the beginning of the fourth century, a further school branched out from the Sarvāstivāda, called the Sautrāntika.
These masters rely solely on the sūtras as authoritative, and do not speak of the Vinaya or the Śāstras; thus, they are the Sautrāntika masters.
Together with the original school, there are eleven schools in total. The original school is called the Snow-Revolution (Himavat-parivarta), and is also called...
Regarding the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*): the Elder [Mahādeva] propagated the Sūtras and Vinaya, but did not propagate the Abhidharma. He opened up the path for its principles and doctrines;
thus, the Elder moved into the Snowy Mountains, and it was named after that location. Second, regarding names derived from metaphors: the Elder proceeded by gradual stages.
It is named as such because it falls gradually like snow being driven by the wind; it resembles snow, and thus it is given that name. Question:
The Ekavyāvahārikas also teach that [dharmas] are conventional, and the Lokottaravādins also teach that [dharmas] are conventional. What is the difference between these two schools? Answer:
The Ekavyāvahārikas maintain that all dharmas possess only conventional names, but they do not say that their substance (*svabhāva*) is also conventional. This...

The Prajñaptivāda school (Sect of Proponents of Designation) maintains that neither essence nor function, nor cause nor effect, possesses any ultimate reality; rather, all things are merely conventional designations. Thus, it differs from the others.

Consequently, its founder established the name "Proponents of Designation" based on his own philosophical perspective. The various differences presented above are all summarized according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* (or *Śāstra on the Wheels of Tenets*).
This distinguishes how the teachings deviate from the single flavor.
As for the second citation of an analogy, it refers to the three subsequent sentences in the commentary. The phrase "water and milk blended together" is based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
That sūtra states: "When a cowherd’s daughter milks a cow, at first the milk is of a single, pure flavor. There is... [text continues]
When people drink it, all their illnesses are eliminated. After some time has passed, water is added to the milk, causing its flavor to become thin and weak.
Although it is now thin and weak, it still surpasses plain water; by drinking it, one’s illness can likewise be cured.

This is a metaphor for the period three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the teachings were divided into many schools. Although the Dharma-teachings had become thin and weak, they still surpassed the teachings of non-Buddhist schools by ten million times.

By practicing solely in reliance upon this [teaching], all attain the fruits of sainthood; therefore, it is said that even bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct surpass those non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who possess superior diligence.
Next, according to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this is illustrated by the analogy of refining gold.
That sūtra states: "During the time when the Buddha was in the world, the Buddha said: 'After my parinirvāṇa, at the beginning of the second century...'"
Since that time, my noble disciples have divided into five schools, or twenty schools, and so forth.
When Śāriputra saw the Buddha’s teaching, he asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, two hundred years after your parinirvāṇa, will there be a division into twenty schools and so forth?"
[The Buddha asked: "If disciples of future generations practice according to which school (*nikāya*), shall they immediately attain the fruit of sainthood?
Which school is the true Dharma of the Buddha? The Buddha replied: "It is like a single gold staff that is divided into five pieces, twenty pieces, and so forth.
Which of these pieces is not pure gold? Śāriputra replied: "All of them are pure gold. The World-Honored One said: "After my parinirvāṇa, although..."
The division into five sections, twenty sections, and so forth, are all the teachings of the True Dharma; by practicing in accordance with them, one shall all attain the fruits [of realization].
Therefore, the commentary states: "It is like refining gold," which refers to the third line of the verse below.

According to a supplementary verse from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, "even when dividing white cotton cloth" refers to the time when human life expectancy was twenty thousand years, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha’s father.
King Kṛkin, having had ten dreams during the night, addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have had ten kinds of evil dreams;
what calamities do they portend? Is it not possible that some wicked person will invade my realm? The Buddha replied, "This matter does not concern the King’s affairs.
This is a prediction regarding the future, when humans shall live for a hundred years: a Buddha will appear in the world, named Śākyamuni. The Buddha...
More than two hundred years after his parinirvāṇa, the noble disciples divided the Buddha’s teachings into twenty schools.

Question: What were those ten dreams? Answer: There is a verse that says: "The great elephant and the well, the parched flour, The sandalwood tree and the wondrous grove, The young elephant and the two monkeys, The broad, firm, and dependent, and strife. The first dream was as follows: [the dreamer] dreamed...
He saw a large elephant in a room that had no doors but possessed windows. The elephant emerged from a window;

its entire body had come out, yet its tail remained caught, obstructed by the frame so that it could not emerge. This was a sign predicting that a disciple of Śākyamuni would sever his attachments and bid farewell to his kin to seek ordination;
yet though his body has left the household life, his mind remains greedy for fame and profit, rendering him unable to practice the Dharma.
It was like an elephant emerging from its body with its tail still not having come out. Second, he saw a single well containing water endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.
There was a person who, though thirsty, looked at this water but did not drink; the well then pursued the thirsty man, and as the man ran, he did not look back at all.
This was a prediction concerning the various disciples of Śākyamuni, both monastics and laypeople, who would experience manifold sufferings in their own bodies.
They are able to hear the Buddha-dharma, yet when the Saṃgha brings the scriptures and the Dharma to lay households to recite and teach them, the minds of the laity do not perceive it;

though they have thirst, they do not drink from it. Third, he dreamed of someone offering one *sheng* of pearls in exchange for one *sheng* of parched flour (*piṣṭaka*), yet the flour would not even be accepted in exchange. This records the legacy of Śākyamuni’s Dharma.
"Disciple, you take the holy words of the Buddha to trade for the wealth and silks of laypeople, yet they are unwilling to trade even for such wealth and silks.
In the fourth dream, you see you take a cubit of sandalwood to trade for a cubit of common wood, yet the common wood is likewise unwilling to be traded.
This records that disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma will take the sacred teachings to trade for secular books and the like."

Even after [the Buddha] had written [the scriptures] and so forth, they still refused to comply. Fifth, he dreamed of a magnificent grove where flowers and fruits flourished, but a band of thieves came all at once and slaughtered them entirely.
This portended that the disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma—the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna—would mutually disparage one another and destroy the Buddha’s teachings.
Sixth, he dreamed of a great many small elephants chasing out a large [elephant].

"Elephant. This refers to a great elephant that goes out with another. This record concerns disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma who, having formed alliances through broken precepts and evil conduct, drove out virtuous and pure bhikṣus. The disciple saw in a dream an extremely inferior monkey.
The multitude of monkeys together supported him as their king; having performed the consecration with the waters of the four great oceans, they established him as king.

This records that among the disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma, those who personally break the precepts and engage in improper conduct will nonetheless support one another, elevating such a person to honor and regarding them as a teacher.
Eighth, he again dreamed of a monkey whose body was smeared with impurities, which suddenly lunged at the others. This records the Śākya... [text ends].
The disciples of Kāśyapa’s Dharma who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct, as well as those who slander pure bhikṣus—this eighth [dream] should actually be the seventh;
there has been a chronological error in their arrangement. In the ninth dream, he sees a single piece of white cotton cloth, worth an immeasurable amount and exceedingly exquisite.
Twenty people then contend over the division of this garment, yet the cloth does not tear.
This prediction concerns the disciples of Śākyamuni, who will dispute the Tathāgata’s teachings and divide them into twenty schools.
Although these many schools differ in their robes and bases of practice, all are the Buddha’s true Dharma; by practicing according to them, one shall all attain the fruits of sainthood.
This refers to the *Pāṃśukūlika* (Wearer of Rags from Dust-heaps). The tenth dream, in which many people attack one another, signifies the [dispersion of the] legacy...
The Dharma-disciples each follow their own school and mutually disparage one another, thereby engaging in strife.
Therefore, the commentary states, "still dividing the white cotton cloth," which refers to the ninth dream. All that has preceded is an illustration by means of analogy.
From here below is the third section, which correctly presents the divergent views; it is divided into two parts. First is the general examination of the heterodox factions. The Commentary states:

"The heterodox factions cause chaos and perversion, and the True Dharma declines. This specifically clarifies their emotional attachments. Regarding the first point, the general examination of the heterodox factions:

What is improper is called *xié* (deviant). It is a mixture of impurity and disorder. *Tú* means merely or casually. *Chè* means sparse or wide. This refers to the traces of the Mahāyāna as taught by the Correct Teaching;

it refers to the texts of the Mahāyāna as taught by the Correct Teaching. A wheel track is called *chè*. The teaching of the Tathāgata is like a wheel track on a road, for there is no further deviation or perversity.

As for the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), [they consist of] the three virtues, the six phrases, and the two... (Note: The final "二" appears to be a fragment or an incomplete enumeration.)
The fifteen [theories of] emptiness and the [notions of] self as real, etc., are explained in detail below regarding the five teachers and three calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
These "heretics" (*cārvāka*) are precisely the non-Buddhists. Alternatively, they are all those within the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) who have become confused;
that is, taking the twenty schools whose mutual views differ and thereby confusing our Buddhist teachings—these are the heretics. Furthermore, taking the Lesser Vehicle as...

They are heterodox followers. What was originally a single flavor of the True Teaching has become a source of discordant views and strife; it is a chaotic distortion of the ultimate traces of the True Dharma.
It is as stated in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*: when the states of Qi and Lu were at war and the army of Qi suffered a great defeat and retreated, the army of Lu intended to pursue them.
Among the troops of Lu was one man named Cao Jue, who said, "Let the army of Lu halt for now; I fear..."

The Qi army was using a deceptive ambush. When the scouts were sent out, if the Qi army’s chariots and horses had been scattered in disorder and their weapons laid crosswise, it would have meant they were truly defeated.
Yet when the scouts looked at the chariots, they saw them arranged in formation; only then did they realize it was actually a retreat.

Now, the followers of the Lesser Vehicle and the non-Buddhists are vying with one another to raise divergent views, throwing my Buddha’s true and correct teaching into confusion. Therefore, it is said:
"Heretical followers cause chaos and confusion. Regarding the phrase "the True Dharma declines" (*zhèngfǎ línyí*):
that which I, the Tathāgata, have taught is called the True Dharma. *Líng* (lur) means high and steep; *yí* (yi) has the sense of being level or plain. The *Erya* states:
"A large mound is called a *líng*; *yí* means level. This refers to various followers of the Lesser Vehicle and non-Buddhists who destroy my true and correct teaching.
Such is the teaching. Furthermore, the various masters of the Hīnayāna claim that the Mahāyāna sūtras were not spoken by the Buddha.
Those of the Hīnayāna who thus slander the Mahāyāna by saying it was not spoken by the Buddha are precisely heterodox followers.

Even if they were to level the mountains of the True Dharma, this is why it is said that the True Dharma is declining. The above constitutes the first section: a general refutation of heterodox followers.

...Furthermore, from here on, the specific attachments of emotional clinging (*saṃjñā-grāha*) are explained separately, divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the emotional attachments of the Hīnayāna; second, the explanation of the emotional attachments of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the first, the analysis of the emotional attachments of the Hīnayāna, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The distinction between the provisional and the real regarding form and mind constitutes their tenet. This refers to...

These are attachments to the conventional as real, which differ from the fundamental tenets of the True Dharma. For example, the Ekavyāvahārikas maintain that both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are conventionally existent;
this is called "attachment to the conventional. That is to say, all phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, possess only a single conventional designation.
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīya masters maintain that both the self (*ātman*) and phenomena exist; this refers to the Sarvāstivādins.
From within [the Sarvāstivāda], they diverge. Thus, their emotional views and attachments hold that all things are my own dharmas and truly existent.

This differs from the Sautrāntika school’s position that the three time periods exist. They maintain that everything is real; that is, the three categories of the dharma-gate and the dharmas of the three time periods are all real.
Alternatively, they reckon that the physical body is the mind-spirit, and that the four great elements and so forth that constitute the five sense organs are all [the self]. This is...
These twenty schools differ in their adherence to [theories of] protection; they differ in their views on whether form, mind, and so forth are provisional or real.

Because they deviate from the True Dharma, those whose tenets differ are said to differ from the school of the Middle Way. The commentary states that "the discourse of existence and non-existence diminishes its reality.

"Diminishes" means to reduce. This is the same intent as that of Buddhapālita and the Sautrāntika school. Question: What is meant by the "discourse of existence and non-existence"? Answer: It is precisely...

Some maintain that external objects are not non-existent in the same way that consciousness is not; this is an exaggeration (*samāropa*). Others maintain that the internal mind is non-existent in the same way that objects are non-existent;
this is a deprecation (*apavāda*), termed "non-existence" (*abhāva*). Question: What is meant by "real dharmas"? Answer: They are neither empty nor existent;

they simply negate the object while affirming the existence of consciousness. To distinguish the mind from emptiness, the Bodhisattvas hold that there is only a single "mind" (*manas*) which is existent, while all else is... [non-existent].
"Provisional" (jia) means that all are non-existent; this detracts from the Mahāyāna’s eight consciousnesses and fifty-one mental factors (caitta-dharma).

If one clings to non-existence, this is precisely the "Blue-Clad" (Qingbian) school. From four hundred years after [the Buddha's passing] until eight hundred years, the Mahāyāna of the School of Emptiness (Śūnyatāvāda) flourished.

This teaching of emptiness clings to the view that all things are empty, making no distinction between the imagined (parikalpita), the perfected (pariniṣpanna), and the dependent (paratantra) natures.

"All are empty" means that internal effects are entirely empty. When Qingbian composed the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there were five masters of śāstras at the same time, known as the "five suns rising," meaning they were born simultaneously in the five regions of India:
Nāgārjuna was in Central India; Aśvaghoṣa was in Eastern India; Āryadeva was in Southern India; Śrīlāta was in Western India; and [Vasuvarman] was in Northern India.
The "soil" refers to Kumāralāta, which signifies the emergence of the five suns. He extensively propagated the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Specifically, in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (The Blue-Eyed One’s Commentary on the *Satya-dvaya-vibhaṅga*), he established logical arguments (*prayoga*) to refute the [notions of] Bodhisattvas and Nirvana. As the verse in that treatise states:

"The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, Like an illusion, they are conventionally produced from conditions. Unconditioned phenomena have no reality; Their non-arising is like flowers in the sky. This is just as the Blue-Eyed One [Kamalaśīla] has explained.
Candrakīrti takes the eight-part *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as his fundamental authority; therefore, he asserts that the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* teach that all things are empty.

As for Bhāviveka, because he does not understand that the Tathāgata’s teaching of emptiness was spoken with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), he clings to the notion that "all things are empty" in a literal sense.

This is Bhāviveka’s nihilistic emptiness (*durgati-śūnyatā*). In the Tathāgata’s *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, the statement that "all things are empty" refers to true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*), which is not [merely] empty.

Because this is "wondrously existent," it is precisely the intended meaning of this sutra to state that objects external to the mind are empty. It does not, however, state that the dependent and perfected natures are also empty.

Qingbian, failing to understand the Buddha’s intention, then clings to the view that everything is empty, asserting even that the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) are empty.

Then, Qingbian’s first inference states: "Conditioned phenomena in their true nature" is the subject (*dharmin*). "Are empty" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because they arise dependently.
The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "Just like a magical illusion. A magical illusion arises dependently, and a magical illusion is empty.

The conditioned nature of true reality is dependently originated and is also empty. This [argument] is a pseudo-inference (*sādhyasama*) and thus possesses fallacies. Specifically, within the reason (*hetu*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished part of the probandum (*ekadeśāsiddha-sādhya*) and the fallacy of the unestablished part of the probans (*ekadeśāsiddha-sādhana*).
Regarding the statement that the reason lacks an established locus: it refers to the subject (*dharmin*) presented in the prior member [of the syllogism]. The intended meaning is...

This is accepted by both schools alike. Since Qingbian establishes "the emptiness of intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena" as the *dharmin* (subject), his statement that "a portion of the *pūrvapakṣa* (the subject) exists" is not accepted by Dharmapāla as having a cause for its arising;
because [the subject] depends upon that [cause], this constitutes the fallacy of the "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*) for one part.
As for the statement that there is a "partial unestablished probans" (*ekadeśāsiddha-hetu*) regarding the example, it refers to the reason...

Regarding the term "arising from conditions" (*pratītyasamutpanna*): it indicates both that which arises from conditions and the other three conditions; thus, the character "arising" (*jāti*) is employed.

As for the analogy of an illusion, since it arises merely through a provisional combination and does not exist by way of causes and conditions, how could the character "arising" apply? Therefore, the word "condition" (*pratyaya*) is combined with "cause" (*hetu*) to form the term "conditioned formation" (*pratyayasiddhi*).
Regarding the statement that "a portion of what is established is unestablished": the analogy of the illusion applies universally to both schools. According to Dharmapāla, the illusion is not...
Emptiness does not exist. The thesis of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) does not apply to that [object]. Thus, regarding the example, the first half exists while the second half does not;

therefore, this constitutes the fallacy of "partial non-establishment of the probandum" (*ekadeśāsiddha*). Second, the syllogism states: "Nirvāṇa is a subject (*dharmin*); it is certainly the thesis of the school of Emptiness; because the reason (*hetu*) is 'because it is unarisen';
the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like a flower in the sky and so forth. This "certainty" refers specifically to the thesis within the school of the Protector (the Buddha).
"Empty. According to our own school, it is not non-empty. You should state that blue is empty according to its own accepted tenet (*svasiddhānta*) in order to distinguish it from other schools.
Since you do not distinguish it from other schools, this is the fault of "non-establishment for the opponent" (*parāprasiddha*).
Furthermore, regarding your statement that "this is dependently originated," how can you say it is empty? Since you commit these various faults, your inference (*anumāna*) is invalid.
[This] is established. Therefore, we know that the Bodhisattva is not empty. If he were empty, for what fruit would you, Qingbian, seek through the Bodhisattva’s cultivation?

Furthermore, toward what dharma would all sentient beings turn in their cultivation? If there is a place to which all sentient beings turn for refuge and veneration, then it is possible to seek a fruit.
Thus, while the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is reckoned as non-existent, the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures are existent. Nirvana...
The "pan" (maṇḍala) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); the four wisdoms are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). These possess both the subject and object of realization;

thus there exist ordinary beings and sages, birth and death, as well as bodhisattvas and nirvāṇa. This shows that among the three natures, it is only the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that is negated.

Therefore, one should know that the correct principle of the Buddha-dharma is this: suffering and its origin are the causes and effects of defilement, while cessation and the path are the causes and effects of purity. II.
The fruit of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is neither empty nor existent; it is the sublime Middle Way of principle, and thus transcends the two extremes.

Because it is free from the deluded conceptualization of external existence, it is called "not existent. Because it is free from the [mere] emptiness of the blue-black evil destinies, it is called "not non-existent.
Thus, by being not non-existent, one correctly accords with the Middle Way. All wise persons should accordingly practice and study this, abandoning those karmas of saṃsāric transmigration.
This is the Unsurpassed Enlightenment. Thus, one may at first cling to existence as firmly as Mount Sumeru, but one must not cling to emptiness even as much as a mustard seed.
Why is it that clinging to emptiness is so? Because such a person stagnates in the extreme of emptiness; the Buddhas declare them to be incurable.
This concludes the section on the divergent paths of heterodox teachers within the Mahāyāna. The above constitutes the fourth of the major sections concerning heterodox factions.
The preceding section concludes with the extensive arising of divergent views.
From here begins the fifth part, which introduces the Middle Way and subsequently presents the heterodox arguments; this is divided into five sections.
First is the explanation of the Master’s name, as the commentary states: "There was a Great Being whose title was Vasubandhu. Second is the praise of his virtues.
1. This refers to the fact that the *Śāstra* states: "He succeeded to the profound wind of the Sages and inherited the noble regulations of the Dharma-King.
2. This refers to the fact that the *Śāstra* states: "He composed this treatise; it is formed by the synthesis of five dharmas. 3.

This refers to the fact that the *Śāstra* correctly reveals the Middle Way, eliminating attachment to the two extremes up to the point of heterodox attachments. 4. This refers to the fact that the *Śāstra* summarizes its profound intent to refute those [misconceptions].

Regarding the deluded attachments: now we further categorize the latter two sections. The fourth section refutes attachments to return to the Middle Way; the fifth section summarizes the profound intent. It is as the Commentary states:
"The text is profound and the principles are vast, making it difficult to examine in detail. These five sections are distinct from one another.
Furthermore, the first part clarifies the person who composed the treatise; this refers to the following two phrases. The word "yuan" (爰) means "at" or "in," and is synonymous with "yue" (粤).
Thus, "yuan-yue" is a single term. The title "Mahāsattva" (Dàshì) is a term of praise and also serves to distinguish him from those of the Two Vehicles.
He is not merely a "great being" (mahāsattva). Because he seeks the great fruit, the great practice, and great nirvāṇa, he is called a "Great Being.

That is to say, he is a being who is a Great Bodhisattva; thus he is named a "Great Being. Some say that one should simply say "Right Being" (samyaksattva), and that this is the appropriate name for a "Great Being."

The "Great Being" (Mahāsattva) is the Buddha. He is named a Great Being because of his unsurpassed state. If one practices the great conduct and seeks the matter of great enlightenment, he is called a Great Being;
this is also true according to principle. The term "Great Being" encompasses both cause and fruit.
However, the "Unsurpassed Being" (Anuttarasattva) refers exclusively to the fruit. The commentary explains: ten "one" (i.e., ten units of one) makes a "sattva" (士); "ten" is the end of numbers.
Furthermore, "one" is the beginning of numbers. This Bodhisattva’s practice of understanding and conduct has both a beginning and an end; therefore, he is called a "Shi" (士).
This is an explanation based on the character itself, which differs from the previous interpretation. He shall appear in the world during the nine-hundred-year period.
The word "jue" (厥) means "his. "Hao" (號) refers to a title of virtue. It is like a person from birth until the age of twenty...

Only upon arrival can one truly receive a name. If a person serves the state as an official, being loyal to the country and fulfilling their duties to the household, then the multitude will bestow upon them a title and appellation.
Because they were loyal to the state, their name was established; Zhang Yan-gong is an example of this.
Likewise, this Vasubandhu was entirely devoted to the Buddha-dharma; he composed treatises to explain the sutras and guided sentient beings.

Because all who are born [in his presence] are able to enter the Buddha-dharma and attain the fruits of sainthood, worldly people compose treatises on account of this Bodhisattva so that the sprouts of all goodness may grow;
thus, he is the world-transcending father of sentient beings, and this is the title established for him.
He was called Devaputra, or alternatively Vasubandhu; this is simply a difference between the Chinese and Sanskrit names.
"Vasubandhu" is the Chinese term; in Sanskrit it is *vasubandhu*, which means "World-Kinsman" (*shiqin* in Chinese). In Sanskrit it is *vasubandhu*.
This person is called Vasubandhu; the old transcription "Poshudou" is incorrect. It is also said that he is named Vasubandhu because he was "intimately known by the world.
Alternatively, it is said that he was obtained through a petition to a celestial deity, and is thus named Devabandhu. Question: Why is he named Devabandhu? Answer:
Because his parents had no offspring and feared that their lineage would be extinguished in the future, they eventually obtained him by petitioning a celestial deity.
In the western regions, there are many who worship celestial deities; specifically, this refers to Maheśvara (Īśvara).
He was named Devaśarman after the deity from whom he sought [protection]. He entered the monastic order within the Sautrāntika school and studied its tenets.

There, he refuted the Sarvāstivāda school in secret by composing the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, thereby covertly undermining the Sarvāstivāda doctrine. Later, there appeared a master of the New Sarvāstivāda school named Saṃghabhadra.
Vasubandhu saw that [Samghabhadra] was secretly refuting the Sarvāstivāda school;

he immediately composed a new forty-fascicle treatise as a Sarvāstivādin, titled the *Abhidharmakośa-puṣpa* (The Flower that Crushes the Abhidharmakośa), which is the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. Vasurāta then pursued him throughout the Five Indies.
Vasubandhu then fled. [The King] asked, "Why did Vasubandhu run away? He replied, "Vasubandhu said that because there was no one to oversee him, he had gone far away.
Fifteen *li* later, when Saṃghabhadra fell ill, he sent his disciples with forty fascicles of his treatise to present to Vasubandhu for his detailed examination.
Upon seeing it, [Vasubandhu] realized its principles were so well-aligned with the *Abhidharmakośa* that he changed the title he had established for it.

The title is the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. This Vasubandhu had previously and subsequently composed five hundred treatises on the Hīnayāna, all of which slandered and reviled the Mahāyāna sūtras, claiming they were not the word of the Buddha.
Because Asaṅga was his elder brother, once he [Asaṅga] understood [Vasubandhu’s] views, he exhorted him to practice the Mahāyāna path.
However, Vasubandhu was unwilling to turn his mind [toward it]. Later, at a certain time, Asaṅga fell slightly ill.
