He sent a disciple to summon Vasubandhu. While Vasubandhu was at his lodging, a disciple of Asaṅga, atop a high tower, recited a verse from the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"If a person wishes to thoroughly know all Buddhas of the three periods of time..."
"One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all things are created solely by the mind. Having heard this verse, he then gave rise to the Mahāyāna mind and cultivated Mahāyāna practices.
Later, he reflected: "I previously slandered and reviled Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras; I shall surely enter hell hereafter.
My prior destruction of the Vaipulya sūtras was entirely due to this tongue. I must now repent for this transgression. He should...
"Only by cutting out your tongue can you offer an apology for your transgression. Vasubandhu immediately took up a blade, intending to cut out his own tongue.

When he was three *yojanas* away from Asaṅga, the latter perceived from afar that Vasubandhu intended to cut out his tongue; he immediately manifested his supernatural powers, shielded the blade with his hand, and said to Vasubandhu:
"You need not cut out your tongue. When a person falls to the ground, they must likewise rise from the ground.
In the past, you used this tongue to slander the Mahāyāna sūtras; now, you should use this very tongue to praise the Mahāyāna sūtras, and that shall be your atonement."
Vasubandhu received these instructions. Later, he composed five hundred Mahāyāna treatises, praising the Mahāyāna and extensively refuting the Hīnayāna;
this *Śata-dharma-śāstra* is one such work among them. He is the "Thousand-Treatise Master" of the Western Regions.
It was at the time of his initial turning of the mind toward the Mahāyāna that he composed the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and subsequently, he composed the *Abhidharmakośa*. That is to say...
Master Cien sighed and said: "Hei isolated his brilliance within the *Abhidharmakośa*. 'Isolated brilliance' refers to the brilliant wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
He manifested conformity with the mundane by teaching existence; this was a demonstration of relying upon the Hīnayāna. He untied the bonds of wisdom within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
As for 'bonds of wisdom,' the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is called the bond of wisdom; now that he has cast it aside, it is termed 'untied. This expresses the liberation of the sages."

He spoke of emptiness; his discernment was cool, his wisdom all-pervasive, and his sagacity exhaustive. He is the Master of the Commentary, whose title is Maitreya (Tianqin), and he is the person capable of composing the treatise who has been thus distinguished.

Second, regarding the praise of his virtues, there are two lines of commentary: "He who succeeds to the profound style of the Ultimate Sage and inherits the mandates and regulations of the Dharma King.
"Succeeds" (*si*) means to carry on a lineage. Just as when a family raises a son, he carries on the lineage of the previous household, so too is this Vasubandhu:
he carries on the lineage of the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*). As for the term "Ultimate Sage," there are three interpretations. First, it is said that Vasubandhu succeeded to [the lineage].
As for Bodhisattva Asaṅga: Bodhisattva Asaṅga is [the stage of] the First Ground (Prathamabhūmi).

Because Vasubandhu was inspired to resolve upon the path by reason of Asaṅga, and because he was Asaṅga’s younger brother, he was a noble practitioner of the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Peak (mūrdhan). The *Shuyao* states that his rank was that of the "Luminous Aggregate" (āloka-skandha).
Daolin was extremely delighted. He maintained that Vasubandhu succeeded Asaṅga Bodhisattva, for Asaṅga was a supreme sage (zhìshèng).
Alternatively, it is said that Vasubandhu succeeded Maitreya, because he took the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as his primary authority; thus, [Asaṅga] is called a supreme sage.
Because he shall attain Buddhahood in the future, he is called a "Sage" (至聖). Thirdly, it means he merely succeeds the Buddha.
Since he does not succeed anyone else, "reaching" (至) carries the sense of the ultimate limit. Furthermore, as a Sage-Dharma King, he is the Ultimate Sage.
This fully exhausts the principle. "Mysterious" (玄) means wondrous. "Wind" (風) refers to a model or standard; thus, this "Mysterious Wind" is the teaching of the Tathāgata. "Heaven" (天)...

Because one is able to succeed to the Buddha’s True Dharma, it is said that one "succeeds to the profound wind (eminent tradition) of the Ultimate Sage. The term "succession" (*shao*) means to continue and inherit.
"Dharma-King" refers to the Buddha himself. Question: Having already used the term "Ultimate Sage," why is the term "Dharma-King" used again later?
Answer: This is merely a phonetic transcription of the family name; there is no further meaning. The "Holy One" (Śāstṛ) is precisely the Dharma King.
Because he has attained mastery over the Dharma, he is a king. Therefore, the sutra continues: "Having already attained mastery over the Dharma, I bow my head to this Dharma King.
*Jīva* is a transliteration; *jīva* means "correctness," and *vitti* means "standard" (*vinaya*).

Thus, the meaning of penetrating the path and transcending conventional barriers was fully realized by both [Vasubandhu] and Maitreya, and they were both able to carry on the lineage; hence it is said that they "succeeded to the mandate and model of the Dharma King.
Third, regarding the explicit clarification of the intent behind this composition, the *Śāstra* states: "The profound creation of this treatise is composed of five elements."
This clearly explains the reasons for composing this treatise. "Yù" (鬱) means to flourish or to be abundant. "Zào" (造) means to compose or to narrate. "Sī" (斯) means this.
That is to say, Vasubandhu flourished and composed this treatise. Question: During the lifetime of the World-Honored One, there were teachings he preached that were not fully understood;
was it therefore necessary for Vasubandhu to further compose this treatise to transform sentient beings? [The Buddha] preached while he was still in the world.

[Question: Since all the Dharmas are already complete teachings, why would a Bodhisattva compose further treatises? [Answer: There is a profound intention behind a Bodhisattva’s composition of treatises.
[Question: What is that intention? [Answer: There are four reasons for composing this treatise: first, to adorn and clarify the Buddha’s sūtras.
It is for this reason that the treatise is composed, because the Buddha’s sūtras are extremely profound, subtle, and difficult to comprehend.
Because of this knowledge, Bodhisattvas compose treatises (*śāstra*) to explain the sūtras; that is, to make the meaning of the sūtras manifest.

Second, they compose treatises in order to suppress heterodoxy and reveal the orthodox. As Ci'en (Xuanzang) said: "When the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are spread like the wind, the heterodox schools lose their elegant doctrines and retreat, whereby the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is made manifest.
Third, Bodhisattvas compose treatises so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. By means of these treatises...

To explain the sūtras so that the True Dharma may manifest and circulate in future generations without its lineage being severed; fourth, to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, which is why he composed this treatise:

to cause sentient beings to eliminate false views and give rise to right view, and by practicing according to the teachings, to transcend the cycle of birth and death and experience the bliss of the Dharma.
Thus, it is called "bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings. Maitreya’s compassion is embodied in these four [purposes].
This is the purpose for composing this treatise. Although there are four purposes, the primary intention is to adorn and clarify the Buddha’s sūtras.

If one does not compose a treatise to explain the sūtras, the profound meanings within them will be difficult to understand. There are five metaphors for the purpose of composing a treatise to explain the sūtras.

The first is like seeing a lotus flower that has not yet opened; although seeing it produces joy, it is not as [joyful] as when it has already opened and its fragrance is rich and pervasive. Thus the Tathāgata said:

First, the meaning and intent of the teachings are profound and hidden; although seeing them may produce joy, it is not as good as composing a treatise to explain them, so that their meaning becomes manifest.
Second, it is like seeing a gold ingot; although seeing it may produce joy, it is not as good as forging it into ornamental jewelry.
The Bodhisattva’s composition of treatises to explain the sūtras is also like this. Third, it is like seeing a sumptuous meal; although seeing it may produce joy, it is not as good as eating it.
Having already known its delicious flavor, it is likewise with the composition of treatises to explain the sūtras. Fourth, it is like receiving a letter of congratulations:

although joy arises upon seeing it, it does not compare to the joy of opening and reading it to learn of the celebratory matter; so too it is with the composition of treatises to explain the sūtras. Fifth, it is like seeing another’s wealth and treasures:
although joy arises upon seeing them, it does not compare to taking possession of them as one’s own wealth; such is the bodhisattva’s composition of treatises.
The explanation of the sūtras is likewise so. The profound meaning of the teachings and doctrines of the various sūtras is difficult to understand;

therefore, treatises are composed to explain the sūtras, as in the four intentions illustrated by the five preceding metaphors. Below, there are three masters who provide different interpretations regarding the purpose for composing the treatise. The first is Sthiramati.
Second, the Fire-Disputation; third, the Protection of the Dharma.
First, regarding the intention behind Vasubandhu’s composition of the treatise as elucidated by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati: it is asked, "Why did the Bodhisattva compose this treatise?"
With what intention? Sthiramati replied: "Because there are three intentions: first, to cause sentient beings to give rise to correct understanding;
second, to cause sentient beings to sever the two heavy obstacles and provide them with salvation; and third, to cause sentient beings to attain the two supreme fruits."

This is the first [point]. Regarding "causing sentient beings to give rise to correct understanding": because all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) are deluded and mistaken, they do not give rise to correct understanding.
Question: Why is it that people of this single stream do not give rise to correct understanding? Answer:

It is because ordinary worldlings are ignorant and, due to their clinging to a self and to phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*), they are entirely [obscured] regarding the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).
Because they do not understand clearly, they are called "deluded. Question: What is meant by "erroneous"? Answer:

For instance, the class of those such as the proponents of the emptiness doctrine of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) and Qingbian (Sthiramati) are termed "erroneous. This is because the Two Vehicles cling to the notion that there is real transformation external to the mind;

thus, this is the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*). These followers of the Two Vehicles are called "foolish" because their understanding is incorrect. As for those such as Qingbian, who cling to [the existence of] evil...
To fall into emptiness and deny cause and effect, or to claim that the dependent and the perfected natures are also empty, constitutes the extreme of nihilism (*apavāda*).

This refers to the erroneous views of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Taken together, these erroneous views of the two vehicles and ordinary beings are collectively termed "delusion.

Now, the author of this treatise, Āryadeva, intends for those who possess such delusions regarding the two kinds of emptiness to give rise to correct understanding; thus, he causes them to... [be liberated from] delusion.

This refers to the arising of understanding; "error" refers to correct understanding. Question: What are called the two emptinesses? Answer: They are the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-śūnyatā* and *dharma-śūnyatā*).

What is now explained as the two emptinesses is precisely the emptiness of the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*) and the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*), because fundamentally there is no essence to either person or phenomena.
This statement of "emptiness" does not mean that there is an emptiness apart from the two attachments; rather, it is simply the two attachments [themselves being empty].

This is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because the essence of self and phenomena has been non-existent from the beginning, this so-called "emptiness" does not mean that there is an emptiness existing apart from the two attachments;

rather, it means that the two attachments themselves are emptiness, having no separate essence. This is the very wisdom that arises by taking emptiness as its object, serving as the gateway through which one enters.
Within this gate of emptiness, one realizes *tathatā* (suchness), which is termed the principle of the two kinds of emptiness. The essence of this principle is not itself empty. This is...

Regarding the term "emptiness" (*śūnya*): it is called emptiness because it is devoid of external, pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita*). Regarding the term "difficult-to-fathom emptiness":

this refers to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) as wondrous existence; that is, the wondrous existence of true emptiness. This correctly negates the two extremes, as will be explained in detail in the following text.
Thus, in Sanskrit it is *śūnyatā*, which means "emptiness. If one says *śūnyatā*, it refers to the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*).
Because one attains the true principle manifested by the two kinds of emptiness, it is the very nature of those two emptinesses; this is an explanation based on the literal meaning (*śabdārtha*).

Some interpret this to mean that "emptiness as suchness" does not exhaust the full meaning of the principle. This is the first [point] intended to produce correct understanding in those who are confused or mistaken.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "I have now composed this treatise because there is confusion and error regarding the two kinds of emptiness."
This is because it gives rise to correct understanding. Thus far, the first part has been to cause sentient beings to develop understanding;
this is why the treatise was composed. From here, the second part is to cause sentient beings to sever their hindrances; this is why the treatise was composed.

Since one can give rise to understanding regarding the two kinds of emptiness, one is then able to sever the two heavy hindrances. As for what are called "heavy hindrances," they possess four meanings, and for that reason they are termed "heavy."
It is an obstruction. First, this heavy obstruction is like a diamond (*vajra*); it is difficult to sever.
Just as all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) in the world can be severed, yet only a diamond is difficult to break, so too is this heavy obstruction difficult to sever, resembling a diamond.
Second, because these heavy afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) exist, it is difficult to transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because these heavinesses exist...

It is an obstruction because it is difficult to cross the four flows (*catur-ogha*). Third, it is because it causes sentient beings to sink into the drowning of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).

Fourth, it causes sentient beings to fall into the wheel of existence and be submerged within the three realms (*tridhātu*); that is to say, this heavy obstruction gives rise to karma and conditions rebirth without cessation.

Because it possesses these four meanings, it is called a "heavy obstruction. If one realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), those obstructions are severed. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says:
The generation of understanding serves to sever the two heavy obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). Because of the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*), these two obstacles arise;

if one realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), those obstacles are severed. This is why Maitreya composed the treatise: it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to sever the two obstacles.
From the third [section] onward, it is for the purpose of establishing the cause and effect for sentient beings. Question: What fruit is obtained?
Answer: One attains two supreme fruits. These two supreme fruits are precisely bodhi. Question: Why are they called "supreme fruits"? Answer:
"Supreme" means extraordinary or preeminent; "fruit" means the recompense for causes. That is to say, by practicing the causes over three kalpas, one obtains the fruit of favorable benefit.
This is a supreme fruit because the cause is supreme, and thus the fruit is also supreme. Cause and fruit mutually encompass one another.

The two vehicles attain two fruits that are not ultimately complete; therefore, they are not "supreme fruits. The ultimate two fruits transcend and surpass the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the two vehicles;
thus, they are called "supreme fruits. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The severing of hindrances refers to the attainment of the two supreme fruits.
Question: Regarding the phrase "severing of hindrances," what are these hindrances? What are their characteristics? How does one attain the two supreme fruits?
The answer states: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says that by severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) which cause rebirth, one realizes true liberation;

and by severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which hinder understanding, one attains the state of a Great Bodhisattva. Question: Why is the afflictive obstruction called "that which causes rebirth"?
Answer: The fifty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "All afflictions are capable of causing rebirth," referring specifically to those that are innate (*sahaja*).
It is "discriminative" (*vikalpita*). It can initiate karma and provide the moisture for rebirth, causing the cycle of birth and death within the three realms to never cease;

therefore, it is called "continuing rebirth" (*anuvartaka*). Before the stages (*bhūmi*), it is both discriminative and innate (*sahaja*); from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is exclusively innate. It is thus named "continuing rebirth" because it provides the moisture for the retribution of the ten kings.
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are precisely the fetters; that sentient beings have not attained liberation since beginningless time is entirely due to being bound by afflictions.

Now, having severed the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that cause rebirth, one is freed from these fetters and thus attains the body of true liberation, which is also called the *dharmakāya*.
Question: One attains the *dharmakāya* by severing the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Why, then, do you say it is attained by severing afflictions?
Answer: This is stated in reference to the preeminent object of obstruction. By severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one attains the body of true liberation;

this very *dharmakāya* is both liberation and the *dharmakāya*. Because the two types of emptiness are manifested simultaneously, that which is specifically mentioned here is the afflictions themselves.

Question: Why is the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) called an "obstruction to understanding"? Answer: It is not that the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are themselves the obstruction; rather, it is the [obscuration] that obstructs...
It is so named because it is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Fourth, *nirvāṇa* is called the "object of knowledge," while that which is inferior to wisdom is called the "knower.

Furthermore, that which is inferior to wisdom is the mind of conceptualization; specifically, this is the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Because it can obstruct the superior wisdom regarding the object of knowledge, it is called the "obstruction to the object of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound, meaning "the obstruction of what is known. By severing this obstruction, one attains Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). That is to say...

The Bodhisattva Sthiramati explains: Because the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu possesses these three kinds of benefit—namely, causing the arising of the mind of understanding, causing the severance of hindrances, and causing the attainment of the fruit—he composed this treatise.
From here below is the second section, which clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva. This intention is to cause sentient beings to realize the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*);
for this reason, the treatise was composed. That is to say, it causes non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox;

it is said that the non-Buddhists reveal this treatise, and it is also said that those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) reveal this treatise, causing them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and return to the Great Vehicle. All are caused to realize and penetrate [this truth].
Because of the two kinds of emptiness, one realizes the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

Since non-Buddhists such as the Sāṃkhyas cling to the three qualities (*guṇa*), the six categories (*padārtha*), and the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), and since the adherents of the Hīnayāna cling to the reality of dharmas because they hold that things exist externally apart from the mind, the Bodhisattvas composed these treatises so that those who have attained the realization of the two emptinesses might realize the principle of consciousness-only. Question: How can one cause others to abandon the false attachments of the non-Buddhists?
It refers to the realization of the principle of the two kinds of emptiness. The answer is: These non-Buddhists have been blinded by ignorance since beginningless time;

not knowing the correct principle, they instead cling to false interpretations. [The notion that] "space and so forth are all produced by ignorance" refers to the specific ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) that directly deludes one regarding the truth of the [Four Noble] Truths—a state of non-cognition associated with the nine types of shared delusion. Because it is a form of incorrect knowledge (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), for this reason...

Regarding "false attachments": because the Bodhisattva’s compassion is such, he composed this treatise through three intentions and four principles to refute the false attachments of these non-Buddhists and cause them to return to right view.

Specifically, because this treatise reveals [the truth] to the non-Buddhists, it enables those who have realized the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) to cease clinging to a self-soul (*ātman*).

This is precisely what constitutes realizing the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). Regarding the "two" [referring to the second category]: this refers to the attachments of the Inner Way (Buddhists) and the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Therefore...

This is the composition of the treatise. The preceding section refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who reveal this treatise; the subsequent passage refers to the Hīnayāna of our own tradition (Buddhism), which expounds this meaning because the Hīnayāna clings to existence.

This indicates that their attachment to phenomena has not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Now, by showing this text, one penetrates the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).
That is to say, it is shown so that those with the false wisdom of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists—who cling to a self and to phenomena—may come to understand [the truth].
Therefore, we know that Vasubandhu composed this treatise so that sentient beings might give rise to correct wisdom, penetrate emptiness, and realize the ultimate principle. Question:

Is this interpretation not merely a product of your own imagination? Answer: Because the holy teachings and correct principles possess a fixed standard of authority. As the first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Furthermore, in order to reveal and dispel the erroneous attachment to a self and phenomena, and for those who are deluded regarding consciousness-only, so that they may realize the two kinds of emptiness."
This is because one knows the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as it truly is. The above concludes the second section, which clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva.
From here on is the third section, which clarifies the meaning of Dharmapāla; that is, Vasubandhu composed this treatise for the purpose of refuting erroneous attachments.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Furthermore, there are those who are confused regarding the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Some maintain that external objects, like consciousness, are not non-existent; some maintain that internal consciousness, like external objects, does not exist; and some maintain that while the functions of all phenomena are distinct, their substance is identical."
Alternatively, some maintain that there are no mental factors (*caitta*) distinct from the mind (*citta*).

To refute these various divergent attachments and to enable them to attain a correct understanding of the profound and subtle principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), this treatise was composed.

To interpret the intention of Dharmapāla here is identical to his previous intent in refuting heterodoxy and revealing the correct doctrine. As the Bodhisattva Qingbian stated: "Within the gateway of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), both mind and objects exist."

There is. From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), both mind and mental objects are empty. Alternatively, one might hold that mental phenomena (*caitta-dharma*) are non-existent just like external objects.

Or, if one is a Sarvāstivāda master, one might hold that external objects are not non-existent, just as consciousness is not. Vasubandhu’s intention in composing this treatise was to refute these two extremes—the dual attachments to emptiness and existence.
This is why he composed the treatise; it is precisely the aforementioned *Śata-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas) which refutes [the attachment to] blue and clarifies [the nature of reality].
This refers to the equal grasping at emptiness. As for the subsequent mention of the "two kinds of selflessness," the intention is to dispel the attachments held by the Sarvāstivādins;
it is for this reason that this treatise was composed. This is precisely the analysis of the teachings of the third period, which are the teachings that are neither empty nor existent.

The three masters mentioned above explain the intention behind Vasubandhu’s composition of this treatise. Therefore, the commentary states: "He earnestly composed this treatise," which refers to the five dharmas.

The "synthesized" refers to the five categories of phenomena (*pañca-dharma*). A question is asked: "Asaṅga was at the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat) or *mūrdhan* (Summit), which are stages prior to the [first] bhūmi.
How could he have composed the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*? Are not the hundred dharmas something composed by a Bodhisattva of the first bhūmi? The answer is:

"A Bodhisattva of the first bhūmi penetrates the 'Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas' (*śata-dharmaka-prakāśamukha*). The Bodhisattva Asaṅga merely expounded it; he did not compose it himself. This is a general clarification of the exposition.
This is the intent of the composition.
Fourth, "Discriminating and Correcting to Reveal the Middle Way and Eliminate Adherence to the Two Extremes" (or, as some say, "The Fourth: Refuting Adherence and Returning to the Center").

The Commentary states: "It opens the two gates of existence and emptiness and clears away the divergent attachments to the two extremes. Regarding the word "opens" (*qǐ*), it means to open [the gate of] existence.
There are two gates to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The "Gate of Existence" refers to the hundred dharmas, as they serve to open up one's attachment to the views of emptiness.

The "Gate of Emptiness" refers to the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*), as they open up the realization that there are no real dharmas existing external to the mind. In composing this treatise, Vasubandhu first presents the hundred dharmas.
This is because Qingbian held the false view that the miserable realms were empty;

for Qingbian adhered exclusively to the doctrine of emptiness, whereas at this second stage, the teaching of the Great Vehicle on emptiness has been established, and now the hundred dharmas are explained as wondrously existent. Therefore, this refutes Qingbian’s deluded attachment to emptiness.

The subsequent mention of the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*) is the gateway of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*). It refutes the Sarvāstivāda attachment to the real existence of the three time periods (*tri-kāla-sad-vāda*).

It further addresses those who claim that atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute existence through the acquisition of the three [characteristics] and the acquisition of that acquisition (*prāpti-prāpti*), thereby clinging to the notion of external, substantial reality. These two forms of selflessness serve to negate such attachments to existence;
they are the Mahāyāna teaching of the Middle Way, which is neither existence nor emptiness. This [teaching] emerged after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, reaching nine hundred years [after his passing].

Throughout the year, these one hundred dharmas are explained; that is to say, they serve to exclude the two extremes, for during the first two periods [of teaching], there was attachment to extremes. The teaching of the first period is the "teaching of existence.

When the World-Honored One spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of "existence," he meant existence in terms of the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature. He taught that consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is not empty.
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda school failed to grasp the Buddha’s intent and thus falsely clung to the notion of real entities external to the mind, remaining stuck in attachment.

This is the second [point]. Regarding those who propound emptiness, their intention is to refute the attachment to existence. That is to say, they exclusively teach the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, speaking solely of emptiness.

As for the Buddha’s intentional teaching of emptiness, it refers only to the fact that the parikalpita (imagined nature) is empty; he did not say that the paratantra (dependent nature) and pariniṣpanna (perfected nature) are empty.
Those such as Bhāviveka failed to grasp the Buddha’s intention and thus falsely adhered to the notion that whether it be form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), [they are empty] because of causes...
The result—bodhi and nirvāṇa—is entirely empty; this is precisely to stagnate in the extreme of nihilism (*apavāda*).

During the third period, the World-Honored One taught the doctrine that is neither empty nor existent, which equally negates both extremes; these include the *Avataṃsaka*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Ghanavyūha*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras.

The "Hundred Dharmas" and "Consciousness-Only" were taught by Vasubandhu; he stated that the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is empty, while the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) [are not].
This exists. A question is asked: "Maitreya [Tianqin] is a bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Why does he not practice for himself, but instead compose treatises?
What is the intent behind opening the two gates of 'existence' and 'emptiness'? The answer is: There are two intentions. First, to generate great wisdom;
second, to generate the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Furthermore, it is to cause all sentient beings to give rise to great gratitude and virtue, and thus contemplate all...
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been deluded and obscured regarding their true nature, erroneously clinging to a self and to phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).

Due to these false attachments, they are either obstructed or driven to give rise to the three karmas, cycling through saṃsāra without end. Their arising follows emotional attachments and occurs in pursuit of views and opinions.

Those who cling to emptiness are deluded regarding both principle and phenomena, asserting that everything is utterly non-existent; those who revel in existence claim that the self and phenomena are all real. Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
The World-Honored One appeared in the world and established this subtle exposition. Its colors are variegated like engraved gold; its literary elegance conceals profound principles.

Thus, it enables those in the evil realms to distinguish between good and evil, while ensuring that even those of unyielding nature realize that all things arise through conditions and exist as illusions.

For this reason, he first clarified the hundred dharmas to dispel the clinging to emptiness, and subsequently described the non-existence of a self to eliminate the clinging to existence. It is because of these causes and conditions that [this treatise] now proceeds.
Chen Yaluon’s commentary states: "Therefore, the sub-commentary says that [this work] opens the two gates of existence and emptiness. To 'open' (pi) means to remove.
By means of the hundred dharmas, it opens up and clarifies the views regarding emptiness; furthermore, it can remove those who cling to emptiness. By means of the two kinds of selflessness..."
This excludes the views held by those of the two vehicles and so forth. By means of these one hundred dharmas and the two kinds of selflessness, one opens up [the path] from the two extremes.
Thus far, the correct analysis has revealed the Middle Way; the refutation of attachment to the two extremes is hereby concluded.
This concludes the profound meaning through the five successive summaries. The commentary states: "The text is profound and the principles are vast, making them difficult to explain in detail.
To say "profound" (*sui*) means deep and far-reaching. "Principles" (*li*) refers to the underlying logic. "Vast" (*bo*) means extensive and broad.

Because the principles are thus deep and far-reaching and extensive and broad, they are difficult to explain in detail. The particle *yan* is a grammatical auxiliary; it is explained in the *Qieyun*. This constitutes the summary.

Above, there have been five topical sections (*pañca-dvāra*), which collectively constitute the fifth major section, opening up that Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) and only then presenting the refined discourse.
From here below is the sixth major section, which briefly presents the title to distinguish it from other texts; this is divided into three parts. First, the general...
The headings: 1. General Explanation; 2. Specific Explanation; 3. Summary. From the initial title down to the specific sub-headings of the individual sections constitutes the general explanation.
Second, from "The Great Function of Apophatic Definition" down to "designated as a number" constitutes the specific explanation.
Third, the summary is indicated by the commentary’s statement: "Therefore, regarding the Mahāyāna... down to "a brief record of names and numbers. Three.
The sections are distinct.
First, regarding the general explanation of the title, it is divided into two parts: first, the general explanation of the seven characters above;
second, the general explanation of the eight characters below. This is the first part. The Commentary states: "The initial reference to 'Great' serves to signal the general scope of the entire work."
"Name" (*ming*) means "foremost," "head," "beginning," or "origin. "To proclaim" (*cheng*) means "to know"; if one acts as a proclaimer, one extols and spreads virtuous deeds.
The above follows the interpretation in the *Yunji* (Rhyme Collection). Others also explain it as "to speak. Thus, these seven characters are explained.
There are three phrases in the commentary, divided into two parts. First, one phrase serves as the title; the following two phrases constitute the formal explanation.
Regarding the title: the term "first" (shou) is as explained previously; that is, the subsequent two phrases explain the preceding one.
That which is first titled the *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra* is the ultimate proclamation of the general grand framework;

that which designates the comprehensive name of this single treatise is precisely that ultimate proclamation of the grand framework. "General" (*zǒng*) carries the meaning of gathering and binding together; by citing these seven characters, [the title] establishes the whole.
The meanings of the hundred dharmas are all fully encompassed therein. "Ultimate" (ji): according to the *Yunjie* (Explanation of Rhymes), "ultimate" means to select with precision;
selection is precisely what constitutes the sublime. "Vast" (hong) means great. "Framework" (gang) refers to a net; it also means great. One should say that the vast is itself the framework.
It is like a fishnet where large ropes are installed and called the framework. By merely grasping the framework, the mesh of the net becomes orderly. Merely...
By raising the seven characters of the title of this treatise, the five categories and one hundred dharmas below are naturally brought into perfect order.

Thus it is said: "When the net is raised by its handle, all the meshes are spread; when the collar of the robe is lifted, all the hairs are aligned. "The ultimate chant" refers to the primary chant, the initial teaching;
it carries the sense of comprehensive inclusion. It signifies that this Mahāyāna Dharma is the most supreme teaching; therefore, it is so called.
"Extremely Chanting. "Chanting" means to proclaim. It refers to the initial proclamation and primary heading of seven characters, the very pinnacle of the beginning of this entire work.

Although there are many meshes in a net, it is by relying on the main ropes that it attains order. Although there are one hundred dharmas, these seven characters serve as the guide for all one hundred dharmas;
thus, they are like the main ropes. As for the term "banner," it refers to a signal flag. Just as a flag leads the way from the front, so too do these words.
Following the *biao* (preface), there are fifty treatises; this constitutes the "Great Army" about to set forth.
The banners and flags must necessarily precede it, for once the insignia of office (*jinjie*) is present, one knows that there is a Commander-in-Chief (*jiandu shi*) leading the Great Army.

Thus, first the seven characters are raised, followed by the *Dacheng* (Mahāyāna) and so forth, totaling one hundred dharmas. These are the insignia of the five categories and one hundred dharmas. Therefore, they represent the banners of each individual section.
This is the general name. Regarding the second point, the total explanation of the eight characters below, the commentary (*śāstra*) states later:

"The names and numbers briefly recorded within the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* section" refers precisely to these eight characters. The following two lines explain the preceding line. Question: [Why is this so?]
What is meant by "a brief record from within the Section on Original Matters" (*Benshi-fen*)? The answer is: it is the grand system for compiling categories of meaning.
Furthermore, what is meant by "the names and numbers briefly recorded from within the Section on Original Matters"? It refers to the specific headings of one selected portion.

The term "compilation" (*zǎn*) signifies the meaning of gathering together. "Categories" (*lèi*) refers to various classes, such as the mind and mental factors, as well as the five categories of phenomena.

"Hóng" means great; for example, in the deep autumn, when the nine-eyed *hóng* geese follow the sun toward the south, those that are large are called *hóng*, while those that are small are called *yàn*.
Now, regarding the term "Hong" (鴻), it takes its meaning from "greatness. Regarding "You" (猷), it means "the Way," "pervasion," "exhaustiveness," and "dharma.
The intended explanation is that this *Bai-fa-lun* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas) records the essential meaning of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, exhausting all its great principles;

therefore, it is called a compendium of the "Great Way" (*hong-you*) of the categorized meanings. That is to say, it is the great dharma of the categorized meanings. As for "simplifying the specific headings of one division," it means to simplify...
This is the selection of the meaning. One should apply this distinction to the characters. This "distinction" (*jian*) is glossed as "pure.

"A single portion" refers to the sense of being one part within that treatise. It is called a "distinct title" because the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, from within the *Mūlabhūmi* (Basic Section), compiled those related dharmas to compose this *Śata-dharma-śāstra*;
hence it is termed a distinct title. Thus concludes the general explanation of the title.

The second [section], the separate explanation of the title, is divided into two parts: first, the individual explanation of the seven characters beginning with "Great" (大); second, the separate interpretation of these seven characters.
Regarding the phrase "the Great Function is established by negation" (大用遮詮): this refers to the first of the eight characters beginning with "Great Matter" (大事).

When the commentary states, "The title of the treatise is established as 'The Treatise on the Path' through the designation of the Great Function by way of negation," at the point of the character "already" (已), there is only negation (遮詮) and no [affirmation].

This expresses [the meaning] through negation; it merely excludes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is called "Great" only by name. What kind of "Great" is this? Is it a Great Person, a Great Dharma, or a Great Deity?
It is simply because it possesses the sense of "Great," as it is able to exclude the Lesser. It is like calling out "fire" to exclude what is not fire;
there is no positive, affirmative meaning [in the word itself]. As for what that "fire" is—[if one asks] is it a firefly? It is merely...

There is the meaning of affirmation (*vidhi*). The meaning of negation (*pratiṣedha*) is like fire; there are also cases where it expresses affirmation. For instance, when one says, "Bring hot fire," this also lacks both negation and affirmation.
Fire does not express itself; it merely negates [the opposite]. If it were to further express [affirmation], one would have to say "Mahāyāna" twice; thus it would be both negating and affirming.
If someone were to formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), then "bringing hot fire" would be that which is exclusively affirmative.
No. How does this differ from what was said previously? In the previous statement, "at the time of fire," there was only negation (*pratiṣedha*) and no affirmation (*vidhi*).

In the subsequent statement, "hot fire," there is only affirmation. If you say it is only affirmation, then in the second phrase one would not mention "fire," because "fire" carries the meaning of negation.
Therefore, "hot fire" is necessary as the meaning of both negation and affirmation. This may be so; however, it is not necessarily so.

Regarding this matter, one must formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). If it were said that the four propositions are fixedly separated, then one should know that even regarding the two truths (*satyadvaya*), there must likewise be four propositions.

What is said here concerning "Great" (*mahā*) merely excludes the "Small" (*hīna*); when both "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) are mentioned together, they possess both the sense of exclusion and affirmation.

If the commentary mentions the single character "Great" alone, it is merely an exclusionary definition (*paryudāsa-prajñapti*), not an affirmative definition (*vidhi-prajñapti*) for establishing the name.

Indeed, there is also explicit definition (paryāya) according to reality, because the character "vehicle" (*yāna*) is present. To speak of a "vehicle," it is so named because of its function of transporting [beings].
Just as ships and carts have the utility of movement, this Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) has the utility of transporting sentient beings to the other shore;
therefore, it is called a "vehicle. Thus, the Commentary states: "Vehicle is so named because of its function of transporting. The Commentary further states: "The hundred dharmas..."

Regarding the statement that "the essence and function are presented together, and the agent and object are raised simultaneously," there are three interpretations. First, Master Zhang Jing says: "The 'hundred' refers to the essence;
'dharmas' refers to the function. 'Clarifying' (ming) refers to the agent, which is wisdom; 'gate' (men) refers to the object of perception.

Therefore, it is said that the essence and function of the hundred dharmas are presented together, and the agent and object of the clarifying-gate are raised simultaneously. Jianfu raises an objection, saying: "As for what was stated previously..."

The "hundred dharmas" are the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Now, since this "gate" (*mukha*) is also an object of cognition, there would be the fault of having two layers of objects within a single topical heading;
that is, the error of exceeding the proper measure. Furthermore, another interpretation states: the hundred dharmas are the objects of cognition and possess both essence and function;
it clarifies that these are the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*), while the "gate" is the provisional function upon wisdom. Thus, the fault of over-explaining is also avoided.

Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Hundred" (*śata*) signifies number; there is no need to discuss essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*vṛtti*). It simply means that within one hundred dharmas, there is both essence and function.

Why is this so? Because within these dharmas, at times there is their own inherent nature, which is therefore called "essence," and at times they possess the sense of generating understanding, which is called "function."
"Function" (*yòng*) refers to the simultaneous presentation of both the essence and function of the hundred dharmas. Regarding "the gate that can comprehensively encompass":
"clarity" (*míng*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the subject that perceives; "gate" (*mén*) is the gate traversed by wisdom, and thus the hundred dharmas themselves constitute the gate traversed.

This is precisely the object of focus (*ālambana*). There is no separate wisdom; when one traverses the hundred dharmas, the sense of having the power of skillful means (*upāya*) is called the "object of focus.
"Gate" (*mukha*) refers to the hundred dharmas; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. The gate is that which wisdom traverses, and is therefore the function (*vṛtti*);
the hundred dharmas are the substance (*svabhāva*). Taking the hundred dharmas as the gates to be traversed is likewise immeasurable and manifold.
This is an error regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*). This interpretation is superior and also accords with the text of the *Śāstra*.

For in the *Śāstra*, the "gate" (*mukha*) is explained by presenting both the subject and the object together. If one were to claim that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the essence and the "gate" is merely a function of wisdom, that would be incorrect.
Why is it that wisdom (*prajñā*) is what can traverse [the path]? Furthermore, why can the "gate" (*mukha*) also be what traverses?

To clarify the distinction between the gate as the agent and the object: wisdom is the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), while the gate is the objective perceived (*ālambana*). Thus, the objects among the hundred dharmas (*śatadharmāḥ*) are the gates.

Regarding the single character "treatise" (*lun*) in the subsequent commentary, the sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "That which circulates and returns to its source is termed a 'treatise'. This is the division.
Second: first, the purpose of the treatise (*śāstra*), which consists of the first two lines; second, the essence of the treatise, which consists of the latter two lines.
"Treatise" (*lun*) has the meaning of coming and going; "coming and returning" is called "cycling. "To investigate" (*yan*) means to grind; "to penetrate" (*qiao*) means to realize.

One must circulate through and investigate the principles of the subtle apertures before one can thoroughly master the True Doctrine (*zhensong*). "Thoroughly" (*jiu*) means to exhaustively investigate;

"thoroughly" (*chang*) means to penetrate. That is to say, by exhaustively investigating and penetratingly clarifying, the true exposition is revealed. Second, regarding the discernment of the essence (*ti*), the Commentary (*shu*) states:
In Sanskrit it is called *mātṛkā*, which is translated here as "Root Mother" (*benmu*). This Root Mother is sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because of this sublime wisdom, one brings to perfection merit and knowledge, and it is able to give rise to and grow all dharmas; therefore, it is named "Root Mother. Furthermore, this sublime wisdom possesses many skillful means;
it investigates the root and exhausts the source, its function being discernment, and it is able to produce intellectual understanding. Hence, it is called "Root Mother."
Furthermore, this *mātṛkā* is the treatise (*śāstra*). The treatise investigates the nature and characteristics [of phenomena], thereby giving rise to sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
Once sublime wisdom has arisen, it understands and is able to refute the subtle [defilements] that subsequently give rise to further treatises.

Because there are questions and answers based on the treatise, and because knowledge arises from these questions and answers, it is said that the treatise is the mother of knowledge. Therefore, it is designated as a "treatise. Thus ends the separate explanation of the first seven [categories].

This is for the sake of specialization. Regarding the second point, the formal explanation of the meaning of the *Lülu* (Abridged Record), the Commentary (*Shu*) answers:

"It is the discerning collection of essential tenets that constitutes this elegant treatise. Here, "discerning" (*zhēn*) means to select; "collecting" (*jí*) means to compile; and "essentials" (*yào*) refers to the concise key points.

Thus, it is the compilation of these concise and essential passages, namely these One Hundred Dharmas (*Bǎifǎ*). Furthermore, it does not take those texts in their entirety. As for the statement that the extensive text is detailed and comprehensive...
Regarding the phrase "because it belongs to other sections" (*tā-bhū-ji-gu*) and so forth: that which is recorded as "other sections" refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

All the elaborate textual expressions of the teaching that serve as exponents belong to its extensive explanations. As for the term "belonging" (*shǔ*), its pronunciation is the same as "candle" (*zhù*);
it means to entrust. If pronounced with the lips slightly open, it means to consign or delegate. Question: Why does this [text] not employ the extensive passages to establish itself?
Regarding the "One Hundred Dharmas" (*Śata-dharma*): The commentary states, "The *Śāstra* is abbreviated so as not to employ redundant words.

Here, "suppressed" (*yì*) means "forced" or "restrained. According to the *Qieyun*, it also means "to press down" or "to constrain. Thus, it signifies that these one hundred dharmas are free from prolixity.

Because this *Śata-dharma-śāstra* has been established by extracting the essential expressive terms (*vācaka*) and the expressed meanings (*vācya*) from the extensive treatises, it is called an "abbreviated record. Chapter One.
Third, regarding the specific analysis of their names: the *Śāstra* (Commentary) states that "that which expresses and designates by calling forth is called 'name' (*nāman*).

This means that names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), phrases express distinctions (*viśeṣa*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) are the basis for these two. However, it is taken here that syllables alone are capable of expressing intrinsic nature.
Question: Since sounds, names, phrases, and syllables can also express and designate all phenomena (*dharma*), why is it said only of [syllables]?

[Regarding] "name" (*nāman*): it does not mention the other two [phrases and syllables]. The answer says: A name expresses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). By citing this "name," the other two are included.
If one were to take "sound" (*ghoṣa*) or "syllable" (*vyañjana*), it would be too narrow; if one were to take "phrase" (*pada*), it would be too broad.

Now, taking "name" avoids being either too broad or too narrow, as it occupies the middle ground. One simply takes "name. Fourth, regarding the separate explanation of the number, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: There are...
That which is measured is designated as "number" (*saṃkhyā*). Because it possesses limits that can be known and its quantity can be measured, it is called "number.
The above constitutes the second section, the specific title. Thus far there have been two parts: first, the general explanation of the title.
Second, the separate explanation of the title. These two [versions] differ slightly; this concludes the correct explanation of the title.
From here on, it is the first [section] of the treatise itself; therefore, it is called the *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*. The above six sections differ; this concludes the introduction.

The end of the first volume of the *Hyōyu Shō* on the *Bai-fa-lun*, and the end of the second volume of the *Hyōyu Shō* on the *Bai-fa-lun*, all state that these are nothing but consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Furthermore, if one were to say that there is no consciousness-only, then conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) would not exist; for conventional truth is dependent [upon it].
Because its essence is mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), since conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) does not exist, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is likewise unattainable.
This is because the two truths, conventional and ultimate, are mutually dependent. If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not exist, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also dispelled.
If one says that both ultimate and conventional truths are empty, then everything is utterly obliterated. One should know that this is what the Buddhas describe as being "incurable."

All phenomena possess both emptiness and non-emptiness; they transcend the extremes of existence and non-existence, correctly abiding in the Middle Way. The above has distinguished how the establishment of emptiness through Consciousness-Only is difficult to explain.
From here on is the fifth [section], concerning the objection that material forms are not mind. The objection states: "If all locations of material form also have consciousness as their essence..."
In that case, consciousness should likewise be like the characteristics of form—evolving as a single, uninterrupted continuity.

Since the mind would then indeed evolve with intervals, the characteristics of form and so forth would be real; mountains, rivers, and the great earth, which are perceived by the world, would be such that the Way exists right before one’s eyes.

If there are real forms external to the mind, how can one say that "there is only consciousness"? Mountains and rivers never cease to exist, whereas the perceiving mind sometimes arises and sometimes does not arise.
Since forms and such are of a single nature and remain stable, how can they be established as "only consciousness"? The intention [of this objection] is:
the mind undergoes arising and ceasing, yet objects do not follow the mind in its arising and ceasing; how, then, can they be established as "only consciousness"?

Below, the Master of the Treatise replies: Because all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have falsely produced a continuous interpretation, the seeds of linguistic habituation reside within the eighth consciousness.
Through the power of that habituation, these mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise and evolve in succession.
These mountains, rivers, and the great earth, which are transformations of the eighth consciousness, are the "aspects" (*nimitta*) of the eighth consciousness.
This is divided [into two parts]. It is called "not separate from the mind"; therefore, one knows that there is only consciousness and no external objects.

If mountains and rivers are considered in relation to the sixth consciousness, then while the sixth consciousness is intermittent, the appearance of mountains and rivers is continuous; this is explained in reference to the eighth consciousness, because they are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) directly transformed by the eighth consciousness.
When sentient beings perish, those mountains and rivers—the first layer of the *nimitta-bhāga*—perish along with those individuals.
Therefore, one knows that nothing exists apart from the transforming mind. Thus, it is known that the principle of "no external objects, only consciousness" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is established.
From here below is the sixth section, which addresses contradictions with one's own tenets through direct valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). The objection states:

External objects such as form and the other five sensory realms are clearly perceived and realized by the five consciousnesses through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since these are obtained through direct perception, external objects truly exist; this is the position of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

This is universally established. How could the Master of the Treatise then deny it by asserting that there are only consciousnesses? In the treatises on Logic (Hetuvidyā), there are three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which serve as the standard for determining existence and non-existence.

If inference (*anumāna*) and the other two were not [valid], one would give rise to attachments through mental inference, such as holding that things appearing as objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are substantially existent.
The phenomena of the five sense-objects and so forth are precisely the five and eight consciousnesses, because they are directly realized. If one says:
If there are no external real objects, how can there be inferential or direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind? When direct perception of the mind exists, it directly realizes external objects.

Since external objects do not exist, direct perception of the mind should likewise not exist. Yet, we currently realize external real objects; therefore, one should know that it is not merely "consciousness-only.
Furthermore, the object of direct perception is a "real object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). That a real object does not follow the mind is clearly understood.

"This refers to external objects that are real. Regarding the respondent's answer below, the treatise states: "When it is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one does not grasp it as external.

It is only later that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates, falsely giving rise to the notion of externality and the conceptualization of external objects. This is the answer given according to the correct tenets of our own school. Its meaning is as follows:
when the five sensory consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*sahabhū-manas*) perceive an object together, they both apprehend it through direct perception.

It is not grasped as being external, because one has attained the essential nature of the self-characteristics of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). That is to say, when the object is not being perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
However, when a subsequent moment of independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, one falsely clings to it, such that an appearance resembling an external object manifests.

One forms a discriminating mind that resembles an external object; this is merely a false interpretation. In reality, there is no external object, because direct perception (pratyakṣa) illuminates its own essence.

This is the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the five consciousnesses. Since it is transformed by consciousness, it is also called the "self-objective aspect" (sva-nimitta-bhāga), as it is not separate from consciousness.
To claim that there is an external object is a conceptual construction and a false attachment born of delusion.

There is both existence and non-existence. This is because, from the perspective of the mind that clings to deluded attachments, there appear to be real objects for the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).
However, when speaking according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), there are no objects existing apart from the mind; they are merely transformations of the internal mind.

If one insists upon the existence of real dharmas external to the mind, such a claim would not accord with the truth. These [objects] exist only as false appearances following deluded sentiment, and thus do not transcend delusion.

It is the mind. It is also called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). When it is the deluded mind, external objects suddenly cease to exist, just as when there is a film on the eye, one falsely perceives flies and the like.
If this is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) accompanying the five [sensory] consciousnesses, it does not form the conceptualization of external objects. The Hīnayāna masters say:
"I am not asking the Master of the Treatise whether the mental consciousness discriminates that external real forms and so forth exist; rather, how is it that the Master himself..."
Is it not difficult for you to answer this yourself? Your response does not accord with the intent of my question. I asked the Master of the Treatise:
"Do the five consciousnesses directly perceive external, real objects? The Master replied: "This answer previously explained that the five consciousnesses do not grasp [objects] as external;

it was the mental consciousness that grasps what is present. This concludes the previous response to your challenge. Now, however, we are discussing the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the five consciousnesses, which resembles [the external object].

"External objects exist" means that their substance is not actually external objects; it merely clarifies the correct principle. This concludes the response to the objections of the Hinayana. The intent is as follows:

the five consciousnesses perceive objects without forming conceptual interpretations and thus do not apprehend the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; therefore, they are called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

As for the second moment [of thought], which conceives of things as truly existing outside the mind and does not follow the mind's interpretation, this is not separate from the "non-departure" [from reality]; hence, one speaks of "consciousness-only."

The seventh point below concerns the objection regarding the contradiction between dreaming and waking. An opponent objects, saying: "It is said that within a dream there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and the dream-objects have no reality.
This is because, upon waking, the subsequent mind realizes that within the dream there were no real objects at all, and they were not separate from the dreaming mind."

This is the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). If one takes the absence of external objects in dreams as the illustration for designating consciousness-only—that the mind during the waking state is like the dream-objects and is thus consciousness-only—then why is it that people in the world do not realize while actually awake that the present objects are consciousness-only?
It is only after waking that one retrospectively contemplates the dream as not being separate from the dreaming mind; therefore, it is called "consciousness-only."

One does not realize that the object perceived subsequent to cognition is merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), because one perceives a real object as being substantially existent external to the mind.
If it is clearly understood that one does not know for oneself that what is perceived is merely consciousness, how can the Master [Vasubandhu] maintain that "all is merely consciousness"?
Below, the Master’s response consists of two parts: first, he provides an established example; second, he gives the formal answer.

Furthermore, regarding the response given by way of an analogy: as for the existence of objects within a dream, it is only after waking up, or subsequently, that one realizes they were merely consciousness-only.
As the treatise states: "Just as one who has not yet awakened from a dream cannot know it for themselves, but only upon reaching the state of awakening can they retrospectively realize it."
One should know that objects and forms during the waking state are likewise so. The explanation says: To properly provide the analogy, it is like when one has not yet awakened from a dream;
while actually dreaming, one does not know at all that it is a dream, and thus clings to it as a real object.

Only upon later awakening does one realize that during the preceding time of dreaming, the dream-objects were entirely non-existent and were all merely consciousness. Thus, it is only upon reaching the state of awakening that one knows the dream.

This is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). It can be understood through an analogy. Regarding the second part, the direct answer, the treatise states: "Those who have not yet attained true awakening are constantly in a dream;
therefore, the Buddha describes this as the long night of birth and death. Because of this, they do not yet realize that the objective realm of forms is consciousness-only. The commentary explains:
The meaning is this: objects perceived during the waking state are just like objects in a dream.

Because one does not recognize that it is a dream—that it is merely consciousness—one clings to them as truly existing external objects, failing to realize that what is currently being experienced is itself a dream.

Only upon reaching true awakening does one finally understand that from beginningless time until now, everything has been a dream-object and nothing but consciousness. (Vimśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi)

The verse says: "As long as one has not awakened, one cannot realize that what is seen in a dream does not exist; this refers to the fact that, having not yet attained true awakening, one can never know for oneself [the nature of reality].

When one attains untainted true awakening, one is also able to recollect the dream-land of the long night of birth and death, and thus realizes that all other ordinary beings are likewise dream-lands, and that their objects do not exist either. All.

All are but consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Question: How is it known that birth and death are a dream? Answer: Because one has not yet attained true awakening, one constantly dwells within the dream of birth and death;
therefore, the Buddha spoke of the "long night" of birth and death, which is as deluded as a dream.

By this principle, one has not yet realized that objects such as form (*rūpa*) are but consciousness-only. The above concludes the response to the objection regarding the contradiction between dreaming and waking.
From here below begins the eighth section, the refutation of the externalist’s objection regarding the apprehension of another’s mind. The externalist objects as follows:
"The Master has already established, through exhaustive reasoning, that the objective realm of form (*rūpa*) is non-existent; since external forms do not truly exist, I shall not debate that point.

However, if the mind of another is indeed substantially existent, why is it not an object-condition (*ālambana*) for one's own consciousness? This implies that one's own mind should directly perceive it."

[The opponent argues: "If one is attached to another's mind, then in this context, if [the cognition] takes that as its object, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is not established, because one would be apprehending another's mind as existing external to one's own mind.
If, on the other hand, one does not become attached while taking another's mind as an object, why is there an object that is not apprehended?
In that case, what could be called 'knowledge of another's mind'? This objection is also found in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. There it says: "If one cannot discern..."

Regarding the "knower of others' minds": what is meant by the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*)? If it were to take [another's mind] as its objective support (*ālambana*), then the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) would not be established.
The Master of the Treatise answers below: Who says that another's mind is not the object of one's own consciousness? I maintain that another's mind is indeed the object of one's own consciousness;
therefore, there exists the knowledge of others' minds. However, I merely do not say that another's mind is the direct objective support (*sākṣād-ālambana*) of one's own mind.

Therefore, one’s own mind cannot directly perceive or grasp another; rather, it perceives another's mind by means of a transformed reflection (*pratibimba*), and for this reason it is still termed "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).

Thus, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is established. When this knowledge perceives another's mind, it does not grasp the object directly as a hand grasps a thing, nor is it like tongs or pincers seizing an object;
furthermore, it is not like the five sense organs directly perceiving their respective objects.

As for the substance: when this consciousness perceives an object, it merely resembles a mirror reflecting things; it obtains only the image (nimitta-bhāga) and does not grasp the underlying substrate (dravya).

Therefore, another person’s actual mind is subsumed under "other-mind-only" (para-citta-vijñapti-mātra), and another person’s five sense organs and five sense objects are subsumed under "another's representation-only" (para-vijñapti-mātra).

The external substrate (bimba) that serves as the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) for the five sensory consciousnesses is the objective aspect of the eighth consciousness. Thus, representation-only (vijñapti-mātra) is fully established.

That is to say, the two divisions of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga) function within the self-verifying division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga), being neither identical with nor separate from the self-cognizing division (svasaṃvedana-bhāga).

When apprehending another's mind, one forms the cognition of "another's mind," which is precisely the grasping of the mental image (pratibimba) of that other's mind; thus, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is established.
The ninth section from here on, "The Objection that Objects of Different Realms Are Not Merely Reflections," begins with the opponent’s objection:

"Regarding the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there are no entities whatsoever apart from the mind. If, however, the objects transformed by another's mind were real, they would differ from the objects transformed by one's own mind;
how then could they be called 'consciousness-only'? [This would apply to] the actual physical sense-faculties and so forth belonging to other persons."

[The opponent asks: "This is an object transformed by one's own body; how can it be established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? For there exist other real forms (*rūpa*) external to one's own mind.
The Master of the Treatise answers and rebukes him, stating: "How extraordinary! You cling to the sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) and thus give rise to doubt.

Does the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* merely speak of a single consciousness? The intended meaning is: "Does the word 'only' (*mātra*) mean that there is only your own single consciousness, and no consciousness belonging to other persons?"
Furthermore, an outsider asks: "If it is not the case that there is only a single consciousness, what would its mode of activity (*ākāra*) be? The Master of the Treatise replies: "Listen attentively!
If there were only a single consciousness, how could there be the distinctions of the ten directions, ordinary beings and sages, the noble and the lowly, cause and effect, and so forth?
Who would preach the Dharma—that is to say, who would be the one preaching the Dharma? What Dharma would be sought? Therefore, [it is] Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*)."
These words possess a profound underlying meaning. The intent is as follows: it is a counter-objection directed at the opponent’s position.
If there were only the consciousness of a single person, how could there be the distinctions between the ten directions, ordinary beings and sages, the noble and the lowly, or cause and effect?

Furthermore, how could there be the distinct existence of other people’s form and mind? If there were only the Buddha alone, for whom would the Buddha preach the Dharma? For there would be no assembly.
Because [the Buddha] is born, there would likewise be no Buddha; that is, there would be no spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). If so, what would there be to seek?

Therefore, the statement of Vijñaptimātra possesses a profound underlying intent (abhiprāya). An outsider asks: "What is this intent? The answer is: "It is the understanding of the meaning of our own school."
That is to say, all sentient beings each possess eight consciousnesses, the six categories of mental factors such as the omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), their respective self-substances,

the two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*) which they transform, the various states of matter and mind, the twenty-four dissociated (*viprayukta*) formations, the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena,
and the true suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the principle of the two kinds of selflessness. One reveals this true suchness by taking emptiness as the gateway.

Thus, that which is permitted as the self-substance of the eight consciousnesses is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness; therefore, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

That which is permitted as mental factors (*caitta*) is that which is associated with consciousness; therefore, it is called "consciousness-only. That which is permitted as form (*rūpa*) is that which is transformed by the aforementioned sovereign [consciousness] and its objects.

The other two positions are easily understood. The term "only" (*mātra*) excludes the existence of external objects; the term "consciousness" (*vijñapti*) excludes the possibility that consciousness itself [is non-existent].
It is emptiness. Because it is free from existence and non-existence, it constitutes *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

If one understands the intent of the teaching on consciousness-only in this way, one will be able to correctly and skillfully prepare the provisions (*sambhāra*), swiftly enter into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and realize unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-bodhi*).

This enables one to rescue sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), rather than allowing them to fall into the nihilistic emptiness of those who deny the existence of the evil realms. For it is only by not contradicting the teachings and reasoning that one can accomplish such a task. Therefore—

One must certainly believe that all things are representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). The preceding section concludes the general response to the previous objection regarding contradiction with reason.

Beyond the nine objections, there is yet another: namely, the objection that if external objects are established as non-existent, then since there would be nothing to forget, cognition should not arise.
The opponent objects: "If there are no real objects of perception external to the mind, from what do these various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise? Conceptual construction...
This refers to the eight consciousnesses. If there were no external objects, by what cause would the eight consciousnesses arise?
The Master of the Treatise answers: Within the eighth consciousness there are all seeds; because these seeds exist, all phenomena arise from them.

Once they manifest as active states (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), they possess a sovereign power capable of drawing forth the various consciousnesses. Therefore, one knows that the arising of consciousness is not separate from the internal mind.

Since there are objects that are transformations [of consciousness], we know that the principle that "all is consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) is established. Although it is said that "it is consciousness-only," this too has its causes and conditions;

only then can it arise. The reason for its arising is precisely the four conditions (catasraḥ pratyayāḥ). Since these four conditions possess the power and function to draw forth and trigger [consciousness], [the principle is established].
If discriminative consciousness arises, how does this contradict the [meaning]? This answers the objection that external objects must exist because they are not forgotten and yet do not arise;
thus, it is concluded that everything is indeed consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). Among the five stages, this occupies the first position because one’s own mind is supreme.
That the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only has been extensively established above. If one follows the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty...
To establish *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), one who employs inference [formulates it as follows]: "The color that is truly and universally established is the subject (*dharmin*).

It is definitely not separate from eye-consciousness; this is the predicate (*dharma*) of the thesis. The reason (*hetu*) is: 'Because it is included within the first three [elements] yet is not included by the eye [organ]. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like eye-consciousness."

By stating "because it is real," one excludes the fault of contradicting worldly conventions; for Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is the ultimate and profound meaning of the Buddha's teaching, which is unknown to the world.
By stating "universally established" (*prasiddha*), one excludes that which is not universally established, namely, non-universally established form (*rūpa*).
