The correct explanation of the meaning of the view of the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is hereby concluded.

Regarding the second point, the identification of the locus where views arise, the *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "That is to say, it refers to those who grasp at the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as 'self' and 'mine'.
The intended meaning is this: one grasps at these very five aggregates of the body as the self and as what belongs to the self.

That is to say, one grasps at form (*rūpa*) as the self, and the remaining four aggregates as what belongs to the self; thus, the five aggregates mutually function as both self and what belongs to the self. Question:
Question: Why are they called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*)? Answer: This is to distinguish them from the five untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates;
therefore, they are called the five aggregates of clinging. Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and clinging (*upādāna*) can moisten and nourish rebirth, these five aggregates come into being.

Since these five aggregates arise from the craving and clinging of others, they are named the five aggregates of clinging. That is, they are named after their cause. Thus, regarding these five aggregates of clinging...
Above, one grasps [them] as "self" (ātman) and "what belongs to self" (ātmīya). It is precisely these five aggregates (pañca-skandha) that give rise to the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi).

The five aggregates are the object-condition (ālambana), while the view of self is the subject-condition (ālambaka). That is, by taking this body of the five aggregates as an object, one gives rise to the views of "self" and "what belongs to self";
therefore, it is said: "one grasps as self and what belongs to self within the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha). This should be understood.

Regarding the sequential clarification of their functional activities (*karmavṛtti*), the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The function [of the view of self] is to serve as the basis for all other views. The explanation (*jie*) says:

That is to say, the remaining three views all arise subsequent to the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). At the very moment this view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises, one further clings to that view of a self-body as being either annihilated or eternal;
thus, this view of a self-body serves as the basis (*āśraya*) for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). This is because [the latter] is based on annihilation...
Because it is always an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, regarding one's own self, the attachment to one's own view as being supreme is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);

thus, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to views serve as its basis. Moreover, the attachment to one's own precepts and conduct as being capable of attaining purity is called the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);
because it serves as the basis for the remaining three views that follow, it is the [view of a self].
This is the functional activity (*karmavipāka*) of views. Therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for all forms of dogmatic attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Regarding the subsequent distinctions among the four types of view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), a question is asked: "What is the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this view of self? The commentary answers:
"These distinctions of the view consist of twenty phrases, sixty-five [phrases], and so forth, which are subsumed under those arising through discrimination (*vikalpita*). To explain:

According to the first exposition in the Abhidharma-śāstra, when one analyzes the aggregates as conditions for formations (*saṃskāra*) without analyzing the place where they arise, there are twenty propositions.
If one analyzes the aggregates as conditions for formations while also analyzing the place where they arise, there are sixty-five propositions.
To set forth the twenty propositions first: each aggregate has four propositions; thus, across the five aggregates, there are [twenty].

There are twenty phrases. Specifically, regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there is one view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and three views of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*), which together constitute four phrases.
This applies to all five aggregates. To illustrate the method applied to the aggregate of form: first, certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon that the aggregate of form is the self;
that is, the very essence of the aggregate of form is the essence of the self. Second, other non-Buddhists reckon that this form is not [the self].
"I. This aggregate of form is my ornament; it is merely the adornment of my household, and thus it is my ornament.

The third non-Buddhist says: "This form is not even an ornament; this aggregate of form is merely my servant, my slave, and my possession. The fourth non-Buddhist says: "It is not even a slave; this form..."

The aggregates (*skandha*) are my dwelling place; they are my cave-abode. Since this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) consists of four propositions, each of the remaining four aggregates likewise has four propositions for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), following the same explanation as for the aggregate of form. Thus, there are twenty propositions in total:
five constitute the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and fifteen constitute the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*). Question: Why are there five views of self?
"Are these fifteen 'mine'? He replied: "Because they arise in accordance with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) through the association of 'mine,' they do not depart from the view of self.
Thus, five are the view of self and fifteen are 'mine. This refers merely to the analysis of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that take the aggregates (*skandha*) as their object;
it does not analyze the basis from which they arise. He asked: "What is called the basis from which they arise? He replied: "If one clings..."
Form is viewed as the self. One clings to the other four aggregates as the locus from which "I" and "mine" arise; "distinctly" means that one specifically identifies the locus from which they arise.
Now, when one does not distinguish the locus from which they arise—meaning, at the very moment one conceives form as the self—one does not further distinguish the locus from which "mine" arises;
it simply arises simultaneously with the view of self. Therefore, it is said that one does not distinguish the locus from which they arise.
There are twenty phrases. If one distinguishes the aggregates that serve as conditions for activity while also distinguishing the bases from which they arise, there are sixty-five phrases.

This concerns the arising of the aggregates separately as "I" and "mine. When one reckons form (*rūpa*) as the self, one then reckons the remaining four aggregates as "mine. Thus, what belongs to the self does not arise within the same aggregate as the self itself.

Because one gives rise to the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) regarding the separate aggregates (*skandha*), this refers to both the statement itself and the basis from which the notion of "mine" arises.
The method of practice is as follows: taking form (*rūpa*) as the self, there are three types of "mine" for each of the remaining four aggregates.
That is: "Form is my self; it is my ornament, my servant, and my dwelling. "Perception (*saṃjñā*) is my ornament, my servant, and my dwelling. "Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are my... [self].

The necklaces, servants, and cave-dwellings: consciousness is my necklace, servant, and cave-dwelling. When one aggregate is taken as the self, the remaining four aggregates each have three types of "mine" (*mamatta*);
thus, three times four makes twelve, and together with the single self, this constitutes thirteen propositions.
That is, with one aggregate serving as the head, there are thirteen propositions; and so it continues as each of the five aggregates takes its turn as the head.
Each [of these] has sixty-five phrases. Question: The commentary states, "sixty-five, etc. To what phenomena does this "etc. refer? Answer:

Since the five aggregates already have twenty phrases, the mention of "sixty-five, etc. refers equally to the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), which also possess the notions of self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).
Now, as for the twelve bases, they are divided as follows: [The text continues with the enumeration of the twelve bases.]
Regarding the section on the conditions for separate practice, as for that which does not differentiate the place of origination, there are forty-eight propositions.
Specifically, there are the calculations of non-Buddhists: the first holds that the eye-faculty is the self. The second non-Buddhist says: "This also is not the self;
rather, this eye-faculty is merely my ornament, for the eye-faculty can adorn me. The third non-Buddhist says: "It is neither..."
"Necklace. This eye-faculty is merely a servant of my house. A fourth non-Buddhist school calculates that it is neither a servant;

rather, this eye-faculty is my dwelling place and cave-abode. Thus, there are four [positions] regarding the eye-faculty: first, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); three propositions are the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Thus, there are four propositions concerning the locus of the eye-faculty. The eleven loci are to be understood accordingly.

The functioning of the eye-faculty consists of ten sets of four, forming forty locations. Furthermore, there are two locations with six and eight phrases, which together constitute forty-eight phrases.

These do not differentiate the places where [perceptions] arise. Specifically, twelve of these are views of "I" (ātman), while the remaining thirty-six are views of "mine" (ātmīya). If one differentiates the places where the formations arise, and further differentiates...
Regarding the "places where they arise," there are four hundred and eight phrases.
Specifically, if one holds that the eye-faculty is the self, then each of the remaining eleven bases has three views of "mine. Thus, eleven times three makes thirty-three;
adding the view of the eye-faculty as the self makes thirty-four phrases. Here, the single base of the eye-faculty serves as the head.
There are thirty-four phrases; ten sets of thirty-four make three hundred and forty. There are two further sets of thirty-four, making sixty-eight.

Thus, there are four hundred and eighty phrases in total. This refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*) mutually being taken as self (*ātman*) or what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), totaling four hundred and eighty phrases.
As for the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), if one analyzes the objects of activity (*ālambana*) in relation to the elements:
Regarding the non-discriminative arising of the elements (*dhātu*), there are seventy-two propositions. Specifically, there are the calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The first group of non-Buddhists maintains that the eye-faculty element (*cakṣur-indriya-dhātu*) is the self. The second group of non-Buddhists says: "This is not the self;
this eye-faculty element is merely an ornament for my home, it is my necklace. The third group of non-Buddhists says: "This is also not a necklace; this eye..."
Regarding the sense-base of the eye: it is merely a servant or laborer for my household. The fourth heterodox teacher says: "It is not a servant or laborer;
this sense-base of the eye is merely my dwelling place, my cave-abode. Thus, for a single base, there are four propositions.
Thus, ten [factors] become forty. Furthermore, each of the eight elements has four phrases, which makes thirty-two.
Combined with the previous, this constitutes seventy-two phrases. If one includes the elements arising from discrimination, there are nine hundred and thirty-six phrases.
That is, one element is taken as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), while for each of the remaining seventy elements, there are...
There are three views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). These three multiplied by ten become thirty. Furthermore, there are seven sets of three; these seven times three make twenty-one.
Adding this to the single view of self makes fifty-two propositions. Thus, with one *dhātu* as the basis, there are fifty-two propositions.
Now, when the eighteen *dhātus* mutually serve as self or what belongs to self (*ātmiya*), there are ten... [etc.]
One set of fifty-two makes five hundred and twenty. There are another eight sets of fifty-two, which constitute four hundred and sixteen.
Combined with the previous five hundred and twenty, this results in nine hundred and thirty-six phrases.

This is according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the first chapter on "The World as Foremost" (*Loka-agradharma*) of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, which analyzes [the teachings] in terms of the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
This can be understood. What has been discussed above is that this conception of a self is not innate (*sahaja*); it is solely a view arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpita*).

Question: How is this known? Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58, states: "The twenty types of *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (personality-belief) are all abandoned through the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
This indicates that they depend solely on afflictions of conceptual construction and do not depend on innate afflictions. This can be understood. Above, there has been...

Fourth: First, the definition of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the identification of the locus where this view arises; third, the analysis of its functional activity; and fourth, the analysis of its distinctions.
These four distinct sections together constitute the completion of the first [section], the definition of the view of a self-identity.
From here below is the second [section], the explanation of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). This is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation.

Regarding the first, the heading, the sub-commentary states: "The view of adherence to the two extremes. The meaning is that this refers to the two types of adherence—the views of annihilationism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*).
Because it does not abide in the middle and because its perspective is one-sided, it is called the "view of extremes" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); this should be understood.

Second, within the formal explanation, there are two parts: first, the analysis of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*); second, the analysis of its distinctions. Regarding the analysis of its functional activity, the Commentary states:

"That is to say, its functional activity consists in leading one away from the middle path—which is itself the locus of obstacles consisting of the adherence to either permanence or annihilation—toward liberation."
This is because one immediately clings to one's own body as being either annihilated or eternal, or clings to the bodies of others as being annihilated or eternal;
thus, one obstructs the practice of the middle way. To "practice the middle way" is precisely to practice the Middle Path. Question: What is called the Middle Path?

Answer: It is called the Middle Way because it is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. This is like the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which, from beginningless time until the path of liberation, is without interruption;

thus, it is free from the view of annihilationism. Furthermore, because the eighth consciousness is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) characterized by the four marks of existence, it is free from the view of eternalism.
Therefore, one is free from the view of permanence. If one perceives True Suchness (tathatā), one is then free from both existence and non-existence; this is called the Middle Way.

Because one is free from the superimposition (*samāropa*) of viewing True Suchness as manifold, it is called "free from existence. Furthermore, because its essence is not entirely non-existent, it is called "free from non-existence.

Thus, by negating the two extremes of superimposition and denial (*apavāda*), it is named the Middle Way. This means that the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) are both [abandoned].

Because it is devoid [of all characteristics], it is called "True Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*); thus it is named *śūnya*. Within this gate of emptiness, there exists the ontological essence of wondrous existence;
therefore, it is named "Wondrous Existence. Thus it is named *śūnyatā*. This term *śūnya* in the Sanskrit language is precisely what is meant by "emptiness.
If one were to further [inquire]—it is simply its nature. It is precisely *śūnyatā*, which in this [Chinese] language is called "the nature of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-dharmatā*). There is...

For this reason, it is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Specifically, one uses the aforementioned hundred dharmas as "wondrous existence" (*prabhāsvara-sat*) to refute the nihilistic emptiness of the evil realms;
one uses the subsequent two types of selflessness (*anātman*) as "true emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) to refute the attachment to existence outside the mind.

Thus, one is free from the extremes of non-existence and free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, correctly abiding in the Middle Way. If these two views of annihilationism and eternalism exist, they directly obstruct progress upon the Middle Way. This...

The "bases" (āyatana) herein include both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, as for the statement that their function is to obstruct liberation (*niḥsaraṇa*), this refers to the practice of liberation itself, which consists solely of the two truths of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*), and is exclusively untainted. These two truths of Cessation and the Path are the dharmas of liberation;

yet these [bases] harbor the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, which prevent the Truth of the Path from arising and prevent the Truth of Cessation from manifesting, thereby obstructing true untaintedness.

Because it functions as such, its activity is defined as obstructing liberation (*niḥsaraṇa*). Question: What is the difference between the practice of the middle way (*madhyama-pratipad*) and the practice of liberation?
Answer: There is indeed a distinction. The practice of the middle way is broad; it encompasses the practice of liberation. However, the practice of liberation is narrow;

it does not fully encompass other aspects of the practice of the middle way. This is because the practice of liberation is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas the practice of the middle way... [is both tainted and untainted].

The "middle course" (*madhyama-pratipad*) refers precisely to the paths with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*). Because this [view] possesses these two meanings, it is said to obstruct the middle course and to obstruct the practice of liberation (*niḥsaraṇa-pratipad*).
This is because these two views—eternalism and nihilism—are able to obstruct these two courses; such is the functional capacity of the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
It should be understood that based upon the aforementioned view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), one then clings to either annihilation or permanence. Thus concludes the preceding section.

This is the analysis of their functional activity (*karmayoga*). Second, the analysis of their distinctions is divided into two parts. First, the presentation of the distinctions; as the Commentary states: "This refers to the distinctions of these views.

Second, the analysis of the distinctions itself, which is further divided into two: first, the analysis of the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*); second, [the analysis of] those who follow the sevenfold theory of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
...and so forth. This is the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Now, to distinguish the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), there are two parts: first, distinguishing the prior limit (*pūrvānta*); second, the subsequent limit (*aparānta*). First, distinguishing the prior limit:
The treatise states: "Among the various types of views, up to the 'Theory of Partial Eternity' (caturtha-ekadeśa-śāśvata-vāda). To first distinguish the four theories of universal eternity:
regarding the phrase "various types of views" (*sarva-dṛṣṭi-gati*), it does not refer to a single name; rather, "various" refers to the sixty-two views, which are termed "all views.
Within these sixty-two views of extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), forty-nine views are subsumed, while ten remain.

The five views are subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Within these forty-seven views, forty are the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) and seven are the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Because there are so many such views, they are called "all views" (*sarvadṛṣṭi*). As for the term "inclinations" (*abhiprāya*), it refers to the underlying intention;
it may mean that which is intended, or it may mean the direction toward which one tends. Therefore, they are called "the inclinations of all views" (*sarvadṛṣṭigati*).
Furthermore, it is said that those who "cling to the prior limit" (pūrvānta) give rise to conceptual views based on the past; therefore, it is called the "prior limit.
If one gives rise to conceptual views based on the future, it is called the "subsequent limit" (aparānta). If one gives rise to conceptual views based on the present...
This is precisely what is indeterminate. It may be called the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*), because it is prior to the future; as the cause of the future, it is termed the "prior limit.
Alternatively, it may be called the "subsequent limit" (*aparānta*), because it follows after the past, or because it is the fruit of the past.
This is called the "subsequent limit" (*aparānta*). Now, first to distinguish the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*): Question: What is meant by the "four theories of universal permanence"? Answer:

These refer to seeing the pervasiveness of birth and death throughout two, four, or eighty eons (*kalpas*). Regarding the "two," these are the practitioners of the lower-tier non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The fourth refers to those of intermediate capacity among the non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*). "Eighty" refers to those of superior capacity among the non-Buddhists. The fourth [category] refers to those who perceive birth and death;

that is, they have attained the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*). Furthermore, regarding the first category, those of twenty *kalpas* are exclusively of inferior capacity among the non-Buddhists;

they have attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*) and perceive all sentient beings throughout the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness within the past twenty *kalpas*.
"Dying here and being born there": at the moment of death it is hidden; at the moment of birth it is manifest. When the world undergoes dissolution and emptiness, it is hidden;
when it undergoes formation and abiding, it is manifest. This is what is meant by "hidden and manifest.

To take these states of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, as well as birth and death, to be permanent—this is the second type of non-Buddhist, the one of middling capacity, who has attained knowledge of past lives.

He attained supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*). Observing all sentient beings throughout the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of forty past kalpas as they died here and were reborn there, he then clung to the view that the self is eternally permanent, existing only through its manifestation and concealment; in reality, it is fundamentally and eternally established.
Therefore, one knows that all sentient beings in the world are eternally abiding. This third type of non-Buddhist is of the highest grade.

Having attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), he observes that throughout eighty eons of formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness, all sentient beings die here and are born there.
He then clings to them as being his self, asserting that they are all eternally abiding; it is merely that they differ in being hidden or manifest. Thus, one knows that they are all [eternal].
They are all eternal. The fourth type of non-Buddhist practitioner, having attained higher meditative concentration, gives rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Seeing how sentient beings arise and die, and how their aggregates (*skandha*) continue in succession, he then clings to the view that both the self and the world are eternal.

While the first three types of non-Buddhist practitioners attain higher meditative concentration and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), and the fourth attains the divine eye, all that they perceive is eternal.

This view of permanence is likewise a defilement pertaining to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Question: These supernormal powers of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) and the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*) are both of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).
How can they be the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), which is a defilement? Answer:

At the very moment one attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives or the divine eye, and correctly observes all sentient beings dying here and being born there, these are indeed of a wholesome nature; it is not [the case that they are defiled].

This is indeed a delusion. That is to say, when a subsequent thought, taking the past object previously observed as its condition, gives rise to the false attachment that it is permanent, this is precisely the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
there is no contradiction here either. Furthermore, this view of permanence also takes the objects of the three realms as its condition.

Furthermore, this view of permanence belongs to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhūmi-saṃyukta*). Because this view arises subsequent to relying upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is connected to the higher stages.

Alternatively, that portion of the view of permanence belonging to the lower realms which takes the objects of the higher realms as its objective support consists of "solely projected images" (*kevala-nirmita-viṣaya*). Question: [What is the nature of these projected images?]
The supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) takes the present as its object. Why, then, is it said to concern the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*)? The answer is:

having already taken a present object, the sixth consciousness then grasps it as past, just as it did when it was present; thus, "dying here and being born there" is stated according to the perspective of the supernormal power's object.

The above concludes the four theories of universal permanence. Next, we shall distinguish the four theories of partial permanence (*ekadeśa-śāśvata-vāda*). Question: What is meant by "partial permanence," and so forth?
The answer is: "The remainder of Brahmā’s great elements (*mahābhūta*), a portion of mental playfulness (*vitarka*), and a portion of anger (*vyāpāda*).

First is the remainder of Brahmā; second is the great elements and the mind; third is the portion of playfulness; and fourth is the portion of anger. Now, regarding the first, the remainder of Brahmā:"
"Brahmā" refers to the King Brahmā (*Brahmā-rāja*). "The others" refers to the Brahma-purohitas, the Brahmapārṣadyas, and so forth.
This refers to the perception of the destruction of the First Dhyāna by fire. When the subsequent kalpa of formation begins, at first there is only the single King Brahmā;
he was born first in the First Dhyāna, and no other beings were present. Then King Brahmā thought to himself: "May all sentient beings come to be born in this place to be my companions."
Having formed this thought, at a later time sentient beings were born into the first dhyāna.
Once born into the first dhyāna, they soon saw a Brahmā King and conceived the notion: "I was born from the Brahmā King. Thus the Brahmā King himself declared: "I am the creator.
Meanwhile, the other sons of Brahmā had short lifespans; they died earlier and became members of external heterodox sects. Thus it was.

Having attained the first dhyāna through the power of his *kalpa* and obtained the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), he saw that the Brahmā King was still present.

He then formed the following conception: "In ancient times, the Brahmā King was eternal, whereas we are impermanent. To conceive that the Brahmā King is eternal is to give rise to a view based on conceiving another as a self (*parātma-dṛṣṭi*).
This is the case where one part is eternal and another part is impermanent. Second is the mind of the great elements (*mahābhūta-citta*). It says:
The "great elements" (mahābhūta) refer to the four great elements, namely earth and the other three. These four great elements are eternal, whereas the mind is impermanent.
When one perceives the earth and so forth, one sees them as eternally existent; when one perceives sentient beings, one sees them as subject to birth and death.
Therefore, it is known that the earth and so forth are eternal, while the mind is impermanent. Third, the "portion of play" refers to the various devas of the desire realm.

At the time of death, he took no pleasure in his own seat and instead desired to engage in play. Because he hoped for such play through the excellence of the environment, he could not let go of it at all.
At that very moment, the Buddha passed away and was reborn in this world; having attained supernormal powers among humans, he observed his previous life.
Because he had harbored hopes for play at the time of death, he formed a fixed attachment, saying: "Therefore, one should know that [it is] play."
Hope is impermanent; that which is free from the play of hope is permanent. Regarding "a portion of the four types of anger":

this refers to when the various devas of the desire realm are approaching their end of life. As their kinsmen depart and the five signs of decay appear, they see their kinsmen surrounding a new deva-king.
Consequently, they gaze with narrowed eyes and give rise to resentment; thus, they suddenly become impermanent. This is reckoned as the "self," as it were. Therefore...

To know that those who harbor anger are impermanent, while those who do not harbor anger are permanent—this is all to have attained a connection with the divine and then give rise to the conceit of a self, [concluding] that one part is permanent and one part is impermanent. This, together with the previous four views of universal permanence, constitutes eight views;
all of these arise based on the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Question: As for the aforementioned view where "another part" is considered permanent, this is...
It is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Since one calculates that one's own self is impermanent, under which view is this subsumed?
If it were the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), how could it be called the view of eternalism? The answer is: it is indeed the view of eternalism; it is not the view of annihilation.

Rather, it is subsumed under defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*) within the category of "distinct objects" (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*), and is not included among the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*). This is because it does not grasp at the annihilation of future lives, but merely calculates that the previous life is eternal.
Alternatively, it may simply be defiled wisdom, which is not subsumed under [the category of] permanence or annihilation.

Regarding the second point, the discrimination of the self arising from the future limit (*aparānta*), the commentary states: "And those who calculate sixteen types of perception regarding the future limit.
Furthermore, concerning the four propositions made with respect to form (*rūpa*): first, the non-Buddhists calculate that "I possess form" and that after death, existence continues.
The "Perception Heaven" (saṃjñā-deva) refers to those calculated to be born in the realms of form and desire where matter exists; that is, the intermediate stage among the nine grounds.

It excludes the two heavens of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), as these are places where consciousness is diminished. This includes the three lower formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) and the seventeen heavens of the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Furthermore, non-Buddhists do not know of the existence of the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), which are the abodes of the noble ones (ārya).
The dwelling place [of those beings] is where externalists (tīrthikas) are born with perception; that is, all other places are locations characterized by perception. That is to say:

"I possess form, and after death, I shall be reborn in a heaven of those possessing perception. The second class of externalists calculates: "I am formless, and after death, I shall be reborn in a heaven of those possessing perception.
What you previously attributed to the first class of externalists—namely, the calculation of "I" and "mine"—is precisely this [calculation of] "I am formless."

Regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), they designate it as "self" while [designating] the other formless aggregates as "not-self. Because they grasp the four [formless] aggregates as the self, after death they are reborn in the heavens of those possessing perception (*saṃjñin*).
The third class of non-Buddhists calculates that the self is both with form and without form; after death, they are reborn in the heavens of those possessing perception.
They grasp all five aggregates as the self: "having form" means they calculate the aggregate of form to be the self, and "being without form" means they calculate...
The other four aggregates constitute the self, which after death attains birth in the realm of those possessing perception (*saṃjñin*).

The fourth non-Buddhist school calculates that the self is neither material nor does it attain birth in the realm of those possessing perception after death; this immediately excludes the third non-Buddhist school.

By saying "not material," they exclude the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); by saying "not immaterial," they exclude the remaining four aggregates. Thus, they conceive of a self as being distinct from the aggregates. All [of these views]...

After death, one attains birth in the Heaven of Those with Perception (*saṃjñin*). These four views may arise within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or they may arise through discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) during the state of distraction.

Regarding the second point, concerning the "limits" (*anta*), four propositions are formulated. First, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) calculate: "Because my self has limits, I shall be born in the Heaven of Those with Perception.
If one clings to form (*rūpa*) as the self, it likewise possesses finite dimensions; therefore, it is called "having limits" (*antavān*).
"Finite. Or it may mean that within the body, [the self] is the size of a finger-joint. Alternatively, it is called "finite" because its reach and location are limited;

or because the other four aggregates also have a finite measure, as their basis and objects of perception are delimited. All such [beings] are born after death into the heaven of those with perception (*saṃjñā*).
The second non-Buddhist school calculates: "The self is infinite, yet after death one is born into the heaven of those with perception. If one holds [this view]...

For those who hold that form (*rūpa*) is the self (*ātman*), because their external paths do not extend to the formless (*arūpya*) realm within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they consider the self of form to be boundless;
since they do not know its limits, it is called "boundless. After death, they are all reborn in the Heaven of Those with Perception (*saṃjñā-deva*).
The third class of non-Buddhists calculates that the self is both bounded and boundless, and subsequently they are reborn in the Heaven of Those with Perception.
O Deva, when it is said that there is also a limit, this refers to the small self, which is "contracted.

If it is said that there is no limit, this refers to the great self, which is called "extended. Thus, at the time of contraction, it is called "having limits"; at the time of extension, it is called "having no limits."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle six, states: "They cling to a self that follows the body; its size is indeterminate, expanding or contracting. When the body is infinite, the self is also infinite;
when the body is small, the self likewise becomes small. After death, such a person is reborn in the Heaven of Those with Perception (*saṃjñā-deva*).
The fourth non-Buddhist school calculates: "The self is neither finite nor infinite. After death, it attains rebirth."
The "beings with perception" (*saṃjñin*) [heaven] excludes the third view. Alternatively, it may refer to the conception of a self within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
It should be understood that regarding the four propositions concerning perception, the first non-Buddhist view asserts: "I possess a single perception;

after death, I shall be reborn in the heaven of beings with perception," which refers to the three lower formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Second, "I possess diverse perceptions," after death... [the text continues].
They are born in the Heaven of Those Possessing Perception (*saṃjñin*), which is located within the intermediate state between the Desire Realm and the Form Realm.

Third, those who think, "I have a small perception," will after death be born in the Heaven of Those Possessing Perception; that is, they reckon a small form to be the self, such as the case of a firefly.
Fourth, those who think, "I have immeasurable perception," are those with the large bodies of the fourth dhyāna; all of them, after death, attain [rebirth there].

Regarding the fourth point concerning the fourfold formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the perception of feeling (*vedanā*) among those born in the Heaven of Perception (*saṃjñā-deva*): The first [position] is the calculation of certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who maintain:
"I shall experience exclusively pleasant feeling; after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Perception," which refers to the Third Dhyāna, as this is established as the pinnacle of pleasure.

Alternatively, they may refer to the Second Dhyāna and below, where pleasant feeling exists but is interspersed [with other sensations]. The second [position] is the calculation of certain non-Buddhists, who maintain: "I shall experience exclusively painful [feeling]."
[They] experience [suffering]. After death, they are born in the Heaven of Those with Perception (*saṃjñin*), where they immediately undergo various sufferings in the Avīci Hell.
The third non-Buddhist school calculates that "I have both pleasure and suffering. After death, they are born in the Heaven of Those with Perception;
they have suffering in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, and they have pleasure in the human and celestial realms within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). The fourth...
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) calculate: "I am neither subject to suffering nor pleasure; after death, I shall be born in the Heaven of Those with Perception (saṃjñin).

This refers precisely to the feeling of equanimity (upekṣā). Alternatively, this may exclude the third calculation. Regarding these, there are four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) for each of the following: superior form, superior [perception], the extremes, and feeling.
Thus, four times four makes sixteen, all of which are theories concerning those with perception. As for the "eight theories concerning those without perception" mentioned in the Commentary:

This refers to the four propositions regarding the possession of form (*rūpin*) and the four propositions regarding having limits (*antavān*). First, regarding the four propositions on the possession of form: (1) "I possess form;

after death, I shall be born in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*). This means that one grasps the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as the self and is reborn in the Heaven of Non-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), which is the fourth dhyāna.
(2) A second non-Buddhist school calculates: "I am formless; after death, I shall be born in the realm of non-perception..."
The third heterodox teacher calculates: "I am both with form and without form; after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception.
He thus clings to the five aggregates as being the self and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The fourth heterodox teacher calculates: "I am neither with form nor without form. After death...
"Subsequently, one may be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought. This immediately refutes the third view, which is the conception of a self as distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*).
This constitutes the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding form (*rūpa*). Second, regarding the fourfold analysis concerning finitude (*antavattva*):

First, certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that "the self is finite," and that after death one is reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought. This refers to the time when they grasp form as the self; its measure is as follows:
Narrowness is called "having limits," or contraction is called "having limits," because one perceives a finite boundary;
thus, after death, one is reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). The second calculation claims: "I am infinite"; after death, one is reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception.
This refers to when one clings to form as the self; it pervades all places and cannot be known as being extended, and is therefore called "infinite. The third calculation...
They say: "The self is both finite and infinite; after death, it is reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception. This refers to the grasping at the contraction and expansion of the formless realm.
When contracted, it is finite; when expanded, it is infinite. In both cases, they claim that after death, one is reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception.
The fourth non-Buddhist school calculates: "The self is neither finite nor infinite; after death, it is reborn..."
The Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*) is not "finite," as it refers to the horizontal dimension; nor is it "infinite," as it is limited above and below.
It should be understood that this also excludes the third alternative. The foregoing constitutes the eight propositions regarding non-conceptualization.

As for the commentary’s mention of the "eight propositions of neither-nor" (*ubhayathānirodha*), this refers to the name "neither-nor" applied to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). These are the four propositions concerning form and the four propositions concerning finitude.

This refers to the four propositions concerning form (*rūpa*) and so forth. First: "I possess form; after death, I shall be reborn in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This is the grasping of form as the self. Seeing that sentient beings enter the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception without clarity, one forms this attachment.
This arises from deluded clinging during the state of distraction (*vikṣipta*), and does not belong to those who have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Second, one holds that "I am formless" and, after death, will be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;
thus, one clings to the four aggregates as the self. Entering the meditative attainment of Neither Perception nor Non-perception without clarity, one forms such an attachment.

Third, one holds that "I am both with form and without form," and after death, will be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; this is the calculation based on the aggregates. Five.
The aggregates are complete. The fourth non-Buddhist proponent says: "I am neither material nor immaterial; after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
This negates the third alternative. This refers to being apart from the aggregates. Regarding the second [category], four alternatives are formulated concerning the finite: first, "I am finite;
after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception"—this may be considered. Second...

1. "I am finite; after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception. Consider this. 2. "I am infinite; after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
Consider this. 3. "I am both finite and infinite; after death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
4. "I am neither finite nor infinite"—this negates the third position. These constitute the eight propositions of the "neither-nor" (ubhayānubhaya) school.
The above has consistently distinguished the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Next, the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) is distinguished. The Commentary states:

"The seven theories of annihilationism and so forth are subsumed under the category of conceptually arisen [afflictions]": First: "I have a self that takes as its nature that which is produced by the four great elements;
this self is annihilated after death among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), becoming ultimately non-existent. This is called 'annihilation. Even the present body..."
1. Regarding those who attain rebirth: they do not take further birth after death. 2. Second, [the view]: "I shall be annihilated after death in the heavens of the desire realm.
3. Third, [the view]: "I shall be annihilated after death in the form realm. 4. Fourth, [the view]: "I shall be annihilated after death in the sphere of infinite space. 5. Fifth, [the view]:
"I shall be annihilated after death in the sphere of infinite consciousness. 6. Sixth, [the view]: "I shall be annihilated after death in the sphere of nothingness."
"Annihilation after death. Seventh: "I am in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and there is annihilation after death.

These seven types of annihilation are also the "subsequent limit" (*aparānta*). Above, there have been two parts: first, the analysis of the view of eternalism; second, the analysis of the view of annihilation. This constitutes the analysis of their distinctions.
Above, there were again two parts: first, the indication of the distinctions; second, the formal explanation and refutation. Thus, the two sections differ.

This section always correctly analyzes the distinctions. What precedes consists of two parts: first, the analysis of functional activity; second, the analysis of distinctions. The two chariots are not the same.

This entire section constitutes the second part, the correct explanation. What precedes consists of two parts: first, the presentation of the two explanations; second, the differences between the two texts.
The second [section] distinguishes the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
From here below, the third [section] distinguishes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This is divided into two parts; first is the heading. As the commentary states:
"The three wrong views," which may be understood accordingly.
In the second section, the formal explanation, there are three parts. First is the general analysis of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Second, from "the distinctions arising from this view" up to "regarding what is not the path as the path," is the analysis of specific distinctions.

Third is the summary, which states: "The commentary says that all such [views] are subsumed under wrong views. These three sections differ. Now, regarding the first part, the general analysis of wrong views: the question is asked: "What..."

It is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The answer states: it refers to the denial of cause, effect, activity, and real entities. To begin with, regarding the denial of cause and effect, we shall first distinguish the denial of the absence of causes.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: "To deny that there is the meritorious cause of giving, and to deny that there are verbal expressions."
There would likewise be no sublime conduct (*sucarita*). This would mean one slanders the existence of untainted sublime conduct (*anāsrava-sucarita*).
There would likewise be no evil cause; thus, acts such as killing would be without fault. Furthermore, even the sublime conduct one performs would lack the cause of merit. How is this known?

Because there are those who, after having practiced giving, subsequently receive the retribution of poverty; therefore, we know there is no meritorious cause for giving. Moreover, one might practice evil...
Having acted, one later obtains the third son of Vaiśravaṇa; therefore, it is known that there is no such thing as a non-existent cause.

All of the above constitutes the denial of causes. As for the denial of effects: this means there would be no holy fruits of the Three Vehicles, nor would there be the fruits of the three evil realms, because causes do not bring about effects;
thus, there would be no attainment of the fruit of outflowlessness through giving. This is called the denial of functional activity.
Furthermore, they slander their parents, claiming that because these individuals are their parents in this life, they will instead become their sons or daughters in a future life;

thus, they know that [the relationship] is not fixed as parent and child, and they conclude that there are no real parents in the world. Beyond this, such non-Buddhists do not even believe in the parents of the present life.

Moreover, they deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) which performs the function of transmitting consciousness to produce a sentient being. Furthermore, they slander [the Dharma] by denying its existence.
This is the function of the *garbha* (womb-matrix). It is the body itself. To slander that which lacks substantial reality is to slander the absence of such things as bodhi, nirvāṇa, and arhats;
it is to have no faith in the fruits of the Three Vehicles at all. This is collectively termed "denying cause and effect," and is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The commentary states:
"And [it includes] those that are not the four views, up to the point where name and meaning are pervasive. The intended meaning is that this wrong view...
Kuan: However, those things not fully subsumed by the other four views are all subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This is just as, for example, those things not fully subsumed by the other three conditions are all subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Now, it is the same with wrong view.
This very wrong view is a view of deprecation (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*). The other four views are mostly views of superimposition (*samāropa-dṛṣṭi*).
To deny cause, effect, function, and substantial reality is called deprecation. The lower "theory of no cause" (*ahetu-vāda*) is also deprecation.
It is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Question: In what sense is it said that the name and its meaning are all-pervasive? Answer:
Whatever is not subsumed by the other four views—all other incorrect views whatsoever—are subsumed under wrong view; this is what is meant by the name and its meaning being all-pervasive.
The above provides a general explanation of wrong view.
Second, regarding the differentiation [of views], there are two parts: first, differentiating those arising from the past; second, differentiating those arising from the future.
First, regarding those arising from the past, the Commentary states: "These distinctions in views extend up to the four types of evasive equivocation regarding immortality.

As for the proponents of the two theories of causelessness: one is a person who, having passed away from the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva), has been reborn here in this world and has attained recollection of their former lives.

Regarding the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*): they are unable to remember the time prior to the emergence of that mind when they were cultivating meditative concentration.

Since the lifespan in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is five hundred kalpas, these practitioners of the highest grade among the non-Buddhists, though they attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives and observe events of eighty kalpas in the past, are nonetheless unable to know the time prior to this Heaven of Non-conception when they cultivated the causes [for their birth]. Thereupon, they give rise to false views, asserting that all things are non-existent.
They arise from causes; therefore, we know that we, too, arise without a cause. Thus, they cling to the view that all sentient beings exist without cause.

Second, because they lack recollection of the deeds performed in previous lives due to discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), they then cling to the notion that everything exists without cause and arises spontaneously (*svayambhū*), as is the case with birds and beasts; who could possibly exhaustively [know their origins]?
As for the source of the mountains, who could have created them? Thus we know they all arise spontaneously; it can be understood that everything exists without a cause.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the four [views] concerning finitude, the first non-Buddhist school calculates that [the world] extends upward to the fourth dhyāna."
Reaching down as far as the Avīci Hell, they grasp at a self that is all-pervasive;
because they thus conceive the thought, "I have limits," it is called "having limits" (*antavān*). Because it has a finite measure, the second class of non-Buddhists calculates:
"The self is limitless (*anantavān*), pervading the ten directions. Because it is beyond the reach of thought, it is called "limitless"; thus, one can recollect the lateral worlds as being limitless.
Because it has a limit, the self is therefore infinite. The third heterodox school calculates that the self is both finite and infinite:

they calculate that because it pervades above and below, it has limits; thus it is "finite. Because they calculate that it extends laterally through the worlds beyond the reach of thought, it is "infinite.
The fourth heterodox school calculates that during the kalpa of formation, the self is not non-existent.

Regarding the "limits": during the period of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), I am not "existent with limits"; during the period of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*), because there are hells and so forth, I am not "non-existent without limits.
During the period of destruction, since even the hells do not exist, I am not "existent with limits. The Commentary states: "The four types of evasive equivocation regarding immortality are:
first, fear of ignorance; second, practicing deceit and crookedness; third, harboring terror; and fourth, fear [of death]."

Yugañña asked: "What are called the four 'immortalities'? He replied: "Because there is an immortal heaven (*amara-deva*) due to its long life, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to it as being eternally abiding and immortal.
That is, the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*) is the immortal heaven. Regarding this, the non-Buddhists themselves calculate that it is 'immortal and undisturbed.
Now, within our Buddha-dharma, we condemn such 'immortality' as deceptive and confused. For now, let us set this aside."
First, there is the fear of being ignorant. This refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who say of themselves: "I do not know what is wholesome or unwholesome;
I do not know the characteristics of the practices for the Immortal Heaven. If someone asks them, "What is the Immortal Heaven like?", they must not provide a definitive answer.
They think that if they were to give a definitive answer, others might perceive their ignorance. This is the secret meaning of the Immortal Heaven.
One should not speak of it. If one were to give a definitive answer, there would be fear that others might disparage me;
therefore, one does not give a definitive answer. This is called "fear of ignorance. Second, practicing deceit:
if someone asks me, "What is the Heaven of the Unfallen like? I then praise them, saying, "It is very good that you ask such a question," though others do not understand why I say this.
Question: Your own insight is profound, such that you praise that person; consequently, that person would not dare to ask further questions.
Third, regarding those who harbor fear: if someone comes and asks me, "What is the Heaven of the Deathless like? and I truly do not know.
He then did not answer, but sat in silence. The person before him could not fathom his depth and praised him, saying, "This is inconceivable.
Fourth is the fear of the ignorant and the conceited. Suppose someone comes and asks me about the Heaven of the Deathless (*amṛta-deva*). I should instead ask them in return:
"Regarding this Heaven of the Deathless you ask me about, what is your own understanding of it? That person will then say: [I thought...]
The "Immortal Heaven" (Amarāvatī) refers to eternal life. The non-Buddhist practitioner then confirmed and agreed, saying: "It is as you have said;

the Immortal Heaven is indeed eternal life. This non-Buddhist practitioner was exclusively devoted to the practice of correct conduct. When someone came to question him, he ought to have asked a counter-question, yet he simply confirmed and agreed.
The preceding sections have all been for the purpose of analyzing the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Next, regarding the analysis of the subsequent limit (*aparānta*), the Commentary states:

"As for those who calculate the subsequent limit and realize *nirvāṇa* in the present": First, there are those who see that they currently experience the fivefold sensual pleasures of humans and devas, and thus reckon this to be *nirvāṇa*.

That is, at the very moment they experience these fivefold sensual pleasures, they believe they have attained the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. Second, there are those who, having become weary of those [pleasures]...

1. Having attained the five sensual pleasures, one immediately attains the first dhyāna. Because one has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and thereby induced pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), one reckons this to be *nirvāṇa*.

2. Third, one becomes weary of the applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna and attains the second dhyāna. Because one is free from applied and sustained thought, one regards it as *nirvāṇa*. 3.
Fourth, one becomes weary of all sensual desires, as well as applied and sustained thought, joy (*prīti*), and feeling (*vedanā*), and attains the third dhyāna.
They take this [state] to be *nirvāṇa*. Fifth, they become weary of all discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*), joy, pleasure, and feeling, as well as the inhalation and exhalation of breath;

having attained the fourth dhyāna, they take it to be *nirvāṇa*. These fifteen views, together with the aforementioned extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), total forty-seven, which constitute the sixty-two views (*dṛṣṭigata*). One should categorize the commentary on this passage as being deluded.
Regarding the aspects of the Truths (*satya-lakṣaṇa*): below the four truths, wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are analyzed.
To first analyze the wrong views regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

"Or, calculating [the cause] as Maheśvara, the Lord of the World, up to that which is eternal and unchanging"—that is, Maheśvara, Brahmā, Śakra, and so forth; all these are fruits of suffering within the three realms and are collectively termed "suffering."
Regarding the Truths: if one clings to these as being permanent, this constitutes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) concerning the Truth of Suffering. The Commentary states:
"Or those who reckon [them] as Maheśvara or the Lord of the World" refers to reckoning Mahādeva as eternally abiding;
that is, the deity Maheśvara is called the Lord of the World. As for "Śakra," this is Śakra-devendra; "Brahmā" refers to Brahmā-rāja. This means reckoning all of these as being eternally abiding.
This is called "reckoning others as self. As for those non-Buddhists who cling to "others" as being eternal, this is precisely what is meant by "reckoning others as self.
Regarding "the remainder and categories of things," these refer to time, space, and the primal limit (*ādi*), which are also capable of producing.
All sentient beings are impermanent and are thus termed "that which is produced. As for the term "time," it refers to the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
Whether it be for a month, or for a day, or for a single kṣaṇa, all sentient beings are born from within time;
they abide by depending on time, and they die by depending on time.
Thus, the birth, aging, and death of all sentient beings are never apart from time. If birth occurs within time, death likewise occurs within time.
Abiding also exists within time; thus, time itself is eternally abiding, whereas sentient beings and the like are impermanent. Therefore, it is called "constant, eternal, and unchanging.
As for "direction," this refers to the four cardinal points—east, west, south, and north—as well as the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir;
all of these constitute direction. That is to say, all myriad phenomena arise from these various directions. Thus, direction itself is eternally abiding. All myriad phenomena...
All things are impermanent; "constant" means eternal and unchanging. As for the term "original limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*), it refers to the time before the world existed.
At that time, there was a *Pangu* (Paṅgu), within whom there was a single substance called *Anta*.

Once *Anta* was broken apart, the pure essence coagulated above to become heaven, the turbid essence settled below to become earth, and the intermediate mixture of pure and turbid essences formed sentient beings. Heaven, then...

As the sun rises one foot higher each day, the earth likewise becomes one foot thicker each day. Those who receive and are imbued with the pure essence (*sattva*) between them will be intelligent and sharp-witted;
those who receive and are imbued with the heavy and turbid essence (*tamas*) will be dull and ignorant.
At this time, the fundamental limit (*prakṛti*) alone is eternal, while all things are impermanent. Therefore, it is said that other categories of things are not eternal and unchanging.
This concludes the first section above, which distinguishes the wrong views regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Second, regarding the distinction of the wrong views regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the Commentary states:

"Or those who reckon Īśvara and so forth to be the cause of all things. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the aforementioned Śakra, Brahmā, and others. A question is asked: "In what way is this [the case]?"
Question: What is the cause for the creation of all things? Answer: The Vedānta masters of the West say that at the time of the kalpa’s formation, a Great Being appears named Nārāyaṇa.
From the navel of Nārāyaṇa, a great lotus flower arises; from within this lotus flower, Brahmā is born.
From the mouth of Brahmā, the Brāhmaṇas are born; from the two shoulders of Brahmā...
Those born as Kṣatriyas were produced from the two thighs of Brahmā; those born as Vaiśyas were produced from the two feet of Brahmā;
and those born as Śūdras were likewise produced [from his feet]. Among these four castes, those born from the mouth constitute the highest caste, while those born from the feet are the lowest.
Thus it is known that all sentient beings are born from Brahmā. This is Brahmā...
The gods and others are the causes of all things. That which is called Maheśvara is composed of eight elements:
first, space as the head; second, the great earth as the body; third, mountains as the excrement;
fourth, rivers and oceans as the urine; fifth, thunder as the breath; sixth, all grasses and trees as the hair; and sixth, all sentient beings [as the internal organs].
These are the worms within the belly. Seventh, the wind serves as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Eighth, all sins and merits are the karmic power of Maheśvara.
Furthermore, it is said that Maheśvara has three bodies: first, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is the empty space of the ten directions;
second, the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which dwells within the fourth dhyāna and is sixteen thousand *yojanas* in height.
Ten days later, as for the three transformation bodies: they reside on Mount Muralaya in the Southern Sea and possess eight hands;
these are also emanations of the Buddha. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist who reckoned Īśvara to be eternal, and he searched for him throughout the Five Indias.
He even went as far as the Southern Sea to search for him. It was this very Maheśvara who had been preaching the Dharma to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Having finished his teaching, he said to those non-Buddhists: "I am not Maheśvara. In Central India, within the Jeta Grove, Śākyamuni is the Great Maheśvara;
he is your original teacher. This was a skillful means to refute the non-Buddhists.
"Way" refers here to the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) calculation that Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, and so forth are the cause of all things;
that is, they do not understand that all phenomena arise from their own causes and conditions. Now, since they calculate that Maheśvara is the universal cause:
This refers to the inclusion of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This is the wrong view under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). The Commentary states:
"Or there are those who recklessly calculate various false liberations"; this refers to the wrong view under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

That is to say, they cling to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as being liberation and *nirvāṇa*. This is like binding oneself with thorns or lying upon thorns, or practicing the five heats (*pañcatapa*).

By burning the body, when suffering is exhausted, one immediately attains liberation; this is called the "liberation of the heterodox" (*tīrthika-mokṣa*). This is the false view regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The Commentary states:
"There are those who falsely cling to what is not the Path as being the Path"; this is the false view regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). That is to say, [they hold]...

The precepts of the chicken, the dog, and so forth, all constitute the false reckoning of what is not the Path as being the Path. Or, such acts as killing horses to sacrifice to heaven likewise constitute the reckoning of what is not the Path as being the Path.
These belong to the category of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The various sections above, though differing in detail, collectively constitute the second [section], which clarifies their distinctions.
Next, regarding the third section, the summary: the commentary states that "all such [views] as these are wrong views.

Above, there have been three parts: first, a general exposition of wrong views; second, an exposition of their distinctions; and third, the summary. These three distinct sections constitute the formal explanation (*viniścaya*).

Above, there have been two parts: first, the presentation of the two [types of] explanations; second, the different textual passages, which together constitute the third part, the analysis (*vibhaṅga*).
The section on wrong views is concluded.
From here below is the fourth [section], which distinguishes the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation.

Regarding the heading, it may be understood that the *Śāstra* states, "the four types of grasping at views. Within the second part, the formal explanation, there are three sections: first, the explanation of the character "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); second...
Explaining the interpretation of the term *dṛṣṭi* (view). Third, explaining its functional application. First, regarding the interpretation of the character *jien* (view):

the Commentary (*Śū*) states, "That which refers to the various views and the aggregates upon which they depend. The Explanation (*Jie*) states: "The 'various views' refers to the three types of views mentioned previously.

The phrase 'the aggregates upon which they depend' refers to the body that serves as their support; it is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of the views, and it is also the retinue (*parivāra*) of the views."
Regarding the explanation of the term "grasping" (*parāmarśa*) below, the *Śāstra* states: "To grasp [it] as supreme and capable of attaining purity.

The intended meaning is that this very "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) possesses these two causes: first, grasping one's own view as superior and other views as inferior, which is called "grasping it as supreme";
second, being "capable of attaining purity," which means that by forming this view, one immediately attains permanence.
They [erroneously] perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, they are said to be "able to attain purity.

If one follows the teachings of the Buddha, these views held by non-Buddhists who calculate [existence] as permanent, blissful, self, and pure are all instances of *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views).

Because they falsely take what is impermanent, without bliss, and so forth—namely, the four [marks of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity]—to be permanent, blissful, and so on, they are subsumed under *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*. Only when these two causes are present does it constitute *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*.
If even one of these meanings were missing, the meaning of "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) would not be established.
Third, regarding its function (*karmaprayoga*), the Commentary states: "Its function is to serve as the basis for all disputes.

This means that when various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) each cling to their own view as being correct, disputes arise among them on this account; because they cling to their own views as being right and superior.

Regarding the view that "others are inferior," the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) immediately conceive the thought: "My view is superior; the views of others are inferior. When they thus cling to their respective positions, conflict and dispute arise.
Therefore, the Commentary states that its function is to serve as the basis for all conflict and dispute.

What precedes consists of three parts: first, the analysis of the character *dṛṣṭi* (view); second, the analysis of the character *upādāna* (clinging); and third, the analysis of the functional activity of the view. These three sections together constitute the whole.

The formal explanation: what precedes consists of two parts—the initial heading and the subsequent explanation—which differ in their respective sections. This concludes the fourth section, the analysis of the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

From here on, the fifth section analyzes the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is divided into two parts: first, the formal analysis of the grasping at precepts and observances; second, from "Now... [the remainder].

The statement that "some sources calculate and explain it as 'lower'" is a commentary intended to resolve textual contradictions. Now, regarding the first [section], the formal analysis of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances), it is divided into two parts:

first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, the heading, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The fifth is clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)," which is the heading, as can be understood.
Within the second part, the formal explanation, there are three sections: first, the analysis of the two characters *śīla-vrata*; second, the analysis of the character *parāmarśa*.
Third, the analysis of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). The three textual passages differ. First, regarding the explanation of the two characters *jie-jin* (precept-restriction):

the *Shu* (Commentary) states, "That is to say, with respect to those precepts and restrictions that conform to various views, as well as the aggregates upon which they depend. The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: "The phrase 'with respect to those that conform' means..."
That is to say, one conforms to the aforementioned views and regards them as superior; thus, one takes one’s own precepts and the retinue of those precepts as the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Here, only that which accords with the prohibitions is taken as the object of focus, while the three views to which it accords are not taken as objects of focus;

this is termed "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Since the [three] views are subsumed under "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), what is grasped here is only the [precepts].

"Holding the precepts" refers to the grasping at prohibitive rules (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). "Prohibitive" (*jin*) means to firmly maintain them without transgression. Regarding the second interpretation of the character *qu* (grasping):

the commentary states, "to hold [them] as supreme and capable of attaining purity. This explains that one holds the specific precepts one observes—such as those of a chicken or a dog—to be supreme, while regarding other precepts as inferior.
Furthermore, it is held that by observing these precepts, one immediately attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity. If...
According to the Buddha-dharma, these are termed the "four inversions. To uphold this precept and thereby attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity is called "being able to attain purity";
this is the analysis of the character *qu* (to grasp). Third, regarding the explanation of its functional activity (*karmayoga*), the commentary states:
"That which serves as the basis for diligent effort toward what is not beneficial is called 'activity' (*karman*). The meaning is that this refers to leaning against a pillar or lying upon thorns.

Practicing the "five heats" by exposing the body to fire, eating only one sesame seed and one grain of barley per day, observing the "chicken-vow" (celibacy), and so forth—though these are indeed forms of asceticism, they provide no benefit whatsoever;
instead, they invite the retribution of the three evil realms. Therefore, their function is defined as being a basis for diligent toil that yields no advantage.

What precedes this consists of three parts, all of which constitute the formal explanation. Of these, there are two sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation. These two passages do not [contradict each other].
The same. This concludes the first section, the correct analysis of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
From here below is the second section, which reconciles conflicting passages; it is divided into two parts. First is the actual reconciliation of the conflicting passages.

Second, from the words "If not so, how... onwards, is the refutation by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*). Regarding the first part, the actual reconciliation of the text: the opponent objects, saying, "If..."
Regarding the statement that "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the grasping of something as supreme and capable of attaining purification, it is called view-grasping;

furthermore, regarding the statement that "precept-and-vow-grasping" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) also has the quality of being supreme and capable of attaining purification—why, then, does the sacred teaching say that grasping something as supreme is named view-grasping, while grasping [it] as capable of attaining purification is named precept-and-vow-grasping? To resolve this textual point: first, the question is restated, and then the commentary provides the answer.

It says: "However, there are places where it is said that [the path] extends to the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); this is such a case. Second, regarding the "correct reconciliation," the *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"This is an abbreviated statement by way of implication (*chāyā-saṃkṣepa*), or it is a 'door of conforming reasoning' (*anuvartana-yukti-mukha*). The meaning is that within this correct reconciliation there are two parts:

first, the abbreviated statement by way of implication; second, the door of conforming reasoning. Now, as for the first, the abbreviated statement by way of implication, it refers to the various treatises.

The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "That which is grasped as supreme is called the 'clinging to views' (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This implies that the clinging to [wrong] conduct as being capable of attaining purification is omitted for brevity.
Furthermore, it states: "That which is said to be able to attain purification is called the 'clinging to precepts and observances' (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This implies that the grasping of [wrong] conduct as supreme is also included therein. Thus, one should understand that the two—views and precepts—are mutually implied when they are stated in brief.

[The grasping at] views and [the grasping at] precepts both possess the most excellent capacity for attaining purification. Therefore, the commentary states in general that this is an abbreviated explanation. Question:
If that is so, what is the distinction between the grasping at views and the grasping at precepts? Answer:

Because the objects of attachment, their bases, the views and their attendants, as well as their excellence and purity, are predominant, they are collectively termed the "grasping at views. If one clings to precepts and the attendants of precepts...

To regard [one's own view] as supreme and pure is called the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). If one says that the two attendants of the view are regarded as supreme but not as pure, this is also not the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
If one clings to [the view] as pure but not as supreme, this is also not the clinging to precepts and observances.
It is only when one clings to one's own view while possessing both of these meanings that it is termed the clinging to views. As for the time of [clinging to] precepts and observances...
Only when these two meanings are present does it constitute the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Second, regarding the "gate of conforming to the principles" (*anuvartana-yukti*):

the intent is that the statements in those treatises—namely, that merely grasping at [a view] as supreme is called the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), while merely grasping at [a practice] as capable of bringing about purification is called the clinging to precepts—are made according to the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
