This is because the masters of the Sarvāstivāda consider [the view of self] to be supreme; thus, they name it the clinging to views.

To grasp [at views] and thereby seek purification is called the "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This is explained solely from the perspective of the Hīnayāna school and is not the ultimate teaching;

therefore, it is termed a "gate of reasoning that follows along" (*anuvartana-yukti-mukha*). "Following" (*anu*) means to conform to or pursue; "turning" (*varta*) means to explain; and "reasoning" (*yukti*) refers to the underlying principle.
The "gate" refers to the gate of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*); it is explained by way of the principles of the two vehicles. Question:
Why do the various treatises not explain solely according to the correct meaning? Since the two types of grasping (*dvaya-graha*) each possess two meanings, why are they omitted?

What is the intention behind this omission? Answer: It is omitted because one wishes to cause practitioners to give rise to knowledge and insight; therefore, it is explained concisely. Question: [Why is this so?]

To hold various treatises as supreme is called the "view of grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). To hold them as capable of bringing about purification is called the "grasping at precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
If these [treatises] were spoken with ultimate truth and were not merely provisional or elliptical, nor were they taught as a pedagogical device (*anupūrvamukha*), what fault would there be?
[The opponent] seeks an answer below. The commentary states: "It is not so; how could it be that they are not subsumed under the two graspings? The intent is: "You, the outsider..."
If one does not accept that this is a concise (saṃkṣepa) explanation, then in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58, regarding the delusions concerning the Four Noble Truths—

specifically under the section on delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*)— the views "that which is not cessation is cessation" and "that which is not supreme is supreme" should be considered the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),

because there is the estimation [of them] as being supreme. Furthermore, under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), the estimation "that which is not the path is the path" and "it can also bring about purification" [would likewise have to be so].

This attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is so called because it regards [a practice] as pure when it is not the most excellent. If this were not the case, one would know that this is a teaching given by way of an abbreviated, conformative door (*saṃkṣepa-anuvartana-mukha*).
Because it regards what is not cessation as cessation and what is not supreme as supreme, and because there is no actual purity, it is merely termed "attachment to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
it is not subsumed under the category of "attachment to views" [*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*] itself. Under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), regarding what is not the path as the path constitutes only...
Regarding "purity has nothing superior," this refers to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is not subsumed under the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

What is stated here—that both types of grasping can each attain purity and each regard [that attainment] as supreme—means that only when each possesses these two meanings are they designated as "grasping at views" and "grasping at precepts and observances.
Thus, one should know that the various treatises state that the grasping at views consists solely of regarding [something] as supreme.

If one clearly knows [a view] and it is not termed "wrong view" (mithyādṛṣṭi), but is instead termed "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), then clearly this is also a case of grasping at what can lead to purification.
If that which can lead to purification were non-existent, it would not be termed clinging to views, but rather wrong view.

Furthermore, it is said that clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) involves only the capacity to attain purification but lacks the quality of being supreme; this too is a case of grasping at the sense of supremacy. If...
If it were otherwise, it would be termed wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) rather than the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
If either one were missing, it would constitute wrong view and not the two types of grasping. These two types of grasping each possess the two meanings of supreme purity.

Therefore, one should know that the cited treatise speaks by way of abbreviation; it is not contradictory, nor is it merely a statement according to a specific methodological approach (*yukti-mukha*).

If one were to say that the *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) is spoken of as being truly characterized only by "supremacy" and lacking "purity," then the meaning of *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* would fail to be established. For *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*, there must necessarily be both supremacy and purity.

Only when [the view of] attaining purity and superiority is present can it be called "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). As for "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it likewise possesses these two meanings;
only when both are present can it be called "clinging to precepts and observances. If either one is lacking, it is merely termed "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, one should know that when various treatises state that clinging to views and clinging to precepts each have only one meaning, this must be a case of abbreviated or elliptical exposition. This concludes the preceding section.
This reconciles the apparent contradictions in the text. Above, there have been two parts: first, the analysis of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);

second, the reconciliation of contradictory passages. These two passages differ; the analysis of the clinging to precepts is now concluded. Above, there were five views (*dṛṣṭi*), which collectively constitute the analysis of their distinctions.
Above, there were two parts: first, the general analysis of wrong views; second, the analysis of their distinctions. These two passages differ; this concludes the primary [analysis].

Commentary: What precedes consists of two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the formal explanation. These two sections differ in their textual presentation, but together they complete the sixth [section], which is the discernment of wrong views.
What precedes consists of six different afflictions, all of which are enumerated individually according to their headings. What precedes consists of two parts: first, the general heading.
The enumeration is presented. Second, the individual items are listed according to their headings; second, the textual passages differ.
This concludes the fourth section, which distinguishes the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). Thus, the commentary states: "The above has distinguished the root afflictions. This should be understood.
From here below is the fifth section, which distinguishes the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The commentary states: "This is the fifth text. It is divided into two parts;

as for the two [sections] up to the main text, they are the same as the preceding ones: first, a general heading enumerating the number; second, a detailed listing according to that heading. These two texts differ.
First, regarding the initial general enumeration of the number, the treatise says: "The secondary afflictions are twenty. The meaning is that the secondary afflictions are...
This is the general heading. "Twenty" indicates the number; this is self-evident.
From here below is the second section, the detailed enumeration according to the heading. The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"The second passage consists of two lines of verse that comprehensively encompass all twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). These are the verses from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* which say: 'Secondary afflictions refer to anger...'"

Envy, concealment, vexation, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, guile, harmfulness, pride, lack of shame, lack of dread, restlessness, lethargy, lack of faith, indolence, negligence, loss of mindfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension. Question: These are twenty afflictions;
why are they called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? Answer: There are two reasons for which they are named secondary afflictions. First:
This is a provisional designation for the specific states of the afflictions; therefore, they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Question:

If the five [minor secondary afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) and the last three of the great secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*) are merely provisional designations for the states of the primary afflictions, then they should be called "secondary" [afflictions].

However, if the two medium secondary afflictions and the first five of the great secondary afflictions are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), they should not be included among the secondary afflictions. Answer: [The text continues...]
It is said: Furthermore, because there is a second sense [to this term], they are called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*).

That is to say, because they are of the nature of being the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the primary afflictions, although their substance is real, they are called "secondary afflictions" because they are the outflow of those other fundamental afflictions;

that is, they are the simultaneous outflow-results (*sahabhū-niṣyanda-phala*) of the fundamental ones. Therefore, they are named secondary afflictions. This combines with the previous general heading.
This is the explanation within the enumeration; it may be understood.

Second, regarding the detailed listing according to the headings, there are two parts. First, a general discussion of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the three stages. Second, a specific discussion of the secondary delusions (*upakleśa*) of the three stages.
Regarding the first, the general discussion, the commentary states that it is divided into three sections. First, it clarifies the minor secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) individually.
"Because they arise separately and because they extend to all defiled minds. To explain this: it is asked, "What is meant by 'minor derivative' (anuśaya)? It is answered:

"They are called minor derivatives because their modes of activity (ākāra) are extremely sharp and each arises individually. That is to say, they arise one after another following the primary [root] afflictions;
they definitely do not arise simultaneously. For example, when anger (*krodha*) arises, resentment (*upanāha*) does not arise, and so forth. It is asked: "What is meant by..."

Regarding the medium-universal [secondary afflictions]: the answer is that they are able to pervade all unwholesome minds. Thus, whenever an unwholesome mind occurs, these medium-universals are present.

This is because they do not pervade all defiled states; for "defiled" is broad while "unwholesome" is narrow. Consequently, these two categories can arise simultaneously, unlike the minor-universals which arise separately.
Question: Why are they called "great-universal" secondary afflictions? Answer: [Because they pervade all minds associated with the three realms].

It is said: This is because the subsequent [section] clarifies that the universal secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-anuśaya*) pervade all defiled minds. Thus, within every defiled mind, these universal secondary afflictions arise.

Among these, the universal secondary afflictions are the most extensive; they pervade those previously mentioned limited secondary afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*), whereas the limited secondary afflictions do not pervade others.
Wherever there is a defiled mind, the eight universal secondary afflictions are present. These eight secondary afflictions are thus attained.
They are co-emergent (*sahaja*). Because they pervade all obscured-unwholesome states (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), they are called "great secondary afflictions" (*mahāparivartin*).
If they do not pervade the obscured but only pervade the unwholesome, they are called "medium secondary afflictions.

If they are unwholesome and also do not pervade [the unwholesome], they are called "small secondary afflictions," because they arise individually. Thus, there are these various meanings; the small, medium, and great secondary afflictions each arise separately.
Thus it is. This first section provides a general analysis of the three secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Second, regarding the specific analysis of the secondary afflictions of the three stages, there are three distinct parts. First, to analyze the minor secondary afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*):
The Commentary states: "This is the first [section]. It is divided into ten parts as in the text.
First, regarding the analysis of *krodha* (anger), it is divided into two: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, the heading, the Commentary says:
'1. Anger'—this is the heading, which is self-evident. Regarding the second, the formal explanation, it is divided into two: first, a brief analysis of its essence and function; second..."

A further explanation of the preceding text. First, regarding the brief discernment of its essence and function, there are two parts: first, the presentation of its essence; second, the discernment of its functional activity.
As for the discernment of its essence, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Its nature consists of the outburst of indignation toward an object that is currently present and non-beneficial."

The commentary explains that "relying on presently manifest objects that are non-beneficial" refers to things currently visible or audible, whether they be sentient beings or the perceptions of others;
it is from these objective conditions that the five aggregates arise. The treatise speaks of "presently non-beneficial matters."
Therefore, it is not an untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma. It is precisely the present encounter with adverse conditions that constitutes anger (*krodha*).

Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is superficial and does not involve deep grasping, if it were directed toward a present untainted dharma, it would be established as a state of hatred (*dveṣa*); this is because such an outburst is the very activity of hatred.
This should be understood. Second, regarding the analysis of its function: the commentary states that "its function is to obstruct non-anger and to grasp a staff. The meaning is as follows:
It is said that "non-resentment" (*anupanāha*) is the state of being free from anger (*avyāpāda*). When resentment arises, it directly obstructs non-resentment;
thus, they constitute a single functional activity. Second, because one is further able to grasp a staff, there are two layers of karmic function.
Using the staff to oppress and punish the other person is the bodily action (*kāyakarman*). Regarding the second layer of karmic function below, the Commentary states: "That is to say, harboring..."
Regarding the phrase "because anger reaches the bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*)," the intended meaning is as follows: one who harbors anger frequently manifests violent and evil conduct;
this is a further explanation of how it obstructs the absence of anger. As for the term "bodily informative action," this is a further explanation of the previous mention of "wielding a staff.
"Wielding" refers to holding with the hand; "staff" refers to a weapon. This is because an evil person is coarse and fierce; thus, it is based on the majority [of cases].

To explain in detail: it is said that wielding a staff constitutes an action (*karman*). At the very moment one grasps the staff with the hand, this is a bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*).

Furthermore, speaking based on the most prominent factor, its actual nature is as follows: there are also cases where one reviles others with evil speech; this should be understood as a vocal informative action (*vāg-vijñapti-karman*).
The second [category], resentment (*upanāha*), is divided into two parts. First, the heading: the commentary states, "The two types of resentment can be understood.

Second, the formal explanation, which is divided into two: first, a brief analysis of its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*); second, a detailed explanation of its functional activity. Regarding the first, the brief explanation of its essential nature and function:
first, to set forth its essential nature, the commentary states, "With anger (*krodha*) as the precursor... it has the nature of harboring a grudge."

Regarding this, the commentary explains: because there is first anger (*krodha*), one immediately treats others with contempt; yet, even when an opportunity to retaliate does not arise, one still harbors malice without letting go.
This is like saying, "I and my enemy have not yet been reconciled after ninety years. Because one thus binds oneself to a grudge, this is the very nature of resentment (*upanāha*).
Second, regarding the analysis of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there are two types of activity. The sub-commentary states that "being able to remain steadfast without resenting" is one.
Regarding its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*): "heat and affliction" (*paritāpa*) are two distinct functions. If resentment does not arise, it is of a wholesome nature;
if resentment arises, it directly obstructs non-resentment—this is the specific functional activity of resentment. Because resentment persists for a long time, heat and affliction are produced.
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, if one follows its explanation, there are five functions: first, it can obstruct non-resentment; second, it can... [text truncated]
Because it obstructs the nourishment of the factors for enlightenment (bodhipakṣa). Third, it leads to rebirth in evil destinies. Fourth, it harms oneself and others.

Fifth, it increases one's karmic limitations. Thus, the aforementioned anger (*krodha*) also possesses these five functions. It should be understood that this resentment (*upanāha*) takes up the aspect of anger with even greater intensity.
Regarding the second detailed explanation of its functional activity, the Commentary states: "One who harbors resentment is unable to endure; constantly..."
"Because of burning affliction (*paridāha*). This means that when one harbors resentment for a long time and is unable to endure it, one immediately experiences burning affliction.
Or, when the burning affliction reaches its peak, it is evident that hot blood issues from the mouth and so forth.
The third [section], the explanation of vexation (*khila*), is divided into two parts. First, the heading: the commentary states that "the three vexations" is the heading, which is self-evident.
Second, the formal explanation, which is divided into two parts: first, a brief explanation of its essence and function; second, a detailed re-explanation of the preceding text.

Regarding the first, the brief explanation of its essence and function: first, as for its definition, the commentary states: "With anger and resentment as the precursor... having a nature of malice and hostility."
The commentary explains: because one previously possessed anger and resentment, one becomes extremely vexed and immediately approaches with a staff to assail others.

Since the enemy has not yet found an opportunity, the resentment increases over a long period; therefore, it is called "vexation" (*pradāśa*). It refers to the mental deliberation directed toward the enemy.

It then becomes violently hot like fire; one then harbors resentment toward previous people—this can be understood. Second, regarding the analysis of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there are two types of functional activity.

The commentary states that "being able to obstruct" and "not being [free from] affliction" constitute one [aspect], while "having the functional activity of stinging like maggots" constitutes the second type of functional activity.
If there is affliction, it directly obstructs wholesome dharmas; if there is no affliction, it does not arise.

It is so because it opposes its counterpart; this is its distinct karmic function. Furthermore, as it can sting and bite both oneself and others, the two characters "sting" (蛆) and "bite" (螫) should be used in both senses.
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it should be understood that this vexation (*pradāsa*) also possesses five functions.

Regarding the second section, which extensively explains the preceding text: first, regarding the re-explanation of its essence, the commentary states, "That is to say, when one pursues past evils and harbors resentment and hostility with a sincere heart.
The meaning is this: if one reflects upon former enemies, resentment and hostility arise; "lì" (戾) refers to being perverse and obdurate.
Second, regarding the extensive explanation of its functional activity, the commentary states, "Frequently manifesting clamor and violence, one even stings and bites others."
The meaning is that, according to the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, it refers to uttering words that are ominous, base, evil, and coarse.
Furthermore, it includes using others as scapegoats for one's own faults. This constitutes the arousal of bodily action (*kāyakarma*) through affliction. As for "violent speech":
These are the "sudden outbursts" (*paryavasthāna*) and so forth. Above, there were two parts: first, a brief explanation of their essence and function;

second, an extensive explanation of their essence and function. These two texts differ, yet both constitute the formal exposition. Above, there were again two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal exposition. These two sections differ, yet both constitute the explanation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) as derived from the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the statement that all three previously mentioned [categories] are classified according to *dveṣa* (hatred), the Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The three types mentioned above..."
It can be understood that its essence consists of a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*).

Below this, the fourth section, the explanation of concealment (*mrakṣa*), is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, the heading: the commentary states, "The four types of concealment," which serves as the heading;
this can be understood. Regarding the second, the formal explanation, it is divided into three parts: first, a brief explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*); second...
The phrase "one who conceals their offenses" refers to [the state] up until the point of insecurity; this is the detailed explanation of the karma.

Regarding the third section, from "due to greed and delusion" onwards, there are three different interpretations by the two masters. First, concerning the brief explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), the commentary first distinguishes its nature.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Regarding one's own or another's offense, up to 'concealment' as its nature": because one has committed it oneself...
One commits various transgressions fearing that others will know of them; if others were to know, one would lose wealth and profit.

Now, fearing the loss of wealth, profit, and reputation, one conceals the transgressions within one's own being and does not repent. Because one claims to be pure, it is said that its nature is to conceal out of fear of losing benefit and fame.
Second, regarding the analysis of its function (*karmaprayoga*), the Commentary states: "It is able to obstruct non-concealment."
Regarding "remorse and affliction as karma": the commentary explains that this also constitutes two layers of karmic function.

Specifically, this concealment directly obstructs non-concealment; this is its distinct karmic function. Because one conceals this transgression for a long time, one subsequently feels self-reproach, saying, "Alas! Alas!
I mean that because one concealed this transgression for the sake of fame and profit and failed to repent, remorse and regret arise. The above has been a brief [explanation].
This explains the essence and function [of the hindrance]. Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation of its functional application, the *Sū* (Commentary) states:

"That is to say, for one who conceals their transgressions, it leads to a state of insecurity. The sub-commentary (*Jie*) explains: This refers to one who, having committed transgressions throughout a lifetime, neither repents nor instructs others;
subsequently, when facing death, they reflect: "In the past, I committed these transgressions. Now that my life is ending, I must necessarily undergo the bitter fruits of retribution."
He then repented, saying, "In the past, I did not repent this sin. Since I have committed a sin, I ought to enter hell.
Having reflected thus, he gave rise to remorse and distress, becoming uneasy. This can be understood. Regarding the third section below, the explanations of the two masters:
the meaning presented here in the commentary belongs to the second master. As for the meaning of the first master, the *Śāstra* says: "There is..."

This *mrakṣa* (concealment) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*). The treatise speaks only of it as a portion of delusion because one conceals one's own transgressions out of fearlessness regarding future suffering.

The meaning is that, being a portion of delusion, it is a state of confusion and darkness toward the object before one; thus, one is not afraid of future suffering and consequently conceals one's sins.
It is therefore subsumed solely under the category of delusion. The second master says: "This *mrakṣa* consists of both greed (*lobha*) and delusion."
Regarding the classification [of the hindrance of concealment], the *Śāstra* states that its essence consists of a portion of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).

As for the phrase "because one conceals one's own transgressions out of fear of losing profit and reputation": if this refers to not fearing future suffering, it is subsumed under a portion of delusion; this is why one conceals one's transgressions.

If, however, it is subsumed under a portion of greed, it is because one desires the wealth, profit, fame, and so forth of others, and thus fears losing profit and reputation, thereby concealing one's transgressions.
It is also subsumed under one portion of greed (*rāga*). Specifically, the previous statement that "one does not fear future suffering" refers to a portion of delusion (*moha*);

the subsequent statement that "one fears losing profit and reputation" refers to a portion of greed, as can be understood. Above, there are three parts: first, a brief discernment of the essence and function;
second, an extensive explanation of the aforementioned functions; and third, the interpretations of two masters. Although these three sections differ, they are all correct.

Commentary: What has preceded consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. These two sections differ in their textual form. This concludes the fourth section, which distinguishes concealment (*mrakṣa*).

From here below is the fifth section, which distinguishes deception (*māyā*). It is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, the heading, the sub-commentary says:
This refers to the fifth [of the unwholesome roots], deceit (*māyā*). This may be understood. Regarding the second part, the formal explanation, it is divided into two sections:

first, a brief explanation of its essence and function; second, an extensive explanation of the preceding text. Within the first section, the brief explanation of its essence and function, we first examine its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Question: What is the essential nature of this deceit? Answer: The commentary states: "Its essence consists of deceiving others for the sake of profit and reputation, up to and including guile and fraud."

Regarding this, the commentary explains: it is for the sake of fame and profit that one immediately practices deception, deceiving all other people by claiming, "I understand the activities of the Buddha-dharma.
Although there is actually no root of virtue or achievement within oneself, because one seeks the benefit of others, one thus feigns and deceives them.
"Arrogance" (*māna*) has the meaning of unreality; "guile" (*śāṭhya*) is a designation for the fabrication of falsehoods. That is to say:
To falsely pretend to possess virtues when one lacks them oneself is called "deceit" (*śāṭhya*); that is, to feign the appearance of possessing virtues.
This is done for the sake of seeking profit and reputation. Next, regarding the analysis of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there are two levels of such activity.
The commentary states: "Being able to obstruct non-deception is one level; taking life as its activity constitutes the second level. If there is one who deceives...
This means that it neither deceives nor arises. Because it is contrary [to non-deception], it is able to obstruct non-deception; this is its specific karmic function.
Regarding the statement that "wrong livelihood is karma": obtaining wealth and profit from others by deceiving them is entirely wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

Therefore, it is called *mithyājīva* (wrong livelihood). This refers to *mithyājīva*, food obtained through wrong means, and so forth. Some explain that because wrong view operates in the same manner as mental karma, it is termed *mithyājīva*.
What is meant here by *mithyājīva* is the act of deceiving others by employing craftiness and contrivances to speak falsely for the purpose of seizing another's wealth;
this is called *mithyājīva* and is also termed "impure wealth. According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang shengjiao lun*), there is also...

[This refers to] the five karmas. Above, the essence and the karma were briefly explained. Regarding the second section, which extensively elaborates upon the preceding text, it is divided into two parts:

first, extensively elaborating on the preceding essential nature; second, extensively elaborating on the preceding functional activity. Third, [it] reveals the basis. The commentary states: "Regarding 'conceit' and 'deception' up to 'unreal'":
this indicates the essence and the karma, as well as the matters of life and death; thus, this explains the functional activity. [The terms] "greed" and "delusion"...

Regarding "one part constitutes the essence," this clarifies the basis (*āśraya*). There are three distinct sections; first, concerning the initial determination of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the Commentary states:
"That is to say, through arrogance and deception... up to 'unreal. The meaning is as follows: because one seeks wealth and goods, one deceives others with arrogance;
the mind harbors improper intentions and various schemes of calculation, and thus immediately feigns the appearance of diligence.

This is the practice of deception. It is called "deception" because it frequently manifests what is unreal in order to delude others. Next, regarding the analysis of its karmic function, the Commentary states:
"Because one obtains wealth and goods by deceiving others through matters of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), these are all improper livelihoods and are termed 'matters of wrong livelihood.
This is because one employs various schemes and stratagems to take the wealth and goods of others; thus, whatever objects are obtained [in this way] are all..."
It is a pure object; therefore, it is known as the matter of "false livelihood" (mithyājīva).

Third, regarding the manifestation of its basis, the Commentary states that its essence consists of a portion of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*). Specifically, because one seeks the wealth of others by deceiving them, it is categorized as a portion of greed.
Because one employs various schemes and plots to deceive others, it is subsumed under a portion of delusion. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Greed and delusion..."
Regarding the two factors that serve as the basis for deception (*māyā*), they are identical to those of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only); this may be understood.

The preceding three types of "provisional designations" (*prajñapti*) collectively provide an extensive explanation of the preceding text. Above, there have been two parts: first, a brief discernment of their essence and function;

second, an extensive elaboration upon the preceding text. This constitutes the formal exposition. Above, there was first the heading and then the explanation; this concludes the fifth section, which discerns deception.
From this point downward is the sixth section, which distinguishes *śāṭhya* (deceit). It is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Regarding the first, the heading:

the commentary states, "Sixth, *śāṭhya*," which serves as the heading; this is self-evident. Regarding the second, the formal explanation, it is divided into three parts: first, a brief discussion of its essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*); second, from "Furthermore, as for *śāṭhya*...
up to "...because of correct instruction," which is an extensive elaboration on the aforementioned essence and function; third, the manifestation of its basis (*āśraya*).
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "Its essence consists of a portion of greed and delusion," which is correct. These three sections differ.

First, regarding the brief explanation of its essence and function, as for the initial analysis of its essential nature, the *Śāstra* says: "Its nature consists of deceiving others up to being treacherous and crooked."
The commentary explains that "flattery" refers to using deceit to mislead one's predecessor. This involves employing various words and fabricating expedients to deceive the person before one.
Regarding the term "险曲" (xiǎnqū): "险" (xiǎn) is not a fixed name; "曲" (qū) carries the meaning of being crooked or not straight.

Because it serves to mislead others, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because of deceiving that person," or "because of overreaching and misleading another. It is like [the story of] Rā... (text fragmentary).
When the net flies through the void, one should consider that it covers over deception; this is its essence.

Second, regarding the analysis of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there are two functions. The commentary states: "That which can obstruct flattery" is one function, because it correctly instructs;
these are the two functional activities. This flattery and non-flattery are mutually contradictory. When flattery arises—
It is the direct obstacle to non-deceit (*aśāṭhya*). Its function is to obstruct the correct instruction of others;
this can be understood. Second, regarding the expansion of its essence and function: first, to expand upon its essence, the commentary states: "That is to say, one who is deceitful and crooked...

up to "...acts in order to grasp another's intentions. The explanation is as follows: because one deceives and flatters others, one crookedly grasps their intentions, or because one troubles their feelings.

That is, one harbors expectations for the favor of others. Because of the pursuit of wealth, one speaks with words that are crookedly compliant to others; thus, one falsely devises expedient means to take what is desired by them.
Therefore, it is said that "one acts to win over the intentions of others. Alternatively, it refers to acting in accordance with what one seeks for oneself.

This can be understood as meaning that one must immediately act in accordance with what is appropriate for the occasion. Next, regarding the reiteration and expansion of the previous application, the *Śū* (Commentary) states:
"Or, because they conceal their own faults until they receive formal instruction. The explanation says:

this means that because such a person practices flattery and crookedness, they are unfit to serve as a teacher or a friend, nor are they fit to be a companion. This is because such a person practices flattery out of greed for fame and profit.
Therefore, it should be understood that since it is not a correct instruction for practicing flattery, it is not a correct principle;

thus, it is not a correct instruction. Third, regarding the manifestation of the basis, the Commentary states: "Its essence consists of a portion of greed. This should be understood. Above, there have been three sections:
first, a brief analysis of the essence and function; second, a detailed analysis of the essence and function; and third, the manifestation of the basis. These three segments differ from one another.
This is the formal explanation. Above, there have been two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. These two sections differ in their textual form.
This concludes the sixth section, which distinguishes flattery (*śāṭhya*).
From here below, the seventh section distinguishes the "deceitful" (*kuhana*). This is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, the heading:

it refers to what is stated in the *Śāstra* as "the deceitful. This may be understood. Within the second part, the formal explanation, there are three sections: first, a brief presentation of its essence and function;

second, an extensive treatment of its functions as previously mentioned; third, the revelation of its basis. Now, within the first section, the brief discussion of its essence and function, we shall first—
Regarding the "essential nature" (*svabhāva*), the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Taking one's own prosperity as the object, up to intoxication and arrogance, constitutes its nature.
The explanation says: "As for 'one's own prosperity,' it may be official rank, wealth and goods, or physical beauty.
When there is such flourishing in the world, one gives rise in the mind to reliance and self-exaltation, failing to see others. This is intoxication and arrogance."

It is similar to a drunken person. Question: How does this differ from pride (*māna*)? Answer: Deceit (*śāṭhya*) arises from being defiled regarding one's own qualities, whereas pride involves looking down upon others.
The *Abhidharma* states that even when referring to things such as longevity or years—which are matters of calculation—there is also an element of deceptive self-exaltation.
This may be understood accordingly. Second, regarding the analysis of its function (*karmaprayoga*), there are two functions. The commentary (*śāstra*) says it can obstruct [the attainment of]...
*Śāṭhya* (deceit) is a karmic function. Its function is to rely upon defilement (*kleśa*). These are two [distinct] karmic functions. When *śāṭhya* arises, it is the direct opposite of non-deceit;
thus, it is said that it can obstruct non-deceit. Regarding the statement "its function is to rely upon defilement":
this means that for one who possesses this *śāṭhya*, defilement serves as its basis. It is because [defilement] arises based on this that it is so named.
It functions as the basis for defilement; this may be understood. Regarding the second point, the detailed explanation of its functional activity, the *Śāstra* states:

"That is to say, it causes those who are deceitful and intoxicated to give rise to and grow all defiled phenomena. The intended meaning is that when such deceit exists, all manner of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) are able to arise and develop.
This is because one becomes defiled by attachment toward one's own prosperity, which constitutes indulgence in intoxication, arrogance, and negligence.
Thus, all defiled phenomena arise based on this; hence it is said that it "gives rise to and grows all defiled dharmas.
Third, regarding the manifestation of its basis (*āśraya*), the Commentary states: "Its essence consists of a portion of greed and delusion. This may be understood.

The three preceding sections—the first briefly presenting the essence and function, the second extensively elaborating on the aforementioned functional activity, and the third manifesting the basis—though differing in their textual expression, collectively constitute the formal explanation.
The preceding section consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. These two distinct segments together conclude the seventh [section], which clarifies "deceit.

From here on begins the eighth [section], which clarifies "malice. This is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Regarding the initial heading, the sub-commentary states: "Eight."
It can be understood that "harming" refers to this very thing. Within the second section, the formal explanation, there are three parts: first, a brief explanation of its essence and function;

second, an extensive analysis of its activity; and third, the revelation of its basis. Now, regarding the first part—the brief discernment of its essence and function—first, as for discerning its essential nature, the *Śāstra* states:
"Its nature consists of a lack of compassion and a mind of malice toward sentient beings, characterized by injury and affliction. To explain this:
Because it is harmful, and because it causes injury and affliction within existence (*bhava*), it is called "lack of compassion" (*akaruṇā*).
If it were non-harming, it would be subsumed under compassion. What is now termed "harming" is precisely the absence of compassion;
because it causes injury and affliction, even regarding the truths of cessation and the path, one gives rise to harm. This very harming—

It arises conditioned by untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). This is explained in terms of "harm" (*vihiṃsā*) as co-arising; that is, it refers to the harm produced through cultivation within the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This also applies generally to the Hīnayāna, though the correct interpretation is that it is spoken of specifically in relation to sentient beings.
Second, regarding the analysis of its functional activity (*karman*), there are two types of activity. The commentary states that "being able to obstruct non-harm" is one of them.
Because it afflicts others, it constitutes two types of karmic activity. At the very moment this harm arises, it directly obstructs compassion (*karuṇā*);

since compassion is immeasurable, it is precisely non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). Because they are diametrically opposed, when harm exists, one necessarily afflicts sentient beings and thus lacks compassionate pity.
This is explained as being the direct opposite of non-harming. If one relies upon...

The *Xiányán* (Exposition of the Manifest) states that this harm also possesses five functions, which may be understood. Second, regarding the detailed explanation of its functional activity, the commentary (*shū*) says:

"That is to say, there is one who harms, because they oppress and afflict others. The sub-commentary (*jiè*) explains: "This very act of harming is able to damage and distress the limbs and joints of sentient beings;
because it causes others to be unsettled and unhappy, it is termed 'oppression and affliction' (*bìnǎo*). This may be understood. Third, the basis [of the harm] is revealed.
The Commentary states that its essence consists of one portion of hatred (*dveṣa*). This is because it does not entirely take life, but rather causes damage to a portion of the limbs and joints;
thus, it takes one portion of hatred as its essence. Above, there have been three sections, all of which constitute the primary explanation.
Above, there have been two [sections], which are the second explanation. These two texts differ, but together they complete the eighth section on the explanation of harm (*vihiṃsā*).

From here below, the ninth section distinguishes envy (*īrṣyā*). It is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the heading, the Commentary states: "Ninth, envy.

The second part, the formal explanation, is divided into three sections: first, a brief analysis of its essence and function; second, an extensive analysis of its essence and function; third, the revelation of its basis.
Regarding the first, the brief analysis of its essence and function: first, the essence is analyzed. The Commentary states:
"Regarding the phrase 'one whose nature is characterized by seeking fame and profit up to jealousy':
the commentary explains that the term *xún* (侚) here means 'to seek,' 'to inquire after,' or 'to pursue. If it were used in the sense of 'half-dead,' it would simply mean death.
Thus, because one seeks fame and profit for oneself, one cannot endure the prosperity of others; that is, upon seeing another person possess flourishing success, wealth, or nobility..."

Regarding "peace and happiness" or "worldly prosperity," these refer to the superior qualities and dharmas from which they are obtained, encompassing both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

To give rise to jealousy toward these is to harbor envy toward such states. If one refers to gods, *māras*, and so forth, it means giving rise to jealousy and resentment toward untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas;
or, in the case of worldly people, it means being envious of others regarding fame and profit—this is the nature of the mind.

Envy (*īrṣyā*) and jealousy (*mātsarya*). Envy constitutes the essential nature [of this category]. Question: What is called envy? What is called jealousy? Answer: That which takes another’s correct Dharma as its object is called jealousy;

that which takes another’s prosperity and happiness as its object is called envy. As the *Yùpiān* states: "To harm the worthy is called jealousy; to harm [another's] beauty is called envy. This may be understood.
Regarding the analysis of its functional activity, the Commentary (*Śū*) says: "It is able to obstruct non-envy, and its result is sorrow and distress. There are also two layers [to this function].

This is its function. If there is no envy, this is precisely the immeasurable state of joy (*muditā*). If one dies while harboring envy and jealousy, it directly obstructs the immeasurable state of joy;
therefore, it is called "directly obstructing non-envy. Because envy obstructs [joy], one becomes sorrowful and distressed whenever things do not go according to one's wishes.
The *Xianyang lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Doctrine) states: "It is able to obstruct... This refers to the *Xianyang*.

Regarding the fourth [immeasurable], among the four immeasurables, the immeasurable of joy (*muditā*) is non-envy (*an-īrṣyā*). It should be understood that its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is as follows.
Second, regarding the detailed explanation of its essential nature and function: first, to expand upon the aforementioned nature, the Commentary states:

"As for those who are envious, when they hear of or see the prosperity of others, there are two [types]. First, seeing that others possess the practices of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), to give rise to anxiety is called envy. Second...

To feel resentment when seeing others’ prosperity and happiness is called *du* (jealousy). The *Yùpiān* states: "To harm the worthy is called *jí* (envy); to harm those of beauty is called *dù* (jealousy).
Regarding the expansion of its functional application, the *Shū* (Commentary) says: "Because it deeply ruins [the mind] with sorrow and distress, one becomes unstable.
This means that once one is already distressed by sorrow, one naturally becomes unstable; this is clear. Third, regarding the revelation of its basis, the *Shū* says: "A portion of *dveṣa* (hatred)."
The essential nature [of this] can be understood.
From here below, the tenth section, "Discriminating the Miser," is divided into two parts. First, the heading: the commentary states, "the ten types of miserliness" refers to this.

Second, the formal explanation, which is divided into three parts: first, a brief discussion of the essence and function; second, an extensive discussion of the essence and function; third, the manifestation of what is... [text truncated].
Regarding the first [section], which briefly distinguishes the essence and function, the commentary states: "Its essence is the secret stinginess that clings to wealth and the Dharma.
This means that "wealth and the Dharma" refers to wives, children, prosperity, riches, and so forth, which are called "wealth";
whereas if they pertain to the teachings, principles, practices, or fruits, these are all called "the Dharma. Thus, it refers to the inability to relinquish such wealth and the Dharma.

Therefore, it is called *mātsarya* (miserliness). "To conceal" (*bimi*) means to be withholding; "to hoard" (*zang*) means to cherish. Because of this attachment, one immediately conceals and becomes miserly;

this is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of miserliness. Regarding its function (*karman*), the *Śāstra* says: "It is able to obstruct non-miserliness and acts as the cause for stingy accumulation. The commentary explains:
"If there were those who are not miserly, they would practice giving (*dāna*), bestowing all their goods and wealth upon others."
This is what is called "giving" (*dāna*). Now, since stinginess (*mātsarya*) exists, it directly obstructs the practice of giving;
therefore, it is said to be that which can obstruct non-stinginess. Regarding the term "mean accumulation" (*kutsita-saṃcaya*): "mean" (*kutsita*) means evil;

because it is mean and evil, and "accumulation" (*saṃcaya*) refers to hoarding—where "hoarding," "collecting," and "gathering" are synonyms—it should be understood that "mean accumulation" is designated as its function (*karman*). Second, the detailed explanation of its essence and function.
Regarding "first extensively explaining its essential nature," the commentary states: "That is to say, one who is stingy has a mind that is mostly secretive and obstructed. The explanation says:

because of stinginess, one's mind is secretive and obstructed, and thus does not practice giving; that is, being base, parsimonious, and obstructed, one is unable to bestow gifts or relinquish things, and is therefore called "stingy" (*mātsarya*).
Next, regarding "extensively explaining its functional activity once more," the commentary states: "Accumulating wealth and dharmas while being unable to bestow them as gifts."
Third, regarding the manifestation of its basis, the Commentary states that its essence consists of a portion of greed (*lobha*).

If one follows the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, there are five types of stinginess (*mātsarya*): first, stinginess regarding dwelling places; second, stinginess regarding families; third, stinginess regarding giving; fourth, stinginess regarding praise;

and fifth, stinginess regarding the Dharma. Now, as for stinginess regarding dwelling places: it is the arising of a stingy thought toward one’s own residence, such that one says, "I alone shall dwell here," and so forth.
He acts with sovereign independence and does not rely on others; this consists of five aspects: first, he does not wish for future bhikṣus to come;
second, because he reprimands and scolds those virtuous bhikṣus who have already arrived; third, he wishes to make them depart early.

Regarding the four types of gifts given to the Saṃgha, if one does not wish to give them away, but instead develops a sense of ownership toward those gifts given to the Saṃgha and calculates them as a personal favor or merit, such a person will be unable to relinquish even the phenomena within that state of suffering, let alone their own possessions.
For such a person, there will ultimately be no liberation whatsoever. Second is the stinginess regarding family; regarding those who have gone...
Upon returning home, one conceives the thought of a lamp. Therefore, it is said: "In this house, I alone always enter and exit;

I do not require others. Even if there are others, I am the most excellent among them. There are also five kinds [of such thoughts]: first, when the layperson encounters an inauspicious event, one shares in their sorrow;
second, when they encounter a beneficial circumstance, one shares in their joy; third, one rejoices in the layperson’s superior achievements.
Fourth, they cause other people to refrain from giving. Fifth, they are reborn in that household as a ghost dwelling in the latrine.
Regarding the third type of miserliness regarding giving: one harbors thoughts of stinginess toward the property of others, thinking, "May I alone obtain the objects of this gift."
Others shall not obtain it; even if one were to give it to them, they would still surpass me. This also has five [consequences]: first, a constant lack of the necessities of life;
second, causing the donor to fail to gain merit; third, causing the recipient to fail to obtain wealth or profit; fourth, disparaging virtuous people;
fifth, being constantly afflicted by anxiety and distress, which will lead to rebirth in the hells and other realms; and even if one is born among humans, one will be poor and lowly.
...and so forth. Fourth is the praise of the stingy person. When others are praised, they give rise to stinginess and jealousy, thinking: "Let only me be praised; do not praise others.
Even if you must praise others, let them not surpass me. Furthermore, there are five [consequences]: first, the minds of others become distressed and agitated;
second, they disparage virtuous people; third, they exalt themselves and belittle others; fourth, [they seek] fame for themselves; fifth, regarding the future...
For hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they will possess no pure mind. Regarding the fifth dharma:

within the True Dharma, they give rise to thoughts of stinginess and envy, thinking, "May I alone know the twelvefold scriptures; do not let others teach them. Even if others should come to know them, they think, "May they not surpass me.
Furthermore, knowing the meaning for themselves, they keep it secret and do not explain it. These faults lead to rebirth as one who is constantly angry and always deluded.
1. Delusion. 2. Having many enemies. 3. Retreating from and losing the noble embryo (āryagarbha). 4. Wisdom does not arise;
because these are enemies and thieves that obstruct the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas. 5. [Obstructing] good people... 6. There is no evil they do not commit, thereby severing the lineage of the Buddha.
The preceding concludes the minor transgressions (*anuvyañjana*).

From here below, the second section concerning the enumeration of the two [unwholesome roots] is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of *āhrīkya* (lack of shame); second, the explanation of *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread).
Now, to specifically distinguish *āhrīkya*, it is further divided into two: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. First, as for the heading, the commentary states:
The phrase "What is called lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*) is the heading; this is self-evident. In the second section, the formal explanation, there are two parts:

first, a brief analysis of its essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*); second, an extensive analysis of its essence and function. Within the brief analysis of the essence and function, the presentation of the essence comes first. The *Śāstra* (Sūtra-commentary) states:
"Taking the slighting and rejection of one’s own qualities and of the noble and virtuous as its nature. To explain: this lack of shame arises with respect to one's own qualities.

"Self" refers to one's own dharmas; that is, the wholesome dharmas within one's own person. Because one does not look back upon the wholesome dharmas within one's own person, one consequently despises and rejects virtuous persons and their teachings. This is the definition of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). As for its function (*karman*): [it is to... (Note:

The original text contains several illegible characters marked by □ and □□□. The translation above reflects the standard interpretation of this passage as found in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* regarding the nature and function of self-conceit.)

This has two types of functional activity (*karma*). The Commentary states that "being able to obstruct shame" (*hrī*) is its specific functional activity, while "producing unwholesome conduct" is its general functional activity.
It is called a general functional activity because it produces unwholesome conduct in common with "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*).
As for the specific functional activity: when lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is present, it directly...
It is the opposite of *hrī* (moral shame), because it stands directly in opposition to *hrī* and *āhrīkya* (lack of shame).
It is a distinct activity (*karman*), because while [other] dharmas cannot obstruct the *hrī* of others, only *āhrīkya* is capable of acting as an obstruction.
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, *āhrīkya* has five activities: first, it can obstruct *hrī*; second, it can obstruct the depth of bodhi; third...
First, it harms oneself and others; second, it leads to rebirth in evil destinies; third, it causes one to lose the support of virtuous friends;

fourth, it causes one to fall into evil paths; and fifth, it increases shamelessness (*anapatrāpya*). Therefore, this [lack of shame] is able to obstruct *hrī* (shame). This is the first of the five functions explained in the *Vyākhyāyukti*.

What follows regarding the production of [evil] is to be understood as referring to the remaining four functions. The above has distinguished the essence and the functions. Second, within the detailed distinction of the essence and functions:
Regarding the first point, "the emergence of the essence," the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "To have no regard for one's own dharmas" means to slight the worthy and good. The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains:
this refers to not regarding or longing for that which is within oneself. The *Śū* [continues]: because of the superior dharma, one slights the worthy person and rejects the wholesome dharma.

This can be understood. Regarding the second section, which expands upon the preceding karma, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Not feeling shame for one's faults and evils obstructs *hrī* (moral shame), because it causes various unwholesome actions to grow.

The intended meaning is that even when encountering evil matters, one does not feel shame; this refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). It is not the same as the preceding characteristic.
As for the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is precisely that which obstructs *hrī*; this is the specific characteristic. Since...
If there is that which is "□□," then all evil deeds will grow and flourish. Because of the absence of shame (*ahrīkya*), it can be known as an unwholesome [root].

Above, there have been two parts: first, a brief exposition of the essence and function; second, an extensive exposition of the essence and function. Although the phrasing differs, these constitute the formal explanation.
Above, there have been two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Altogether, this is the first section of the analysis.
The discussion of *āhrīkya* (lack of shame) is concluded.

From here below is the second section, which analyzes *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread of blame). This is divided into two parts. First is the heading; it may be understood that the commentary states, "Lack of dread of blame" refers to this very point.

In the second section, the formal explanation, there are three parts: first, a brief explanation of the essence and function; second, an extensive and reiterated explanation of the essence and function;
third, the explanations of two masters. Regarding the first, the brief discernment of the essence and function:

first, as for the definition of its essence, the commentary states, "It does not regard those who are esteemed by the world as being of a violent and evil nature. The explanation says: "The world" refers to other phenomena that serve as conditions.
Because one possesses this lack of shame, one does not heed the reproaches of people in the world, nor does one heed their punishments and executions;
thus, one honors and values those who are violent and evil, and consequently honors and values evil dharmas.
"Violent speech" refers to those who are impetuous and reckless. "Evil" refers to a single unwholesome dharma;
because one does not heed the world's censure and loathing, one thus honors and esteems evil dharmas. This is the essential nature of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*).
Regarding the analysis of functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there are two types: first, specific functional activity; second, general functional activity.
As for specific functional activity, the Commentary states that it is the functional activity capable of obstructing shame (*hrī*).

That is to say, only the absence of shame (*āhrīkya*) alone is capable of obstructing shame, while other factors cannot [obstruct it] independently; therefore, it is called "specific functional activity. As for general functional activity:
The *Śāstra* states: "It causes the growth of unwholesome conduct. This is because shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) is also capable of causing the growth of unwholesome conduct;
since they coexist, it is called its pervasive karmic function. According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) also has five functions:
first, it can obstruct shame (*hrī*); second, it can obstruct bodhi and nirvāṇa; third, it harms oneself and others; fourth, [it...]
One proceeds toward the evil realms. Fifth, it increases shamelessness (*anapatrāpya*). In this commentary, the statement that it "can obstruct shame" refers to its first function;
the statement that it "gives rise to and grows unwholesome conduct" refers to its remaining four functions, as should be understood.
Second, regarding the extensive and detailed explanation of the essence and function: first, as for the actual presentation of the essence, the Commentary states:

"That which has no regard for the world, and honors and values the violent and evil. The intent is this: because it disregards neither the world’s reproach and aversion nor the world’s punishments and executions, one proceeds to commit various unwholesome deeds; thus, it honors and values those who constantly practice unwholesomeness.

This can be understood. Next, regarding the re-examination of its function, the Commentary states: "Not feeling shame for one's transgressions and offenses obstructs *hrī* (moral dread), because it causes various unwholesome actions to grow.
The intended meaning is that even when committing various [unwholesome deeds], one does not feel ashamed; this lack of shame for one's transgressions and offenses [is what obstructs *hrī*].

This is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). As for the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), shamelessness (*anapatrāpya*) and lack of remorse (*anottappa*) are the specific characteristics.
Since there is lack of remorse, from this all various evil deeds are fully produced. The above is the second section, the extensive explanation of the essence and function.
The third section below, concerning the explanations of the two masters, also serves to reconcile textual contradictions. First, the ancient master asks:

"Is this lack of shame regarding one's faults and evils a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect), or is it a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)? The second master answers:

The commentary (*vṛtti*) states that "not feeling shame for one’s faults and evils" is a general characteristic of both. The intended meaning is that this lack of shame regarding one’s faults and evils is...
This is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), because they are co-present. An ancient master said:

"If these are the general characteristics, how is it that various sacred teachings (*āgama*) speak of 'not feeling shame for one's faults and evils' as the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of lack of shame and lack of dread?
This is indeed the text of the *Abhidharma*.

The second teacher’s section below consists of three parts: first, the reconciliation of the teachings; second, the critique of the ancient masters; and third, the characteristics of understanding and practice.

Regarding the first, the reconciliation of the teachings: you ancient masters state that within the various holy scriptures, it is said that one should not feel shame regarding one's faults and evils.
Regarding these two distinct characteristics (*bipakṣa*), the Commentary states: "Because they are understood through convergence, the various sages provisionally designate them as the essence.

The meaning is that, based on shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), both involve a lack of remorse for faults and evils; thus, they are provisionally named as distinct characteristics.

In reality, however, they are universal characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Why? Because it is precisely through shamelessness that one disregards and rejects the noble Dharma and the virtuous and good, which constitutes the distinct characteristic.

Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaḥaṇa*): lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) consists in not regarding oneself; lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) consists in not regarding the world. These are their respective specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
As for the statement that taking no shame as the specific characteristic [of lack of dread], this is a figurative designation (*prajñapti*) and not a literal one.
Thus, it should be understood that all the holy teachings employ such figurative designations. Second.
Challenging the ancient masters, there are four challenges herein: first, the challenge that there is no distinction in essence; second, the challenge that they do not arise simultaneously;

third, the challenge that they are not substantially existent; and fourth, the challenge that they are not pervasive across all unwholesome states. Regarding the first, the challenge that there is no distinction in essence:

if you claim that shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread-of-blame (*anapatrāpya*) are the distinct characteristics of not being ashamed of one's own faults and not fearing the censure of others respectively, then these two would be identical.
If that which consists in a lack of shame constitutes their essence, then the essence of *ahrī* (lack of self-respect) would be identical to the essence of *anapatrāpya* (lack of decorum).
This is because both are of the same nature—namely, a lack of shame—and thus the essences of these two dharmas would be indistinguishable. The treatise states:

"If one maintains that 'lack of shame' is the distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of these two, then the essences of these two must be indistinguishable; they would be like suffering and pleasure."
The two feelings (*vedanā*) should likewise be of the same nature. Why? Because both painful and pleasant feelings are merely characterized by experiencing (*anubhava*).
Since they are both of the nature of experiencing, would it not follow that the very essence of the feeling of suffering is the feeling of pleasure?

If, however, the two natures of oppression and gratification are distinct characteristics, then the same applies to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Shamelessness and lack of dread are...

There is a phenomenon (*dharma*) that ought to possess its own distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding this subject (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*) is stated: "Because both are characterized by a lack of shame regarding faults and evils.

The concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is like the two sensations of suffering and pleasure; because both [sensations] possess the quality of experiencing (*anubhava*), each of these two sensations has its own distinct entity.
Likewise, because both *hrī* (moral shame) and *apatrāpya* (moral dread) possess a lack of shame, they too—just like the two sensations—each have their own distinct entity.

Each has its own distinct essence. If it were the case that both feelings (*vedanā*) possess the quality of experiencing (*anubhava*), then the Master [Vasubandhu] should have stated that the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) is itself pleasure (*sukha*). If that were so, what difference would there be between suffering and pleasure?

Since both [feelings] possess the quality of experiencing, and experiencing is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of these two feelings, within that [commonality], the feeling of suffering is precisely that which oppresses...
[The opponent] presses: "Pleasurable sensation is precisely that which is agreeable; thus, the two sensations are each distinct in their essential nature.

Now, since both lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) involve not feeling ashamed of faults and evils, it is clear that these too share this common characteristic. As for the second objection regarding their non-simultaneous arising:
It is also like the two feelings of suffering and pleasure. Since both feelings consist of experiencing [an object], the feeling of suffering and the feeling of pleasure do not arise simultaneously.
When there is a feeling of suffering, there is certainly no feeling of pleasure, because suffering and pleasure are mutually contradictory.

Now, since non-ashamedness (*āhrīkya*) and non-conscientiousness (*anapatrāpya*) are identical in their lack of shame regarding faults and evils, they likewise should not arise together; for they are identical in this regard.

Because they have the characteristic of shame (*hrī*). If it were the case that lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) arose simultaneously, it would be clearly understood that these two dharmas possess distinct intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and that "not feeling shame" and so forth do not constitute their respective distinct characteristics. An ancient master offers this defense:

"Although I take 'not feeling shame' as the basis for the two, their distinct characteristics nonetheless arise simultaneously; this is because their objects of focus (*ālambana*) are different. Thus, while they arise together, they are [distinguished by] lack of dread.
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): the power of the world and the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) are directed toward others.
Thus, because the objects of the self and others differ, they may also arise simultaneously. For this reason, there is no difficulty regarding their actual existence.
If you, the ancient masters, say that because the objects are different, the power of the lack of shame is distinct from the power of the world, [it is because] there is a difference between them.

It is taught that they arise simultaneously, and it is taught that there is no sense of shame (*anapatrāpya*). Regarding the power of the world and the power of self and dharma as their respective objects, the objects are also distinct.

As for why they arise simultaneously, it is because they exist in mutual dependence. Since they are established through the distinction between self and other, the entities of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) would then be devoid of reality, just like [the concepts of] long and short. The measure [of the teaching] states that shamelessness and lack of dread do indeed exist.

[The opponent states: "Dharmas must not be definitively existent; this is our thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because they are established through mutual dependence. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like length and shortness, which is easily understood.

The ancient master further defends [the position], saying: "I do not say they exist through mutual dependence; rather, they arise sequentially, and thus they may still be substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Because of this, there arises a fourth faulty objection regarding lack of pervasion (*avyāptidoṣa*): "If you, the ancient master, say that they arise sequentially, then..."
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) do not pervade all unwholesome minds, because there are times when one lacks shame but possesses no dread;

thus, they do not mutually pervade one another. Why, then, are they called "middling" and "pervasive" among the unwholesome? The four objections above constitute the second set of objections from the ancient masters.
Below this follows the third [section], the explanation of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, the ancient masters say: "If one says that one does not feel shame..."
Regarding the statement that "transgression is always a universal characteristic," one wonders what its specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is. The Master of the Treatise replies:
"As for the specific characteristic, it is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); it consists of not regarding one's own qualities and of slighting and rejecting the virtuous.
As for lack of embarrassment (*anapatrāpya*), it consists of not regarding the world and of honoring the violent and evil; this is its specific characteristic. If that is so, then...

It is not that [the mind] is not pervasive regarding evil. If a wholesome object arises, one immediately gives rise to [wholesome thoughts], and thus simultaneously and lightly rejects [the unwholesome].
If no evil object arises, how could there still be a lack of reverence and respect? The answer says:

The commentary states that "at the time of an unwholesome mind, regardless of whatever object arises, there is no fault of [the wholesome mind] failing to arise. The meaning is simply that as long as there is even a single wholesome [thought], [it prevents the unwholesome from arising].
When the conditions arise, all give rise to the attainment of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread-of-blame (*anapatrāpya*).

If, regarding the power of oneself and the Dharma, one treats the virtuous and good with contempt and rejection, there will invariably be the principle of honoring and respecting the violent and evil. If one disregards the world and honors the violent and evil, there is already the principle of slighting and rejecting the virtuous and good.
Thus, the very moment one honors the violent and evil is precisely [the moment of moral transgression].
To lightly reject what is wholesome means that at the time when one is virtuous and good, there is no basis for honoring or respecting the violent and evil.
It is not necessary to wait for both conditions to be present; rather, as soon as even a single object arises, shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) arise accordingly.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, these two types [of mental factors] merely pervade the unwholesome mind; they do not depend on specific objects."

There is no distinct arising of difference. Question: Within the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaḍ-vyākhyāna*), how are these two factors, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), subsumed?
Answer: The commentary states that these two aforementioned [factors] are both "concomitant" (*anuśaya*) and do not possess the six types of analysis;

this may be understood. Above, there are two parts: first, the individual analysis of the "concomitants"; second, the reconciliation of the explanations of the two masters, whose textual versions differ. In total—
This concludes the second section, the analysis of the two *anuvyañjanas*.

From here below begins the third section, the analysis of the *mahābhūmikas*. The commentary states that they are divided into eight as per the text; however, the latter seven have not yet been reached.
Furthermore, the thirteenth section, which analyzes lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, the heading:
it may be understood that the *Śāstra* states, "Thirteen: lack of faith... Second, within the formal explanation, there are three sections:

first, a brief analysis of its essence and function; second, two [sections] that explain the preceding text; third, from "the three characteristics of lack of faith" onwards, it concerns defilement (*saṃkleśa*).

This is the opposite of the pure characteristics (*śubha-nimitta*). There are three [aspects] that differ. First, regarding the brief discernment of its essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*): first, to correctly set forth its essence, the commentary states:
"Its nature consists of the mind’s impurity regarding reality, virtues, and capabilities, characterized by a lack of faith, lack of endurance, and lack of desire.
To explain: "Reality, virtues, and capabilities" refers to the objects of non-faith; "lack of endurance and lack of desire" refers to the causes of non-faith.
That is to say, regarding actual virtues, it is the inability to endure, the lack of delight, and the absence of desire.
As for its nature being "mental defilement" (*citta-mala*), this refers to its essential character. It is the opposite of faith, which has as its nature deep endurance, delight, and desire;

thus, mental defilement has as its nature the inability to endure, lack of delight, and lack of desire. Next, to distinguish its functional activity, the commentary states: "It is able to obstruct purity and follows its basis."
Regarding "acting as a cause" (*kāraṇa*): the commentary explains that when non-faith arises, it directly opposes faith and thus prevents faith from arising.
Regarding "acting as a basis" (*āśraya*): this means that this very non-faith serves as the basis for [the subsequent state].
This is because there is indolence (*kausīdya*). That is to say, it is laziness (*ālasya*) rather than diligence (*vīrya*). Because non-faith (*āśraddhya*) serves as its basis, one becomes indolent.
It acts as the foundation for indolence; this is the functional activity of non-faith. According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun), non-faith also has five aspects.
[The first] is that which can obstruct pure faith (*śraddhā*); the second is that which can obstruct...
[It leads to] neither enlightenment nor nirvana; third, it harms oneself and others; fourth, it leads to evil destinies;
fifth, it increases the lack of faith in others. This is a brief analysis of its essence and function. Regarding the second point, which explains the preceding text, the commentary (*śūtra*) states:
"Because those who lack faith are mostly indolent. The meaning is that if one lacks faith, there will be indolence, as [lack of faith] serves as the basis for indolence.

Because of this basis, since indolence is itself a falling away into [evil], if one does not believe in the Buddha-dharma, one will then perform evil deeds and give rise to various unwholesome states and indolence;
therefore it is said that "indolence is much. Thus it should be known. Regarding the third point, the mutual inversion of the defiled and the pure:
as for the statement that the three aspects of non-belief are inverted to become belief, the intended meaning is that the three aspects of non-belief...
